en: The three bodies (trikāya) abide within the center of the body in the form of wheels (cakra);
the thorough knowledge of the three bodies is known as the wheel of great bliss.
This great gnosis (mahājñāna), residing within the body, is free from all conceptual constructions.
Pervading all things, though residing in the body, it is not born of the body;
sentient beings are indeed Buddhas, yet they are merely veiled by adventitious defilements.
Through the removal of those [defilements], sentient beings are undoubtedly Buddhas.

The Hevajra Tantra: The First King of Rituals. The First Chapter on the Family of Hevajra. Oṃ, homage to the glorious Hevajra! Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the bhagas of the Vajra Ladies, which are the heart of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas. (1)

The *Muktāvalī*, a Commentary (*Pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the Master Ratnākaraśānti. Oṃ. Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva! May the wild dance of Heruka protect you—he who, with the placement of his feet upon the earth, shatters the mountains; who, with his loud laughter and the sounds of his banner and bell, brings about the destruction and creation of the three worlds; and who employs such terrifying means to subdue the arrogant, while holding within his heart the essence of the Three Secrets of the Jina. (1)

A commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* is being composed—clearly following the sequence of the sūtras, established by the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), lucid, and as heart-pleasing as a string of pearls. (2)
Lack of faith is the root enemy and the sole ground of destruction; indeed, this faith arises from valid cognition, for one does not become omniscient through mere reverence. || 3 ||

He who says that what was done by the Jina was not done, and he who says that what was not spoken by him was spoken— he casts aspersions equally upon both of those who are the supreme authority for the world, the Tathāgata.

In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the first chapter, the *Hevajra-kulapaṭala*]: The Victors have spoken what is beneficial in many ways; people accept it according to their own inclinations. *vimadā* (variant: *visadā*) — *ka*; *agre truṭitaḥ* (broken off) — *ka kha*. END_OF_PDF_PAGE_052
Therefore, here too, this Pañjikā elucidates the meaning for the sake of generating interest. (5)
"Without hearing there is no awakening; without hearing there is no reflection; without the pair [of hearing and reflection] there is no yoga; and with the loss of yoga there is no attainment.
May this "Necklace of Pearls," bound here in the heart, remove for a long time the anguish of those who yearn for it within this Tantra. 6.

The introductory formula beginning with "Thus have I [heard]" is as follows: some maintain that this is merely an abridgment of another tantra, since these two ritual sections (*kalpa*) were extracted from an extensive tantra and thus represent exactly what was recited therein; others, however, hold that the introductory formula uses the word "by me" (*mayā*) for the purpose of declaring that it was extracted by me.
Others maintain that its ultimate, most secret meaning is something entirely different; however, that is incorrect,
because it would be improper to state it at the beginning, since it is intended to be explained only later, and furthermore, because it is not established by the literal words.
Therefore, these [commentators] forcibly construe the meaning about to be explained into a text that has a different purpose, merely for the sake of bewildering the ignorant.

Consequently, even here, this very introductory statement (*nidānavākya*) is uttered, as the Blessed One said: "O monks, my Dharma should be compiled thus: 'Thus have I heard. For this reason, the compiler says: "Thus have I heard," indicating that the Dharma was taught by one who has attained self-enlightenment.

Because it is recited from what was heard from the teacher, the term "heard" (śruta) indicates the communal recitation (saṅgīti); for if it were not heard directly, or if it were heard otherwise, the communal recitation would lack authority due to the possibility of deception.
To exclude these two [possibilities], there are the two words "evam mayā" (thus by me).
Therein, "mayā" means "by me alone" it was heard from the Teacher, and not something that has come down even through a lineage of hearing.
"Evam" means exactly as I shall relate; the sense is: "it was heard by me precisely thus, and not otherwise."
The occasional dwelling of the teacher in a suitable place and the assembly of a suitable retinue constitute the occasion for the teaching; thus it says, "at one time," and so forth.
"Time" (*samaya*) refers to the period.
"The Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) is Vajradhara in the form of Hevajra.
The six qualities, beginning with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), are the *bhagas* when complete,
as it is said in the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: "Sovereignty, complete knowledge, fame, glory, beauty, and the exertion for wealth— the tradition holds that these six are called *bhaga*."
He is called "Bhagavān" because he possesses fortune (*bhaga*);
he "dwelt" (*vijahāra*) means that he dwelt by means of the Buddha-dwellings.

There are four Buddha-dwellings: the dwelling of deportment (*īryāpatha*), the dwelling of teaching (*deśanā*), the dwelling of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and the dwelling of solitary retreat (*pratisaṃlayana*).
For movement and abiding are concentrated,
and the Blessed Buddhas are always concentrated;
therefore, whatever bodily action belongs to the Blessed Buddhas, that is their abiding in the modes of deportment.
Whatever verbal activity they have is their dwelling in teaching;
whatever mental activity they have that is naturally concentrated during meditative absorption and attainment is their dwelling in attainment;
and whatever mental activity they have regarding the dwelling in happiness in the present life and the approaching of deities and others is their dwelling in seclusion.

Where did he dwell? He dwelt within the *bhaga* of the Vajra Consorts of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. This refers to the gathering of the three secrets—body, speech, and mind—of all Tathāgatas;
it is the form of the Blessed One Vajradhara known as the *dharmodayā*, which consists of the perfectly pure *tathatā* (suchness) of those very secrets of the Tathāgatas.

For since it is the synthesis of the three secrets, it is triangular; since it is perfectly pure suchness (*suviśuddhatathatā*), it is white as the autumn moon and hollow within; and since it is purified through the progressively wider sequence of the stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*), it is increasingly expansive. Furthermore, these very [triangles] are the wombs (*bhaga*) of the Vajra Ladies (*vajrayoṣit*), Locanā and the others, because they possess bodies consisting of the uncontaminated bliss of the *dharmadhātu* and *dharmatā*.
Therefore, it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, which are also the wombs of the Vajra Ladies."
"In them" means in the gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) located there;
for example, when one says "he lives in the city today," it means he is in the palace situated within the city.

Having perceived the Blessed One’s dwelling in a place more secret than the most secret, [one thinks]: "Surely the Blessed One will teach here a Dharma more secret than the most secret. Thus, the gathering of a suitable assembly is stated by implication.
Furthermore, that assembly consisted of Bodhisattvas such as Vajragarbha and others, as well as Vajrayoginīs such as Locanā and Gaurī and others. || 1 ||
The traditional teaching (śruti) states that "bhaga" refers to the six qualities: complete sovereignty, beauty, fame, prosperity, knowledge, and the effort for one's welfare.
The traditional definition of *bhaga* is the possession of these six qualities: complete sovereignty, beauty, fame, splendor, knowledge, and the effort toward one's goals.
[The Chapter on the Family of Hevajra: Therein the Blessed One said: “The heart of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, the Lord, the most secret of secrets.

“O Vajragarbha, well done, well done! O Great Compassionate One! Listen to the heart of the Mahābodhisattva—of Vajrasattva, the Mahāsattva, the Samayasattva, and the Jñānasattva—which is called Hevajra. (2)
Regarding the phrase "therein," that is, in that monastery, he says [something]; for what purpose does he say it? For the sake of arousing the eagerness of the audience.
What does he say? "All," and so forth.

They are called *tathāgatas* because they have gone (*gata*) exactly as it should be gone (*yathā gantavyam*); that is, because they have abandoned all obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsana*).
Alternatively, the word *gata* has the sense of "knowledge" (*jñāna*);

they are *tathāgatas* because their knowledge has gone exactly as the phenomena (*dharmas*) are; that is, because they possess the correct knowledge of all objects of knowledge in all their aspects at all times.
Alternatively, there is a metathesis of the letter *da* for the letter *ta*,

such that they are called "Tathāgatas" because they speak exactly as it should be spoken; and since they all correctly teach the Dharma to those to be trained according to their dispositions, lineages, and times, they are both "all" and "Tathāgatas," and their body, speech, and mind are that very Vajradhara.

His heart-essence is the Lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*), the supreme deity; for all the body, speech, and mind of the mantra-deities— who are of the nature of non-conceptual wisdom— are secret, being difficult to believe in, and among those,
the most secret are the "secrets beyond the secret" (*guhyātiguhyāni*),
which are associated with the wrathful ones.
That which is called Hevajra is the body, speech, and mind, supremely fierce and overflowing with passion;
therefore, it is more secret than the secret,
and the sense is that those who will have faith in it are extremely rare to find.
"Thus" means "in this manner.
In this way, three reflections arose among the members of the assembly who were filled with longing:
"If this is a secret more secret than any other, then one must state what kind of person is worthy [to hear] it in this world."

The first reflection is that the established tenet is that there is nothing superior to Vajradhara; [the second is] whether this essence belongs to him alone, or to another known by the names of body, speech, and mind;
and the third is what the name of this Lord (bhaṭṭāraka) is.
Therefore, in order to refute these [objectionable] discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), he says "Aho" and so forth.
Here too, at the end, the word "iti" from the preceding sentence should be understood as recurring; and since the sense of "and" (*ca*) is implied, the meaning is "and thus he said."
The word "iti" is not read even earlier in some manuscripts; for its meaning is understood even without it.
[First: *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: "O Vajragarbha!"—the meaning is that all bodhisattvas are Vajragarbhas, as they belong to the lineage (*gotra*) of the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, the five—delusion, hatred, pride, passion, and envy—are the *kula-tathāgatas*.

Among them, he who belongs to the lineage of hatred is named Vajragarbha; this name is significant according to its etymology (*anvartha*), and this lineage of a bodhisattva is difficult to encounter.

For this very reason, there is an address of wonder: "Aho! Well done, well done, O Greatly Compassionate One, O Great Bodhisattva! He is "Greatly Compassionate" (*mahākṛpa*) because his intention is to accomplish the welfare of others through all means, such as the most fierce [activities].

His awakening, which accomplishes the infinite welfare of the world by those very same means, is "Great Awakening" (*mahābodhi*); he is a "Great Bodhisattva" (*mahābodhisattva*) because his resolve (*sattva*) is directed toward that [awakening].
He whose intention for the welfare of others and his intention for his own welfare are such as this is supreme among the lions of men;
therefore, he enjoins [the listener] to hear the two praises, "Excellent! Excellent! By this much, he indicates that a virtuous person of such lineage and such disposition is capable in this matter.
How is it known that "this person belongs to such-and-such a lineage"?
It is known through signs such as a particular degree of faith and inclination toward its qualities.
And it is said in the *Ārya-Laṅkāvatāra*: "Fire is known by smoke, and water by the crane."
The lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known by its signs.
By this much, the first reflection has been refuted.
To refute the second, he says: "The heart of Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, and Samayasattva. It is true that there is nothing superior to Vajradhara;
however, because the Vajra family is characterized primarily by great compassion, Hevajra is the supreme form of Vajradhara.
Therefore, this is called its "heart" (*hṛdaya*); the sense is that the meaning of "heart" is indeed the essential meaning (*sārārtha*).
By this, the second type of discursive thought (*vitarka*) is refuted.
By the phrase "called Hevajra," the third type of discursive thought is eliminated.

Vajragarbha said: "The Blessed One spoke in the Hevajra Tantra [Chapter 1: The Family of Hevajra]: 'Why would one become Vajrasattva? How would one become Mahāsattva? By what would one become Samayasattva? May the Blessed One explain this to me.'"
That which is indivisible is called "vajra"; by this logic of wisdom, the being who is the oneness of the three realms is known as Vajrasattva.
It was said: what was it that he said?
Three questions.
For what purpose did he speak?
For the sake of explaining the majesty of the Vajradhara, which was indicated by the three preceding quarters [of the verse].
He asked: "What did he say?"—[the reply was: "The three subsequent answers are 'indestructible,' meaning they cannot be broken."
"It is said to be 'vajra'"— because of its similarity to a vajra,
all three existences (bhava) are "existences" (bhava) in the sense that they become all the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma).
Why are the Buddha-qualities alone [the subject] here? Because of their predominance.
Why all [of them]? Because they are complete.
How are there three by way of pervasion and logical principle?
By means of the distinction between body, speech, and mind.
The three realms of existence constitute the "three worlds" (*tribhava*). Their unity is their equality; how is that unity?

It is through the exhaustion of the seeds of all *sāsrava* (defiled) phenomena and the cessation of those consciousnesses that manifest as the foundation, the body, and enjoyments. When the stains of the mind have been cast off, it resembles the surface of a sky of pure bliss; it is characterized by the *ālayavijñāna* [purified], has attained the characteristic of the *anāsrava* (undefiled) realm, possesses the characteristic of potentiality, and serves as the support for the seeds of all Buddha-qualities. Being of the nature of luminosity without appearance and consisting of great bliss, it is the abode of the three worlds as far as space extends—this is the unity of the three worlds.
Why is it called "existence" (*sattva*)?

Because its very state of extreme purity is what is meant here; for the word *sattva*—which denotes the state of being existent (*sataḥ bhāvaḥ sattvam*)—is used in its most excellent sense to refer to this supreme purity, meaning the *dharmakāya*.
For the purity of a person is the liberated body;
the extreme purity is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
It is called the dharma-body because it is the body, the dwelling place, and the support of the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*), since it is the substratum for their seeds.

Furthermore, the primary body of the *dharmakāya* is the *dharmadhātu*, which is without beginning or end, naturally luminous, and remains exactly as it is at all times; thus, it is called *tathatā* (suchness). [It is] Vajrasattva—[the Great Being (*mahāsattva*)]. (Note: The bracketed portion reflects the variant readings provided in the source text: *vajrasattva-ka.cha, vajrasattvaṃ-kha.gha, vajrasattvā-ga*;
and *mahāsattva-ka.cha, sattvā-ga*.)
Samayasattva (ka, cha); Mahāsattva (kha);
"Speak! (ka); "Speaking" (ga);
the Blessed One said (gha); "You" (ja).
In the indestructible [state], the oneness of the *sattva*—ka; the oneness of the three worlds—cha;
joined—ka, kha, gha; joined—ga; the revelation—ga.
Regarding the characteristics—
*ka* being a term for what is praiseworthy—
*ka-kha*: "One who is filled with the essence of great gnosis (*mahājñāna*) is called a *mahāsattva*," according to the *Hevajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*.
Because he is constantly engaged in the commitments (samaya), he is called a "being of commitment" (samayasattva).
By means of this summary of the conduct of awakening, one is called a bodhisattva;
through the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and gnosis (*jñāna*), he is a gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) and a Tathāgata.
For this very reason, he is never divided; because he is indivisible, he is a *vajra*.
The meaning is that [the Buddha] is eternal by virtue of the eternity of his *prakṛti* (intrinsic nature);

only its purification from adventitious stains is differentiated, because it was previously non-existent, because it increases gradually on the stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*), and because it exists in its entirety up to the stage of a Buddha and as far as space. "By this wisdom" means by means of the knowledge that discriminates between the two referents; "by reasoning" means by means of the yoga that is the knowledge of their very co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
"He is both a vajra and a sattva"; by this he is known as Vajrasattva.
The reversal of gender has been stated according to Vedic usage, for such is the speech of the Ṛṣis.
All this is merely conventional designation, or perhaps nothing at all.
"With the essences of great gnosis," and so forth:

"great gnoses" refers to the white dharmas whose intrinsic nature is the Mahāyāna; their "essences" are the tastes or enjoyments. [This occurs] with a body adorned with incomparable primary and secondary marks, within a perfectly pure buddha-field—arrayed with various ornaments of qualities and emitting great rays of light that radiate throughout infinite other world-systems—consisting of the seven most brilliant jewels.

"Enjoyments" (*saṃbhoga*) refers to those things enjoyed in common with noble Bodhisattvas; "full" means being satisfied at every moment together with those very Bodhisattvas, because it never perishes and is thus eternal by virtue of its non-interruption—this is the meaning. It is a stream that holds the jewel of non-interruption.
For instance, in the utterly pure Buddha-fields, the sustenance of sentient beings is provided by the joy and bliss of the great flavor of the Dharma, not by food such as morsels.
What, then, is that which is filled with the flavor of great gnosis?
It is the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body) of the Buddhas; it is called "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*), and thus it is designated as "Great Being."
How so?
He exists, he persists, and he does not perish; thus he is a "being" (*sattva*).
A great being is a "great being" (*mahāsattva*).
The meaning is that it does not perish at all;
"pūrṇā" is *gha*, "pūrṇam" is *cha*;
"mahāsattva iti nirodyate" is *ga*, "mahāsattveti" is *gha*.
*nitya*—ka; *nitye*—kha. *gha*—*samayasattva vidhīyate*—ka; *samayasattvābhidhīyate*—kha. cha. ja.
This verse does not exist in manuscripts ka, kha, ga, and ṭa; it is enclosed in brackets in the reading of manuscript *ca*, and this reading is found in manuscript *gha*.
The *Bodhisattvasamāgama*,
beginning from the very first folio marked "gha" (as indicated by the sequence a, b, c, gha), this white manuscript is now commenced.
—The manuscript here is damaged by a tear: *ka*, *kha*; due to constant fraying—*gha*;
the reading is broken: *ka*; "asraṃsanamaṇidhanaḥ"—*kha*, *gha*;
the reading is broken: *ka*, *kha*.
In the *Kavaḍī-gha Vajra Tantra*, [the first chapter, the *Hevajrakulapaṭala*], from the *Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*, Vajragarbha said: "By what means does Hevajra possess such a compendium of names?
What is signified by the syllable *he*, and what is expressed by *vajra*?"
Regarding "eternal" and so forth, here the word *samaya* should be understood as *mahāsamaya*,
because a single part of a term indicates the whole term.

Just as "Bhīma" or "Bhīmasena" refers to one who moves everywhere through the application of his power, so too the *samaya*— the great *samaya* (*mahāsamaya*)— is that which, according to the disposition [of beings], is the convention of subduing the universe through all possible means and forms.
The "Great Pledge Being" (mahāsamayasattva) is so called because he is a being (*sattva*) due to his constant activity; this is according to etymology (*nairukta*), through the elision of syllables.
For this very reason, it is said: "Because he is constantly engaged in the pledge (*samaya*)."

The meaning is that the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddhas, which has infinite divisions and is eternal by virtue of its continuity, is designated by the term "Great Being of the Great Pledge" (*mahāsamayasattva*). For example: just as a fire set in a vast forest burns in some places, remains burning in others, and goes out in others; so too the emanation body of the Buddhas arises in some Buddha-fields, dwells having arisen in others, and passes into final nirvana in others, yet all world-systems are never at any time left empty by it—this is the meaning of "eternal by virtue of continuity."
Thus, these three bodies are infinite through their divisions; those belonging to each individual Buddha belong to all Buddhas, and all of them belong to a single Vajradhara alone,
for everything of theirs is dependent upon him and consists of him.
Thus, this Blessed One Vajradhara is called Vajrasattva by means of the Dharma-body, Mahāsattva by means of the Enjoyment-body,
and Mahāsamayasattva by means of the Emanation-body.
By this exposition of the majesty of Vajradhara, the majesty of Hevajra is also explained by implication, because Hevajra is his very heart. || 5 ||
Vajragarbha said:

What did he say? For what purpose did he state the other three questions? It was for the sake of explaining that very reason—indicated by the name itself—for why Hevajra is the heart of the Vajradhara, and not merely for the sake of the literal meaning of the words.
"Hevajra" is the complete summary of such names; by what [analysis] would it be [formed]? "By Vajra"—that is, by the word *vajra*. (6)
He said: "Who is there who does not exist like this? [The syllables] *ka*, *na*, *asti*, *kha*, *idṛśa*, *gha*.
The summary: by the author of the *Hevajra*, "gha"—even by the *vajra* thus what?—"ka"; even by the *vajra* thus what?—"kha"; even by the *vajra* thus what?—"ga, cha, ja, jha".
The text is missing here—Ka.Kha; "samayeti"—O, the text is missing here—Ka.Kha;
it does not exist—O.
Because it is constantly active;
the reading "gha" is missing here in the manuscripts ka and kha.
The fire of the rising sign (lagna) is indeed sometimes—
sometimes never.
In terms of their divisions, they are infinite—
all of them indeed being samayasattvas.
The reading is missing— ka kha do not have it—
gha states "by the word Hevajra."

The Blessed One said: "By the syllable *he*, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is expressed, and by *vajra*, wisdom (*prajñā*). Listen as I declare that Tantra which consists of the nature of wisdom and means. (7) The connection is: "it is called 'great compassion'. The intended meaning is that there is an elision of the suffix *mal* and the substitution of *it* for the word *karuṇā* according to etymological rules (*nairukta*).

Great compassion and wisdom, which manifest as supremely fierce physical and vocal actions for the sake of disciplining those who are utterly wicked and violent, are called "vajra"; the meaning is that they are expressed by the word "vajra."
*Prajñā* is preeminent knowledge; the meaning is non-dual knowledge.
However, in this context, emptiness itself is called *prajñā*, because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) of wisdom.

Thus it is said in the glorious *Guhyasamāja*: "How is that called 'vajra'? That which is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is *prajñā*; the characteristic of existence is the means (*upāya*)."

(Secret Assembly Tantra, 18:32) This essence, which is without cavities, characterized by being uncuttable and indivisible, and which is neither burnable nor destructible— emptiness is called the vajra.
Regarding the term "firm" (*dṛḍha*), according to the statement in the *Vajraśekhara*, it means "consisting of wisdom and skillful means" (*prajñopāyātmaka*).

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and skillful means (*upāya*) is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); these two are wisdom and skillful means. That which has these as its essence (*ātman*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is "consisting of wisdom and skillful means."
By this, the analysis "He and Vajra" as "Hevajra" is indicated;
the meaning is that Hevajra is great compassion (mahākaruṇā) which has the emptiness of all phenomena (sarvadharmaśūnyatā) as its object.
"Tantra" means a continuous composition (prabandha).
And that is threefold: the tantra of cause (*hetutantra*), the tantra of result (*phalatantra*), and the tantra of means (*upāyatantra*).
For this very reason, Hevajra is also threefold: causal Hevajra (*hetuhevajra*), resultant Hevajra (*phalahevajra*), and means Hevajra (*upāyahevajra*).
Cause, lineage (*gotra*), and family (*kula*) are synonyms.

In this context, however, it is precisely the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*)—as the vessel for those virtuous ones for whom great compassion and wisdom are predominant—who is called *Hetuhevajra* (Causal Hevajra) and *Hetutantra* (Causal Tantra).
How so? Because Hevajra is the cause.

How is it a continuum (*prabandha*)? Because there are many sentient beings belonging to the Vajra Family, the state of Mahāvajradhara—which is attainable through the power of *Hetuhevajra* and the long-term cultivation of *Upāyahahevajra*—is called *Phalahevajra* (Fruitional Hevajra) and *Phalatantra* (Fruitional Tantra).
How, then, is it Hevajra? He is so called because of the fruit of the vajra.
How is it a continuum (*prabandha*)? Because it consists of the infinite qualities of a Buddha; for that causal and resultant tantra has already been explained previously. || 7 ||

A different reading is seen in the *Hevajra Tantra*: "The wise know the great mudrā of attraction through the gaze, as well as manifold powers such as paralyzing, expelling, immobilizing armies, and malevolent rites. (8)
The cause of the arising and abiding of the yoginīs according to the rule, their capacity, their knowledge and realization, and the emergence of the deities as they arise. || 9 ||
First of all, there is one cause for the arising of Heruka; by means of that very state of being, O Vajragarbha of great compassion, they are liberated. 10.
"Seeing," and so forth, refers to the capacity [to perform] such acts as splitting open the clouds that pour down rain. 12 || 8 ||
Arising according to principle and according to application refers to the forms, signs, and so forth;
abiding refers to the foundational mandala.
The cause is the moon, sun, and so forth;
the capacity is the excellence of recitation and meditative cultivation; the power is the knowledge of astrology and the like, as well as skill in all the activities of a teacher.
"Of the deities" refers to Śrī Heruka with his retinue or to Nairātmyā;
"according to their arising" means their generation according to what is appropriate. || 9 ||
"One" refers to what has been described as the drawing forth by vision (*dṛṣṭyākṛṣṭi*) and so forth;
*Heruka* is the resultant *Hevajra*. His "origination" (*utpatti*) is the attainment of that state, and the meaning is that its cause is the *Upāya-tantra*.
Why is this [the] first? Because the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), which abounds in great means such as the forms of deities and so forth, is more excellent.
In the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, it is stated: "This triple world is mind-only.

For manifestation (*prakāśa*) is the very nature of representation (*vijñapti*). That which does not have this [manifestation] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not manifest, because of the contradiction [between the two].
Therefore, that which manifests—such as blue, yellow, and so forth—is not an object external to consciousness.

First: The Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī states: "No external object exists in the way it is conceptualized by the ignorant;
rather, the mind, stirred by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), proceeds appearing as an object. (Laṅkāvatārasūtra 10.154). Here, *luṭhita* means "afflicted" or "impacted."
Moreover, this blue and so forth is not an external object, because it lacks the nature of being either one or many:
for it is not one, since it appears with distinct parts; nor is it many, since it does not consist of atoms, due to the impossibility of joining atoms together.
For instance: if it has parts, how can it be an atom?

If, on the other hand, it is partless, then atoms joined together would occupy the same location as one another because they are conjoined in their entirety; thus, every aggregate would be a mere atom. Even an elephant, a mountain, the ocean, and the earth [would be so].
And it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*: "Just as a form in a mirror is devoid of both unity and difference..."
And though it is seen, it does not exist there; so too is the nature of things in all entities.
(Laṅkāvatārasūtra 10.709) Therefore, there is no external object of apprehension apart from consciousness;

because that [object] is absent, the state of being an apprehender—which depends upon it—also does not exist for consciousness. Thus, all objects are non-dual, consisting of neither the apprehended nor the apprehender.
Since duality is absent, there exists only the delusion that manifests as duality.
That very error is the imagination of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*).

Or rather, the emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—the state of being devoid—of that imagination of the unreal by means of those two [subject and object] is the representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), which exists eternally.
That very duality is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of things, because it does not exist according to its [apprehended] characteristics.
Unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it is made dependent on others—that is, it is produced by causes and conditions.
The emptiness of duality (*dvayaśūnyatā*) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it exists eternally as such.
And it has been said by the venerable Lord Maitreya: "The imagined, the dependent, and the perfected."
"It is taught [as such] because of the object, because of unreal imagination, and because of the non-existence of duality" (*Madhyāntavibhāga*, *Lakṣaṇapariccheda* 10.6).

In that regard, a bodhisattva should cultivate three concentrations: first, the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), because its objective support is the non-existence of imagined aggregates, bases, and elements; for it is understood that "all entities do not exist by way of the characteristics of the imagined aggregates, bases, and elements."

Suffering and the cause of suffering—the three realms—exist as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), yet they do not exist as the form of duality because they manifest through unreal imagination (*abhūta-parikalpita*). This is the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), because it acts as an obstacle to the aspiration for renewed existence.
The emptiness of duality is the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena, because it is not adventitious.
That itself is suchness (*tathatā*), which is eternally just so. [End of] folio *ka kha* of the *Pāṇḍulipi*.
