That itself is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because it is the foremost of all principles. That itself is the signless (*animitta*), because it manifests when the signs of delusion—the various mental forms (*ākāra*)—have been completely abandoned. That itself is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because it is the objective domain of the supreme supramundane gnosis.

That very [emptiness] is the *dharmadhātu*, because it is the cause of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*) such as the powers (*bala*) and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), since the noble qualities arise for those who take that very [emptiness] as their object.
Furthermore, this emptiness of duality is neither an entity (*bhāva*) nor a non-entity (*abhāva*).
Why is it not an entity?
Because it has the characteristic of the non-existence of duality.
Why is it not non-existence?
Because it is the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
This is the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*), because its object of focus is signlessness.
Furthermore, these three concentrations are the derivative *prajñāpāramitā*, because they are its application.
Therefore, one should investigate in this manner.
This form that appears as blue, yellow, and so forth, is neither an external nor an internal entity, because it lacks the nature of being either one or many, as previously explained.
It is merely that the intellect of the ignorant—overwhelmed by the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless ignorance—appears in that very form despite being non-existent.
Taking that very form as its cause and its objective support (*ālambana*), the world's dualistic conceptualization and the grasping subject of duality proceed, serving as the root of all misfortune.

As long as this appearance manifests, the ultimate reality is not seen, just as those suffering from ophthalmia who perceive hairs, gnats, and the like do not see the emptiness of those hairs and so forth.
Having investigated in this way, he completely abandons all names and all signs.

Then, for one who is established in that non-conceptual, non-manifesting samādhi which takes all phenomena as its object, there arises—by the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) from previous practice, effortlessly and without volitional construction—the vision of the emptiness of all phenomena, which is free from conceptualization and devoid of appearances. This supramundane gnosis (*jñāna*), resembling a sky of pure and solitary bliss, is the ultimate bodhicitta, the primary perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the path that serves as the antidote to all obscurations.

By means of that antidote, through the complete exhaustion of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of all seeds of defiled phenomena residing in the *ālayavijñāna*, and through the cessation of those consciousnesses which manifest as the environment, body, and objects of enjoyment, one abandons the characteristics of that *ālayavijñāna* and assumes the characteristics of the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
That very untainted realm is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas.
The established doctrine is that upon its attainment, the attainment of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* follows as dependent upon it.
In this system, it is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) alone that is cultivated for the sake of Buddhahood.
And that is the correct knowledge of the non-existence of objects differentiated by duality.

Through the ascertainment of the non-existence of duality and the subsiding of the false forms of duality, there arises the manifestation of infinite mere luminosity. Therefore, this cultivation of Heruka with his forms, of the yoginīs, of the mantras, symbols, and the celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*), and so forth, is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), a delusion that leads to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Someone might have the doubt that effort does not bring about liberation; therefore, to dispel that, he says: "They are liberated by means of *bhāva* alone.
*Bhāva* is so called because it brings to fullness (*bhāvayati*), establishes [the mind], and causes one to attain all the qualities of a Buddha—that is, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
By means of that alone are the Great Compassionate Ones liberated.
Therefore, he is addressed as "O Great Compassionate One.
In the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: "Beings are bound by attachment to existence (*bhāva*) and are liberated through the thorough knowledge of it.
The wise one should contemplate existence as existence, and non-existence through thorough knowledge."
In the same way, one should meditate upon Śrī Heruka, while thoroughly understanding non-existence.

For if they were liberated by the single perfection of wisdom alone, they would very quickly realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions, and thereby attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, but not the enlightenment of a Buddha.
However, the Bodhisattvas, who possess great compassion, desire supreme enlightenment—the ultimate means for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings—and not an inferior one.
Therefore, these [Bodhisattvas] are liberated by means of all six perfections, not by a single one.
If, then, they are liberated by the six alone, what is accomplished for them by the five, and what by the sixth? To this he says: "They are bound," and so forth.
Here, by the word *bhāva*, the five perfections (*pāramitā*) are meant, because they are predominant in the act of establishing and bringing [the result] to completion.
Bondage is indeed existence (*bhāva*) because it acts as a stabilizer; thus, there is "bondage by existence.

By means of that, even those who are liberated are bound, for through its power they remain within the three bodies (*kāyatraya*) as long as space exists, in order to perform the welfare of the world in all its aspects without limit.
The thorough knowledge of that existence is the knowledge of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-jñāna*); that is "thorough knowledge thereof."
And that is the perfection of wisdom; by means of it, they are liberated.

Precisely through that, because of the abandonment of all obscurations along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*), there is the complete exhaustion of all defiled phenomena together with their seeds.
Thus, for them, this is called "non-abiding nirvāṇa" (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), because of not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Summarizing, he says: "The entity," and so forth.
"Entity" refers to the wholesome [deeds] consisting of the five perfections.
"To be cultivated" means that it should be produced within the continuum of one's own mind through effort and made into one's very nature by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

"And [he understands] its non-existence through thorough knowledge" means that he understands the non-existence of that entity by means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) through the thorough knowledge of both the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) natures. For one who does not cultivate the entity is liberated [only to] fall into the awakening of a *śrāvaka*, while one who does not thoroughly know it remains in cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); thus, in either case, one would be dull-witted.
But the wise Bodhisattva performs both;
for this very reason, there is the address "O Wise One."
By this much, that which is to be accomplished in the Mahāyāna has been established in brief, because the Mantra system is a compendium of the Mahāyāna.
Demonstrating that very point in the *Hevajra* as well, he says "tadvat" (in the same way), etc.
"Heruka" refers to Heruka, his insignia, his seat, the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), and so forth.

Because the inclusion of the "principal" implies the inclusion of its "retinue," as it is said in the *Vajra Tantra*, in the first chapter on the Family of Hevajra: "The great gnosis residing within the body is free from all conceptual constructions;
it pervades all things, and though it resides in the body, it is not born of the body."
"Who is this who goes? The King.

This is the meaning: the sovereign of the mandala is the single-flavored perfect awakening (*samyagbodha*) of all those wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharmāḥ*) that are cultivated in the Mahāyāna; having differentiated that very perfect awakening as the mandala, the performance of the welfare of the world by means of those [qualities] is the radiation of the mandala.
These three [meditations] are to be cultivated here for the sake of swiftly attaining the three bodies;
the remaining [virtues], however, are for the sake of the swift and easy accomplishment of this very cultivation.
And all of this is to be thoroughly understood as being mind-only and as non-existent in accordance with how it appears.
Thus, one method-based system (upāyatantra), relying upon the generation stage (utpattikrama), has been explained and established.
Now, in order to explain the second *upāya-tantra* based on the *utpannakrama*, he says: "Residing in the body," and so forth.

It is "Great" (*mahat*) because it is the substratum for the seeds of all the qualities of a Buddha; and it is "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) because its intrinsic nature is luminosity—thus, it is "Great Knowledge" (*mahājñāna*).

"Residing in the body" means it is the presiding principle of the body, because sensations—which are the fruits of that [body's] karma—are experienced as inseparable from the body, and because the sense faculties, which are the supports of sensation, function as inseparable from the body.
Although that gnosis is established within this body, it is nevertheless the great gnosis.
For instance, its true nature (*dharmatā*), which is suchness (*tathatā*), is itself the lineage (*gotra*) of the Buddhas;
and that which is the Buddha-lineage is the lineage of all the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*).
And by virtue of that body of reality (*dharmatā-śarīra*), that gnosis is naturally pure; consequently, it is free from all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*).

This is because all stains of conceptualization—which manifest as the appearance of a foundation, a body, objects of enjoyment, and so forth—are adventitious (*āgantuka*) therein, since they do not consist of its very nature, just as clouds, darkness, frost, and other impurities are adventitious in the sky.
For this very reason, the *dharmakāya* is said to be eternal by virtue of the eternity of its intrinsic nature.
Just as the *dharmadhātu* of the Buddhas is without beginning or end, so too is the purity of the Tathāgata, as well as his state as the vessel for the seeds of all Buddha-qualities.
"Hevajra" is the subject under discussion;
that very Great Wisdom (*mahājñāna*) is Hevajra.
"It is pervasive of all things" because all things appear within my consciousness; thus, although it resides in the body, it is not born of the body.
Why is it not born of the body?
Because there is no body external to consciousness, and even the body in the form of consciousness is unreal; and that which is non-existent cannot function as a producer.
The implicit meaning is this:

although he is all-pervasive, he is not composed of all things, because all things are subsumed within the two [categories] and thus do not exist, and because their respective appearances are likewise unreal; yet, due to the vastness of his activity, the Buddha is designated as "all-pervasive."

And because of its very inexhaustibility, it is called "eternal. In the *Hevajrapañjikā-muktāvalī*, it is said: "In reality, the cognitions that appear as the body and so forth are themselves the entities of the body and so forth; this relationship of cause and effect between them is well-known in the world and in the treatises.

And it is stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*: 'The cessation of causes and conditions is the establishment of the mind-only as the [ultimate] cause. Non-arising was also stated by the venerable Nāgārjuna: 'The negation...'"
I speak.
No phenomenon whatsoever arises, nor does anything whatsoever cease;
it is only conditions that arise and cease.

Mind-only, representation-only, and phenomena— these are merely representations; external objects do not exist, for they are simply conditions, being nothing other than the representations of the forms of objects.
If it is argued that, according to the view of the venerable Nāgārjuna, cognition is nothing other than the form of cognition itself?
No; for they say: "The great elements and so forth, which are said to be contained within consciousness, vanish when that consciousness is known; indeed, they are falsely conceptualized."

The meaning of this is as follows: "Whatever is taught in the treatises as the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) is subsumed within *vijñāna*—that is, it is included within worldly cognition—because it is only consciousness itself that appears in the form of the primary elements, their derivatives, and so forth. That [world of] great elements and so on "goes to its disappearance" within *jñāna*, meaning it sets or vanishes in supramundane cognition. Indeed, it is false, because those great elements and so forth are merely imagined by deluded consciousness and are not its own inherent nature; therefore, they set within non-deluded cognition."

Therefore, the concordant tenet of both the Mādhyamikas and the Yogācāras is superior: that not everything exists as duality or in the form of dual aspects, and yet not everything is non-existent as mere manifestation without duality.
The other three Madhyamaka positions and the four Yogācāra positions have been refuted by those expert in the treatises on valid cognition and scripture.
Furthermore, how is such great gnosis (mahājñāna) Hevajra?
Because its intrinsic nature is that of great wisdom and great compassion.
Why is that?

Because he is by his very nature a vessel for all the qualities of a Buddha and the qualities of a Bodhisattva—which consist in accomplishing the welfare of the entire world in every aspect without limit—and whose intrinsic nature is to be attained through cultivation;
if this were so, it would be merely a causal tantra (*hetutantra*).
In that regard, how is it the "Method Tantra" (*upāyatantra*)?
This is true:

because He abides as the substratum of the body, because He is all-pervasive, because He is mere luminosity, because He is mere non-manifestation, and because He is great bliss—in all the *Vajra Tantras* [the *Hevajrakulapaṭala*], Vajragarbha said: "O Blessed One!"
"What are the channels in the Vajra-body?
The Blessed One replied: "There are thirty-two channels; these thirty-two carry the bodhicitta and flow into the place of great bliss."
Among them, three channels are primary:
lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī.

The continuous flow of mental attention (*manasikāra-prabandha*), by virtue of being a vessel for the qualities of the Buddha and by virtue of encompassing the entirety of the Mahāyāna, is empowered by all the Tathāgatas; that alone is the primary *upāya-tantra*.
Furthermore, because the mental attention and the object of mental attention appear as non-different, that very [mental attention] is also called the *upāya-tantra*.
Moreover, for the sake of cultivating that great gnosis (*mahājñāna*), the mudrā is also empowered by all the Buddhas.

For example: [the practice may consist of] a subtle, complete *hūṃ* syllable, or one devoid of vowels and the measure of the moon, or merely the *bindu*, as subtle as a mustard seed or even more extremely subtle; or, according to the division of the four wheels, the four syllables together with their retinues.
If it is argued that this pertains to the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) and not the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*) in the context of the mudrā, this is not so.
For the term "generation stage" (*utpattikrama*) used here is technical (*paribhāṣika*), not worldly;
it refers to the deity's body produced from the transformation of mantras, symbols, and so forth, and not to the mantra alone.
Thus, according to the position of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), Hevajra is precisely that aforementioned great gnosis (*mahājñāna*).
The adamantine body (*vajradeha*) of yogins is their very own body presided over by that [wisdom];
that itself is their mandala of the support.
It is understood that the mandala to be placed consists of the channels (nāḍīs) themselves, which have the nature of the fifteen yoginīs;
however, this is not yet known: are there only fifteen channels, or are there thirty-two? Therefore, he asks, "O Bhagavān," and so forth, [stating] "thirty-two channels," and not merely fifteen.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Thirty-two," and so forth;
because thirty-two bodhicittas carry thirty-two deities, therefore these thirty-two are also vajrayoginīs.
The "place of great bliss" (*mahāsukhasthāna*) refers to the center of the head;
here the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative.

From there they flow and stream forth, just as rivers flow water from mountains, so too do they flow with the *bodhicitta* from the center of the head. First, it is said in the *Vajrapañjikā-muktāvalī*: "If there are thirty-two channels (*nāḍī*), how is their inclusion [accounted for] by the fifteen *yoginīs*?"
Lalanā, Avadhūtī, and Rasanā are the three Nairātmya Yoginīs;
they are indivisible and subtle in form, and two of them are declared by the Victors to be Vajras.
That which is divine and that which is called Vāmā—these two are designated as Gaurī; she is described as Vāmanī, Kūrmajā, and Vāriyoginī.
Bhāvakī and Sekā are declared to be Vajraḍākī;
Doṣāvatī and Mahāviṣṭā are both considered to be Pukkasī.
Mātarā and Śarvarī are proclaimed as Śavarī; and both she who gives cold and she who gives heat are Caṇḍālī.
Pravaṇā and Hṛṣṭavadanā—these two are considered to be Ḍombinīs;
then there are Svarūpiṇī and Sāmānyā, who are the two Gaurīs and gatekeepers.
She who is both the giver of causes and the cause of separation is called Caurī by the sages;
she who is both the beloved and the perfected one is designated as Vetālī.
She who is Pāvakī and she who is remembered as Sumanā are indeed Ghasmarī; Trivṛttā and Kāminī likewise constitute the pair known as Bhūcarī.
The three final ones are Khecarī, Gehekā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā;
thus, there is a complete collection of fifteen Ḍākinīs.

And so he will state in the *Sarvamantramudrāṇapiṇḍārthapaṭala* (the chapter on the summary meaning of all mantras and mudrās): "In the *Akulapaṭala*, the channels that have been described as consisting of thirty-two are considered to be yoginīs, two by two, one by one, in succession;
Lalanā, Rasanā, and Avadhūtī are considered to be the yoginī Nairātmyā."
The bodhicitta becomes the moon consisting of fifteen digits;
its form is the *ālī*, which is great bliss, and the yoginīs are its constituent parts.

(*He Ta . .*) In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the first chapter on the Family of Hevajra], it is stated by implication that just as the first Yoginī, Nairātmyā, consists of three channels (*nāḍī*), so too the final Yoginī, Khecarī, consists of three channels; otherwise, there would be no inclusion of the two channels within the Yoginīs. This is because of the statement, "The carriers of bodhicitta are thirty-two," for in the Yoginī-tantras there are indeed thirty-two divisions of bodhicitta, and their very foundation is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha-cakra*).
Therefore, there are exactly thirty-two channels that individually carry the *bodhicitta* and originate from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Among those flowing from it, the locations where they exercise sovereignty are taught as their respective sites.

However, the distinction of their nature as *yoginīs* varies according to the different tantras and is not uniform across all tantras; furthermore, their mutual interconnection through the movement within each individual channel should be understood by observing their functions in their respective locations.

And it is said in the *Sampuṭa*: "There are two channels (nāḍyau) in the middle of the womb, on the left and the right; one should know that the semen is in the left and the blood is in the right. Thus.
(First Chapter in the sixth [section] of the Sampuṭatantra): It is stated in the *Sampuṭa* and the *Vajraḍāka*:
"Starting from the throat and extending to the left, the channel belonging to the Saṃbhogakāya rests in the center of the navel; though facing downward, it brings about intoxication."

"The channel that rises upward from above the navel and rests in the middle of the throat is proclaimed as the carrier of blood (*rakta*). Intoxication (*mada*) is known as the moon (*candra*), and blood (*rakta*) is remembered as the sun (*sūrya*); indeed, these two, the moon and the sun, are proclaimed to be the two channels. Thus [it is said].

(Third chapter of the sixth [section] in the *Sampuṭatantra*) And it is said in the *Sampuṭa*: "In the center of the heart is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp; situated in its center is a channel (*nāḍī*) whose nature is like oil and fire."
Resembling a plantain flower, it hangs with its face turned downward;
in its center stands a hero, no larger than a mustard seed.
The syllable HŪṂ, which is the unstruck sound (anāhata), the seed of coming and going, flows like snow;
it performs its function while residing within the entire body.
In the *Hevajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: Lalanā exists as the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), while rasanā is established as skillful means (*upāya*);
avadhūtī is in the middle region, free from subject and object.
The short [vowel] is proclaimed to be in the form of the letter *na* at the navel;
the syllable *hūṃ* is situated in the heart with two long measures (*mātrā*);
and in the throat, in the form of the syllable *oṃ*, it is called the protracted (*pluta*) with three measures.
On the forehead is this syllable *Haṃ*, the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) consisting of resonance and the point (*bindu*);
it sports here at ease in the form of Śrī Vajrasattva.
And on the four petals situated in the four directions, there are four elemental channels (bhūtanāḍī) by virtue of their nature as oil and fire. Thus it is said.

(*Sampuṭatantra*, Chapter Six, Second Section): Regarding this triad of tantras, how is there consistency (*ekavākyatā*) in the description of the channels (*nāḍī*)? Since that which is not stated in one place is established from another, the intended meaning here is as follows: *Lalanā* and *Rasanā* [begin] from the throat down to the navel; within this interval, the two channels on the left and right sides are named Moon and Sun. Below the navel, the two channels of the *yoni* are indeed those named *Lalanā* and *Rasanā*.
The channels of the heart are five: Trivṛttā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā. Furthermore, it is recited in the *Sampuṭa*:
"One hundred and twenty [channels] arise from the differentiation of the four wheels;
by way of the nature of bodhicitta, there are thirty-two supreme channels."
(Sampuṭatantra, first [section], second chapter: Even by that, no contradiction is perceived;

for in that [text], those [channels] are not intended to be numbered according to the petals of the lotus, since there is no statement to the effect "according to the number of the petals of the lotus," and because the channels are enumerated within the heart-lotus, where *lalanā* alone carries *Akṣobhya*, while *rasanā* primarily carries blood.
For this very reason, he says: "In their midst," and so forth.
"By way of the nature of wisdom" means that she primarily carries the moon;
"by way of skillful means" means that she possesses the nature of skillful means because she carries the blood.

"Avadhūtī is devoid of subject and object" means that she is called *avadhūtī* because she has shaken off (*avadhūta*) conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and she is devoid of subject and object because she carries only non-dual bodhicitta.

Regarding the phrase "in the Middle Country," the word "is situated" (saṃsthitā) is understood from the *Vajra Tantra* (*Hevajratantra*, Chapter 1 on the Family): "Lalanā is the bearer of Akṣobhya, and Rasanā is the carrier of blood;
Prajñā is known as the bearer of the moon, and she is proclaimed as Avadhūtī."
She is indivisible, subtle in form, divine, Vāmā, and Vāminī;
she is born from Kūrma, Bhāvakī, Sekā, Doṣā, Viṣṭā, and Mātṛ.
Śavarī, Śītadā, Ūṣmā, Lalanā, Avadhūtī, Rasanā, Pravaṇā, Kṛṣṇavarṇā, Surūpiṇī, Sāmānyā, and Hetudāyikā.
What, then, is the Middle Country (madhyadeśa) here?
It is the head, throat, heart, navel, and the center of the womb; these are the three principal channels (nāḍītraya) here, which are the Yoginīs of Selflessness (nairātmyayoginī).
The final three channels, beginning with Gṛhā, are Khecarī.
The remaining thirteen pairs of channels are the Yoginīs beginning with Gaurī;
therein, whichever channel gives birth to, nourishes, or moves toward a particular [deity], it is designated as "flowing toward that" (tadvahā) according to its specific function.

Abhedyā is situated at the head, carrying nails and teeth; Sūkṣmarūpā is at the crest, carrying hair of the head and body; Divyā is at the right ear, carrying skin-dirt; Vāmā is on the spinal column, carrying flesh; Vāmanī is at the left ear, carrying sinews; Kūrmajā is between the eyebrows, carrying the chain of bones; Bhāvakī is at the two eyes, carrying the gall-bladder; Sekā is at the base of the arms, carrying the heart; Doṣā—that is, Doṣāvatī—is at the armpits, carrying the eyes; Viṣṭā—that is, Mahāviṣṭā—is at the breasts, carrying bile; and Mātarā is at the navel, carrying the lungs.

Śarvarī carries the intestinal chain at the tip of the nose; Śītadā carries the lateral fibers in the mouth; Ūṣmā carries the belly at the throat; Lalanā, Avadhūtī, and Rasanā—these three have already been explained—flow downward into the heart as the carriers of feces (viṣṭā); Hṛṣṭā, whose face is joyful, resides in the middle of the perineum (sīmānta) at the penis; Svarūpiṇī, carrying phlegm, is at the glans (mer̤ha); Sāmānyā, carrying pus, is at the anus; and Hetudāyikā, carrying blood, is in the thighs.

Vajrapañjikā, Muktāvalī, Viyogā, Premaṇī, Siddhā, Pāvakī, Sumanā, as well as Vṛttā, Kāminī, Gehā, Caṇḍikā, and Māradārikā. Vajragarbha said: "The Blessed One spoke: 'O Blessed One, what are these thirty-two channels like? || 1 || 18 ||
All things transformed within the three realms are devoid of subject and object; alternatively, they are conceptualized as the characteristics of existence by every means. || 20 ||

*Viyogā* flows with sweat from the calves; *Premāṇī*, carrying fat, is in the toes of the feet; *Siddhā*, carrying tears, is on the tops of the feet; *Pāvakī*, carrying phlegm, is in the big toes; and *Sumanā*, carrying the mucus of children, is in the two knees. In the pericarp and the petals of the heart-lotus, in due order, are *Trivṛttā*, *Kāminī*, *Gehā*, *Caṇḍikā*, and *Māradārikā*. (18)

"O Blessed One, what are these thirty-two channels like? This is the question; and the intention of the questioner is as follows: if the channels were to be meditated upon in a form well-known in the world, then even that meditation would not be merely wholesome, let alone become the path to enlightenment. On the other hand, if they were to be meditated upon in the form of non-dual luminosity, then the yoginī-maṇḍala characterized by the saṃbhogakāya would certainly not be meditated upon at all. (19)
Therefore, he says: "transformed into the three existences" (*tribhavapariṇatā*).

The single-flavored nature of all the qualities of a Buddha is the Dharma-body, which is the "three existences. Since all these channels are transformed into—that is, included within—that [Dharma-body], they are free from subject and object; the meaning is that they consist of non-dual luminosity.
Alternatively, the word *vā* in the phrase *athavā* has the sense of *ca* (and); thus, the meaning is "even though they exist.
The form of the channels (*nāḍī*) is well-known in the world as a characteristic of existence (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*). By that [form], these [channels] are imagined and even sealed by all the Tathāgatas;
by what reality (*tattva*) are they so?

The Buddha-dharmas manifested as the *saṃbhogakāya*, which are the causes for the welfare of the world in all its aspects through every means (*sarvopāya*), constitute "all means. In that sense, whatever is the reality (*tattva*) of the *yoginīs* is indeed the reality of the channels (*nāḍī*). Therefore, it has been established here that the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) itself is the *yoginī-maṇḍala*.
Thus, the Great Gnosis (*mahājñāna*) residing within one's own body is the *vajra*.
The very wheel of channels within one's own body is his maṇḍala of yoginīs. || 20 ||
Prasamanī (ka), Premaṇī (kha, ga, gha), Sumanā (tathā) — (ka); Sumanā (kha), Trivṛttā — (ka); Trivṛttā — (ga).
Caṇḍīkā—what? Kātyāyanīkā; Māradārikā—a; Māradāyikā—b; Kāmācadāyikā—c; there is none—a.
nāḍyaḥ – ka, cha; nāḍya – gha; kīdṛśam – ka; kīdṛśa – gha;
there is no visarga – gha; tribhāvapari0 – ṭa.
All that is grasped and the grasper are conceptualized— what [is there]?— what [is there]?; the characteristic of existence— ga.
Carrying the vehicle of the child’s elixir—ka; carrying the child’s elixir—kha;
bestowing immortality—gha;
[this phrase] does not exist—ka, kha.

In the Vajra Tantra, the chapter on the family of Hevajra and the classification of the vows are explained: "Āli, Kāli, moon, sun, wisdom, means, dharma, enjoyment, emanation, great bliss—body, speech, and mind—thus by me. (21)
The extremely profound *utpannakrama* has been explained;

now, in order to describe the *utpannakrama* that is not so profound in its many varieties, he says: "The classification of the vows (*saṃvarabheda*), etc. That internal transformation of external phenomena which a yogi perceives or determines is their "vow" (*saṃvara*), because they are restrained by the body, or because they are gathered together in brief. Its "classification" (*bheda*) consists of many types.
Regarding *āli-kāli* as moon and sun, or wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*): *āli* consists of the fifteen vowels, and *kāli* consists of the thirty-four consonants.
However, here, by way of summarizing them, the syllables *va* and *hūṃ*, situated respectively at the navel and the heart, reach the jewel and the crown of the head;

these are *āli* and *kāli*, which are themselves the moon and sun, wisdom and means, having the nature of Nairātmyā and Heruka. These two alone meet at the tip of the *bola*; they are the supreme *samaya-mahāmudrā* of the Hevajra yogins, meaning that there is no [separate] pair of bodies.

The *dharma*, *sambhoga*, and *nirmāṇa* [wheels] refer to the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), the wheel of enjoyment (*sambhogacakra*), and the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*). These are the body, speech, and mind;
thus, these three wheels are, respectively, the secret forms of the mind, speech, and body of all Buddhas.
The thorough knowledge of those very three secrets of the Tathāgatas as having the single flavor of unsurpassed bliss is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
Now, in which locations within the body are these to be seen?
Respectively, in the heart, throat, vulva, and head; for it will be stated in the *Sarvatantramudraṇapiṇḍārthapaṭala*: "The *saṃvara* of the syllable *AṂ* resides in the center of the Yoginī’s body.
Just as it is externally, so too is the internal *saṃvara* fully revealed: the bliss of *bola*, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), the vajra-sphere, and the means (*upāya*)."
By means of this secret union, the external duality is illustrated.
The three bodies (trikāya) are said to exist within the body in the form of wheels (cakras); the thorough knowledge of the three bodies is considered the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukha).
"The Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Emanation-body, as well as Great Bliss—
these three bodies are established in the navel, heart, throat, and head" (Hevajra-tantra). Now, the classification of the vows (*saṃvara*) is explained— Ka, Ka, Tha, Te— Ga.

In the moon and sun of Āli and Kāli, which are wisdom and means, [are] the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies, speech, and mind—*ka*, *ālikāliścandra*—*ga*. "Mahāsukha" does not exist in the readings of *ka*, *ga*, and *gha*.
"Māyā"—*ka*, *gha*; "māyā"—*ṅa*.
In that regard, among these, *ka*...
The external restraint— O [deities], those who uphold it— Kali and Nairātmyā-Heruka— Gha.
And the emanation wheel is Kha, body, speech, and mind—
Gha is the secret of body, speech, and mind— Ka.

"With the single flavor of bliss" (sukhaikarasena) refers to the fourth [wheel], the Great Bliss Wheel (mahāsukhacakra). They will say: "The protection (saṃvara) of the syllables KA, KHA, and A. Regarding "KA, KHA, A": this is the reading in the root text: "Hevajra Pañcamudrā Vajrapañjara Hevajra Pañcayoginī Māyājāla; that which was revealed by them."
The first reading in the root text is "the wheel of the three bodies, four [mudrās], and five wisdoms.
In the *Hevajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: by the syllable *E* is the goddess Locanā; by the syllable *Vaṃ*, Māmakī is remembered.
By the syllable *ma* she is Pāṇḍurā, and by the syllable *yā* she is known as Tāraṇī. || 22 ||
In the nirmāṇacakra there is a lotus of sixty-four petals;
in the dharmacakra, one of eight petals;
and in the saṃbhogacakra, one of sixteen petals.
In the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), there are thirty-two petals; this is their arrangement according to the sequence of the number of wheels. || 23 ||
And here, immediately after the phrase "the three bodies," the term "together with their thorough cognitions" (*saparijñānā*) is to be supplied.

Then, as to what the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these wheels is, he says: "Thus by me"—meaning that the wheels of emanation (*nirmāṇa*), dharma, enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), and great bliss (*mahāsukha*) have, respectively, the intrinsic nature of "thus by me" (*evam mayā*); that is to say, they have the intrinsic nature of the four goddesses beginning with Locanā. || 21 ||
For this very reason, he says: "By the syllable *eka*, etc. (22).
He asks, "What are their forms? and replies with the words beginning "nirmāṇa" (emanation), etc.;
here the locative case is used in the sense of the nominative, meaning that the sixty-four-petaled lotus is the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*).
The same applies to what follows.
"Eight" means eight petals; "sixteen" means sixteen petals; "thirty-two" means thirty-two petals.
Now, among these lotuses, which deity should be visualized in the center?
[The deities are] the syllables *A*, *Hūṃ*, *Oṃ* (Praṇava), and *Haṃ*, respectively.
Therein, the lotus of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is downward-facing; the syllable *haṃ* is also situated in its center, facing downward, dripping with the liquid of nectar.

Regarding the phrase "of the wheels" (*cakretyādi*), the sequence of the number of wheels is the "sequence of the number of wheels" (*cakrasaṃkhyākrama*); by means of that, there is an arrangement. Of what?
Of the fourfold sets beginning with the moments (*kṣaṇa*), which are to be explained immediately hereafter.
What is the purpose of mentioning "number"?
It is for the sake of making it known that the arrangement is according to the sequence of counting, and not necessarily by some other order. || 23 ||
— at the syllable *e*, *ka* is *rocanā*; at the syllable *vaṃ*, *ga* is *ka*.
Recalled—ka. gha; in the syllable *ma*—ka; Pāṇḍarā—ka, Pāṇḍulā—kha.
The Goddess: Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, Yā—these are the forms of Kā;
Tāriṇī is Ka. Ṭa, Tāraṇī is Kha; Ca, Cha, Ja, Jha, Bho are [the forms of] Tāraṇī.

[The four mudrās] are remembered—[the reading "karmamudrā, dharmamudrā, mahāmudrā, mahāsamayamudrā" appears as an addition at the beginning in manuscripts *ka*, *gha*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, and *bho*; however, in manuscripts *kha* and *ga*, the initial reading is "the sixty-four-petaled lotus of the nirmāṇacakra"]. *ka*, *gha*.
petal—ka. gha; petal—ka. gha; wheel—ṅa
In sequence:
when *ka* has gone below, there is no *ka*— *gha*.
In the Tibetan text, there is no fixed arrangement;
rather, it appears in a different order— (gha).
In the Hevajra Tantra, there are four moments: the variegated (vicitra), the ripening (vipāka), the crushing (vimarda), and the signless (vilakṣaṇa). || 24 ||
There are four limbs: service (sevā), near-service (upasevā), accomplishment (sādhanā), and great accomplishment (mahāsādhanā). || 25 ||
The four noble truths—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. || 26 ||

The four principles (tattvas) are: the principle of the self (ātmatattva), the principle of mantra (mantratattva), the principle of the deity (devatātattva), and the principle of knowledge (jñānatattva). || 27 ||
There are four Ānandas and Nanda as the fifth. || 28 ||
Ānanda, supreme bliss, and the bliss of cessation; the innate [bliss]—these are the four classes: Sthāvarī, Sarvāstivāda, Saṃvidī, and Mahāsaṃghī. || 29 ||
The definition of the moments beginning with Vicitra is found in the third chapter of the second Kalpa.
Regarding the phrase "the four noble truths," this refers to the yogi’s activity directed toward the objects of the four noble truths;

he explains that very point with the words beginning with "suffering" (duḥkha), meaning: the full comprehension of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path. || 26 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "ātmatattva" and so forth:

the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*) is the very nature of the self, which is representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*); the reality of the deity (*devatātattva*) is Hevajra and the others; the reality of the mantra (*mantratattva*) is the syllables such as *A* and so forth; and the reality of gnosis (*jñānatattva*) is the non-conceptual gnosis of unsurpassed bliss. || 27 ||
The characteristics of the four joys are described in the eighth and tenth chapters. || 28 ||
"Schools" (*nikāyāḥ*) refers to the communities of monks (*bhikṣusaṃghāḥ*).

For it will be stated in the fourth chapter of the second *kalpa*: "The [four] divisions are: outflow (*niṣyanda*), maturation (*vipāka*), human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and expansion (*vaipulya*);—[the degrees] mild, medium, intense, and extremely intense;—this is the additional reading. (ga)

In the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*, it is said: "The moon and sun, the *āli* and *kāli*, the sixteen transits (*saṃkrānti*), the sixty-four *daṇḍas*, the thirty-two *nāḍīs*, and the four watches (*prahara*)—thus, all are fourfold. (30)
Sthāvarī is in the nirmāṇacakra because emanation is stable therein; Sarvāstivāda is in the dharmacakra because the Dharma arises from discourse.
Because consciousness exists in the sambhogacakra at the throat, there is sensation;
and because great bliss resides in the mahāsukhacakra at the head, it is called the Mahāsaṃghī. Thus it is said.
He will later state the phrase "all these four" at the end of that section; because its sequence is different, it should be understood immediately after the *Mahāsaṃghī*.
Thus, all these sets of four are to be resolved within the four wheels—this is the conclusion. || 29 ||

Now, because it is formless, consists of mere luminosity, and is the generator of all mantras, one should resolve that the very bodily wind is Vajradhara and Hevajra; with reference to the yoga that characterizes this, he says "Moon and Sun," and so forth.
"Moon and Sun" refers to *Āli* and *Kālī*:
the channel (*nāḍī*) on the left side, extending from the throat down to the navel and facing downward, is the Moon and *Āli*, because it carries the *bodhicitta*.

The channel that rises upward from the navel and extends to the end of the throat on the right side is the Sūrya and Kālī; because it carries blood, the left channel should be made the path of entry there,
while the right channel is the path of exit.

Both nostril apertures are the two gates; there are sixteen transitions (*saṃkrānti*) in those very two nostril apertures, which are the movements occurring every half-hour (*ardhārddhayāmika*). Thus, there are sixteen [transitions] in a day and night, which constitute sixty-four *daṇḍas*; in a day and night, a *daṇḍa* is half a *nāḍī*.
Regarding the thirty-two *nāḍīs*: a quarter of a *prahara* within a single day and night is indeed a *ghaṭī*, and that itself is a *nāḍī*.
Since there are four *praharas*—both by night and by day—there are eight [nāḍīs] in a day and night.
Regarding this, there are these verses:

At night there are four watches (prahara) and so forth; these consist of nāḍīs, ghaṭīs, and pādas of a watch. A daṇḍa is half a ghaṭī, and a breath (śvāsa) is the inhalation and exhalation through the nose by means of the vital air (vāyu).
Six breaths constitute one *prāṇa*; three hundred and fifty breaths, along with a quarter of that [number], constitute the first day and night of the northern and southern solstices respectively.
In the *Hevajratantra*, the *Muktāvalī* commentary on the *Hevajra*: "The staff increases daily until the end of the two solstices;
likewise, from those days and nights, the staff decreases day by day."
The increase and decrease of the transition [of breath] occur through the breaths increased by one-sixteenth [of the total],
and those two [decrease and increase] occur through one-third of a breath and one-twelfth of a breath respectively every day;
in this manner, the movement of the wind in the two channels is to be observed.

And the transition between mandalas is as stated in the Sampuṭa and other sources: "In the southeast, the northwest, the northeast, and likewise the southwest, there is movement upward, sideways, and downward."
In that mandala, movement by the Māhendra wind results in kingship; by the Vāruṇa wind, the acquisition of wealth; by the Āgneya wind, death; and by the Vāyavya wind, the loss of wealth.
Thus [it is said].
(*The first chapter in the sixth [section] of the Sampuṭatantra*)—Much more of this kind could be stated here, but it is not mentioned for fear of excessive length.

However, mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*) must indeed be explained as being sixfold, for the sake of mastering the winds and stabilizing the mind, as it has been said in the Abhidharma: "Counting, following, placing, characterizing, and turning back..."
This mindfulness of breathing is considered to be sixfold.
Thus it is said.

And purification. (In the *Abhidharmakośa*, the summary verse states: *Āna* is inhalation, the air entering; *apāna* is exhalation, the air exiting. Wisdom (*prajñā*) that has these as its object is "mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānasmṛti*). It is called "mindfulness" because mindfulness is the cause [of it].

In this regard, "counting" (*gaṇanā*) means withdrawing the mind from both body and thought, and directing the mind toward the mere inhalation and exhalation, counting one, two, up to ten, and repeating this again and again.

In this practice, there are three faults: counting too fast, if one takes two as one; counting too many, if one takes one as two; and confusion, if one takes an inhalation for an exhalation, or an exhalation for an inhalation.
Counting correctly otherwise, if distraction occurs in the interval, one should count again from the beginning until one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Following" (*anugama*) means that as the breath enters, one follows it effortlessly through the throat, heart, navel, hips, thighs, and calves, down to the feet;
as it exits, one follows it for a span (*vitasti*), two spans, or up to the distance of a fathom (*vyāma*).
The blazing *caṇḍālī* burns the five Tathāgatas at the navel.
And it burns Locanā and the others; when she is burnt, the Moon flows forth. || 31 ||

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Establishment," from the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittaherukavajrakula-paṭala*. Regarding the practice called "Observation": one perceives [the breath] situated from the tip of the nose down to the big toe like a thread through a jewel. One observes whether it is beneficial or harmful, cold or hot. This is not merely wind alone; rather, one discerns these four great elements, the derivative material forms dependent upon them, and the mind and mental factors—thus the five aggregates.

"Turning back" (*vivartanā*) means turning away the cognition that has the wind as its object and establishing it in progressively higher roots of merit, up to the application of the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) and so forth. "Complete purification" (*pariśuddhi*) is the establishment [of the mind] up to the supreme king of the mandala of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth. || 30 ||

Now, having resolved that the *bodhicitta* itself is Hevajra, in order to explain the internal yoga (*adhyātmayoga*) which characterizes its stages such as the cause (*hetu*), and to explain the internal fire-offering (*homam*) of the *bodhicitta*-oblation joined with the *caṇḍālī* residing at the navel or with Hevajra descended from the heart in the form of the drop (*bindu*), seed-syllable (*bīja*), and so forth, he says: "The *Caṇḍālī*" and so on.

The Blessed Lady Nairātmyā, whose form is the first syllable, always resides in the region of the navel; she is called *Caṇḍālī* because of her ferocity (*caṇḍatva*). "Blazing" means that, being of the nature of the fire of passion (*rāgānala*), she burns—that is, she heats.
"The five" refers to Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Amitāyus, and Amoghasiddhi; "of Locanā and the others" refers to Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā.
How does he burn them?

Having drawn them in from the ten directions by means of rays from the seed-syllable in his own heart and having dissolved them into the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), he burns them with the rays of the blazing, arisen Caṇḍālī.

Regarding what is stated in the *Sampuṭa* concerning the burning of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions within the Dharma, Saṃbhoga, and Mahāsukha wheels of the yogin: such burning of the Mahāsukha wheel is not applicable here in this tantra, because of the mention of the burning of the five Tathāgatas and so forth, whereas there is no such mention for the Dharma wheel and the others. As stated in the *Hevajra-kulapaṭala*: "When [the body] is burnt, the moon (bindu) flows as the syllable *haṃ*. Thus, when those [wheels] have been heated and the Caṇḍālī—comprised of Hevajra—has returned to her own place, the Mahāsukha wheel is moistened by those [elements] melted by the heat; the meaning is that the syllable *haṃ* situated therein emits gnosis (*jñāna*). || 31 ||

Regarding the "Vajra Family Chapter" (*vajrakulapaṭala*): Hevajra himself, whose nature is innate great gnosis (*sahajamahājñāna*), is the "Vajra. His "family" (*kula*) is his abode, which is the yogin’s own body; the meditation upon that very [body] is here called the "Vajra Family" because it has the Vajra family as its object of focus (*ālambana*).
The chapter that elucidates this is the "Vajra Family Chapter. This is designated by its primary feature.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Vajra Family Chapter, in the *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti.

The second chapter on mantras. We shall now explain the chapter on mantras. The mantra for the bali offering to all spirits: Oṃ, the letter A is the mouth of all phenomena because they are unarisen from the beginning—Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā. || 1 ||
The seed-syllables of the Tathāgatas: BUṂ AṂ JRĪ KHAṂ HŪṂ. || 2 ||
Power is considered to be of many kinds, including paralyzing, causing flight, immobilizing an army, and malevolent sorcery.

Having stated this, he speaks the second chapter concerning that, titled "The Chapter on Mantras" (*mantrapaṭala*). It is called "mantra" because it protects the world through the contemplation of the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*); its meaning is the *bodhicitta* born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Furthermore, it is called "mantra" because it is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that [reality], such as the syllable *Oṃ* and so forth; the chapter which elucidates that is thus described.

We shall explain—that is, we shall speak of—that mantra for the *sārvabhautika* offering; that is, the offering (*bali*) or gift for worship belonging to all beings (*sarvabhūta*), namely Indra and the others together with their retinues, who are the deities (*devatā*) of this [offering]. To that [mantra].
"Of all phenomena" means of conditioned things, such as the object of worship, the worshiper, and the act of worship.
"The letter *a* is the entrance" means that the letter *a* is the beginning of the knowledge of their true reality (*tattvajñāna*).

Why? He says: "Because they are unproduced from the very beginning. For they have never been produced from the outset; by way of the nature of the grasped and the grasper, they are eternally unproduced.
The knowledge of reality regarding these [phenomena] is that "they are eternally unarisen"; the meaning is that the letter *a* is the beginning of that [knowledge], hence "*āḥ*".

And therefore, *Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ* means the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*) between the body, speech, and mind of those who are to be worshipped and those who worship, and the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas; therein,
[the syllable] *Oṃ* signifies that all this is merely mind (*manomātra*), devoid of objective referents (*arthaśūnya*).
Even for that which is mind-only (*manomātra*), there is the power of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) characterized by the emptiness of forms;

through the transcendence of even that power which defines the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is the vision of the ultimate. This is indicated by the syllable "HŪṂ," because therein there is no conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of the grasper and the grasped within mind-only, because the appearances thereof have set, and because even the verbal expression (*jalpa*) that defines the emptiness of duality has ceased.
The manifestation of all body, speech, and mind has the single flavor of luminosity;
therefore, this body is "hū" and the mind is "ti," thus forming "hūṃ."
The syllable *phaṭ* is for the purpose of causing the downfall of those who conceptualize diversity.
"Of the Tathāgatas" refers to Vairocana, Ratneśa, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Akṣobhya, respectively.
The heart-mantra of Hevajra is: *Oṃ deva picu vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. (3)
All mantra-words: beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, interspersed with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
The mantra for agitating the city: *oṃ a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa svāhā*.
The seed-syllables of the Yoginīs are: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, lṛ, lṝ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ. || 6 ||
"Baṃ" is the mind in the state of mere cognition;
"I" is the mind in the equality of all Buddhas with the Self;
"Āṃ" is the mind for the determination of the purity of the world; "Jrīṃ" is the mind as the Lord.
"By means of emanations, the mind pervades space," thus *kha~*.
Furthermore, "this body (*deha*) and the invocation (*hūti*) and the mind (*manas*)" constitute *hū~*.
As it has been said: "The syllable *HŪṂ* brings about the indivisibility of the three vajras of body, speech, and mind."
He is called *deva* because he sports (*divyati*) by means of his mastery over all things;

he is *picu* because, like cotton (*picu*), he is excellent and soft, sharing the common nature of cotton in that he bestows grace upon all, and he is *vajra* because, like a thunderbolt (*vajra*), he subdues the wicked—thus he is *picuvajra*.
"Mantra-words" refers to Hevajra;
this rule applies to the mantras of Hevajra for the sake of avoiding confusion despite their diversity,
whereas for others, it applies according to what is appropriate.
"Beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*" means that they begin with *oṃ* and end with *svāhā*.

"Interspersed with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*" means that after three *hūṃ*s there is one *phaṭ*, which is the *hūṃ-phaṭ*; by this [formula] they are extensively strung together, because it is inserted before the word *svāhā*.

In that regard, the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning of mantras is for the purpose of praising them, because they arise from the vision of [reality] as being mere mind; the word *svāhā* at the end is for the purpose of honoring them;
and the syllable *hūṃ* is for the purpose of threatening the wicked.
The syllable *phaṭ* is for the purpose of striking down the wicked. // 4 //
