Vajrā, Gaurī, Vārī, Vajraḍākī, Nairātmikā, Bhūcarī, and Khecarī—through their yoga, the practitioner performs [rites] such as immobilization (*stambhana*). This is the second chapter on mantras.
Regarding the phrase "Vajrā" and so forth, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is applied after "Vajra" and the others; its elision (*luk*) is according to Vedic usage.
"Nirātmikā" refers to Nairātmā.
"One should do" means "one should perform."
The chapter that illuminates the mantras is the Mantra-paṭala.
This is the second chapter. [Note:

There is an additional reading—"the mantra is the heart of the bound soul" (paśuhṛdayā mantraḥ)—and another additional reading—"the mantra is the heart of the bound soul" (paśuhṛdayo mantra). Gauri, Kha, Ga, Gha.
Vāriga;
Vajraḍākinī and Ka; Khecarī—Kha and Ga.
One should perform the rites of immobilization and so forth—ka, gha; [the reading] "stambhādīno" is found in gha.
"Kuryāt" (one should do) is found in ga and ja; "kare" (in the hand) is found in cha. This is the second chapter on mantras in the *Hevajra-ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. —ga.

Nairātmā—Gha. The third chapter on the deities. We shall now explain the chapter on the deities: first one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and likewise compassion (*karuṇā*) in the second.
In the third [dhyāna], one should cultivate joy; [in the fourth], equanimity in every respect.
Regarding the phrase "the chapter on the deities" (*devatāpaṭalam*): in the *Hevajra*, the deities are the Vajrayoginīs, and this is their chapter. Why is it "their"?

Because here the yogas of the generation stage of Hevajra are explicitly taught in an increasingly extensive manner, and by those very [teachings], the yogas of the goddesses are also indicated by way of analogy.
In that regard, concerning the first yoga of Hevajra, he says "first," and so forth.
Its status as "first" is relative to [the preceding stages of] compassion and so on.

First of all, having performed the protection of the place and oneself, one should enter the temple, sit upon a comfortable seat, and place the Blessed One’s image on a cloth or similar support before oneself. Having worshipped him and consecrated the *arghya* offering with mantras, one should assume the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), establish mindfulness, perform the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit, and the taking of the three refuges. Then, having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should first cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward all sentient beings—loving-kindness characterized by the bestowal of divine happiness—and cultivate it during the first moment.
In the second moment, one should cultivate compassion toward those very beings, characterized by the removal of all their suffering.
In the third, one should cultivate sympathetic joy toward those same beings, characterized by the establishment for as long as saṃsāra lasts of whatever happiness has been bestowed upon them.

One should cultivate equanimity toward all of them in every respect, in order to exhaust all unwholesome factors such as the afflictions and to bring about the complete accumulation of all wholesome factors pertaining to future lives and the supramundane.
The word "should cultivate" carries over [from the previous context].
(Gha.cha.ja.jha)
The second—ka, kha, ga, cha, ja, jha;
*muditām*—ka, ṭa, he0paṃ0, mu0va0;
*upekṣī*—ka; absent—kha, ga; *upekṣyām*—gha.
There is no *visarga*: Ka, Gha, Cha, Jha. *Hevajre*: Ka, Kha. *Paṭalam*: Ka, Kha.
The house of concentration—Bhoṭa; the offering of water—Ka Kha; the confession of misdeeds—Ka.
Having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)—this reading follows the manuscripts *ka* and *gha*. As for the simile of the "stolen" (*hṛta*), it is according to manuscript *ka*.

Therefore, again in the *Hevajratantra*, [Chapter 3: The Chapter on Deities], the *Muktāvalī* commentary on the *Hevajra-pañjikā* states: "Having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *ra*..."
First is the realization of emptiness, second is the gathering of the seed-syllable, third is the accomplishment of the image, and fourth is the placement of the immutable [syllables]. (2)
In this way, one should cultivate these four immeasurables.
For what purpose?

To support all roots of virtue, beginning with the thought of awakening; to provide no opportunity for malice, violence, and the like; and to protect oneself from suffering, miserable rebirths, Māra, and the Lesser Vehicle.
This preliminary equipment (*parikara*) belongs to the first yoga and is common to all yogas.
The body of the first yoga is the fourfold vajra; he states this with the words beginning "therefore" (*tasmāt*). (1)
"Therefore, once again" means that after that as well, the word "one should meditate" (bhāvayet) continues [from the previous context]. What should one meditate upon?
"Awakening to emptiness," and so forth.

The universe has the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*); its being devoid of duality—the grasped and the grasper—is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Awakening to that is the non-erroneous vision of emptiness; one should cultivate that awakening to emptiness.
How should one cultivate it?

In this, there is nothing whatsoever to be grasped (grāhya) nor anything that grasps (grāhaka), because it cannot withstand analytical investigation. Rather, one should reflect: "Since the duality does not exist, it is merely the deluded mind itself that arises as the appearance of this entire universe to me, like a dream and so forth. Having thus removed the appearance of duality—the cause of delusion—one should perceive that very mind which appears as the universe, resembling pure crystal, consisting of mere luminosity, infinite, and non-dual.
This is the second stage, the "Collection of the Seed" (bījasaṅgraha).

Having withdrawn that very same infinite, non-dual mind of one's own into one's heart, and having visualized it as having become the orb of the rising sun, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable above it—mounted on the sixth vowel (Ū), adorned with the lunar drop (bindu), and garlanded with blazing rays. From that seed-syllable, one should emanate the infinite yoginīs, such as Vajragaurī and others, and then their reabsorption back into that very seed-syllable is the "collection of the seed" (*bījasaṃgraha*); one should contemplate that.
This is the third [stage], the "accomplishment of the image" (*bimbaniṣpatti*).

By means of that seed-syllable, one should meditate upon the manifestation of the image—the manifestation of one’s own body in the form of Hevajra, seated upon a corpse situated on the pericarp of a large lotus, mounted upon a sun disk, and possessing a halo of solar radiance.
"The fourth is the placement of the syllable" means:
then, having visualized a sun disk in one's own heart, one sees the seed-syllable placed upon it.
The meaning is that one should meditate on one's own mind as being perfected in the form of the seed-syllable mounted upon the sun at the heart, which is the nature of the mind of one’s own deity.
And here, the words "the second" and so forth are adverbs modifying the action. || 2 ||
Arising from the seed—kha; accomplishment—ka, ga, gha;
common—gha.
This is indeed one's own mind—ka kha; to be removed—gha;
it does not exist—bhoḥ.
Hūṃ, adorned, O Bhagavatī!
Established in the state of non-duality—ka;
the mind—gha.
In that [space], from the syllable *hūṃ* at the navel, there arises the Viśvavajra;
with that very vajra, one should visualize a rampart and a cage-binding. (3)
First, the wise one should meditate on the corpse as being of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; standing upon it, the yogi should visualize himself as Heruka. (4)
Regarding the second yoga, he says "by means of the letter *ra*" and so forth.
Here, the preliminary preparation (*parikara*) up to the realization of emptiness is as before;
he explains what is additional by means of the two verses beginning with "by means of the letter *ra*."
In that regard, the cultivation of loving-kindness and so forth is the first protection;
the realization of emptiness is the second.
He describes the third protection with the verse beginning with the syllable *repha*.

This is its meaning: having first meditated on a solar mandala with a fire-colored *rephe* (the letter *r*), and having visualized a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) in its center by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should conceive of a rampart through the extreme densification of the subtle vajras radiating from its corners in the four directions. With those [rays] extending upward, one should conceive of a lattice (*pañjara*) rising from the peaks of the rampart; and with those radiating from both [the lattice and the rampart], a boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that with those extending downward, there is a ground made of vajras reaching down to the depths of the netherworld (*ārasātala*).
And by means of the sun and the universal vajra, which have become rays and spread forth in all directions, one should make all that firm. || 3 ||
"First" means prior to the body of the yoga (*yogaśarīra*).

"One should meditate on a corpse" means that one should visualize a dead body within the pericarp of a broad eight-petaled lotus rising from the surface of the ground made of vajras, situated in the midst of the fourfold enclosure.
Why is this the support (*ādhāra*) of the Blessed One? To this he says: "They know it to be of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

For that which is dead is devoid of self (*nirātman*), and selflessness (*nairātmya*) is the *dharmadhātu*; the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) has the *dharmadhātu* as its object, and the Blessed One has the nature of the thought of awakening.
Therefore, the sense is that this is the support of the Blessed One.
"Standing above" means having resolved that one's own self is situated [there].
This is because such a resolution has the nature of the mind of great awakening (*mahābodhicitta*).
Thus is the preparation for yoga.
The body of yoga is the sequence of Sūryavajra; he introduces that very [sequence] with the words "the state of Heruka," etc., [meaning] the state of Heruka of oneself. (4)

In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the third chapter, the Chapter on Deities]: One should visualize the syllable *repha* within one’s own heart, from which arises a solar mandala; and right there, one should likewise visualize the syllable *hūṃ*, whose nature is wisdom and means. (5)

One should meditate upon the reality of the syllable *hūṃ*, which is black in color, most terrible, born of the *vajra*, and situated in the center of the *vajra*-pedestal; one should contemplate that very reality. || 6 ||
Having seen [the seed-syllable] transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, one should visualize it as having the nature of hatred;
[one should meditate on] Vajrajanma as great black, resembling a blue lotus, or indeed, one should contemplate him as having a dark-red luster according to one's desire. (7)
"In one's own heart," and so forth.
"The syllable HŪṂ" means that the syllable HŪṂ has the nature of wisdom and method; this is because its essence is the bodhicitta, which is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion. (5)
"Vajrasambhava" means the arising of the vajra.
"Varaṭaka" refers to the central sphere.
The syllable *HŪṂ* itself is the reality; thus, *HŪṂ* is the reality. (6)
The transformation of the syllable *hūṃ* is its evolution.
"Born from the vajra" refers to Hevajra.
"Having seen, one should meditate" means that having seen him with the first moment of mind, one should cultivate the visualization with subsequent moments.
"Having hatred as his essence" means that he possesses the flavor of artificial anger for the sake of destroying the faults of the wicked;
for this very reason, he is "mahākṛṣṇa," meaning exceedingly black.
"Paṅkaja" refers to the blue lotus (utpala).
"Blue and reddish luster" means having a blue hue with a reddish tint, for the purpose of indicating the passion (*rāga*) of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
"With faith" means according to one's preference.
If one has a preference for blue, one should meditate on blue alone; if [one prefers] blue and red, then one should meditate on that very [color]. (7)
In the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*, having beheld the Lord of Great Compassion, born of the Vajra, in the sky, one should worship him with the eight goddesses who wear all ornaments. (8)
Caurī holds the deer-marked moon; Gaurī is the vessel for the sun;
Vetālī has water in her hand; and Ghasmarī holds medicine.
Pukkasī holds a vajra in her hand, and Śavarī likewise holds nectar;
Caṇḍālī plays the hand-drum (ḍamaru)—by these [goddesses] the Lord is worshipped.
With his neck embraced by Ḍombī, he is impassioned with great passion (mahārāga). The seed-syllable consisting of the moon, the letter *la*, and the sun (*mārtaṇḍa*) should be situated in the center.
They say that he alone is the *sattva*, whose intrinsic nature is supreme bliss.
Regarding the third yoga, he says "In the sky," and so forth.
Just as there was a preliminary arrangement (*parikara*) in the second [yoga], so too in the third;
however, it is more extensive at the beginning. He explains that with three and a half verses beginning with "In the sky."

Having entered the meditation chamber, and having performed worship with flowers and other offerings to the Blessed One—or whether he has performed them or not—he should sit cross-legged and, with a concentrated mind, visualize the Blessed One in the sky and worship him along with the eight goddesses.
The moon is Mṛgalāñchana (the deer-marked),
the sun is Mārtaṇḍa,
and Vairocana is the thunderbolt.
How is it that the essence is honey, and how is it worshipped by the Ḍombī as "Ḍombī"?

Having performed worship of the Blessed One with his neck embraced—that is, with his throat closely clasped—one should perform the entire preparatory equipment for yoga, from the confession of misdeeds up to the visualization of oneself seated upon the corpse, just as in the second yoga. (9–10)
The body of yoga is the fivefold manifest enlightenment; he explains these with the words "the lunar line" (*candrālī*) and so forth.
*Āli* means a row; *āli* is the row beginning with the letter *a*.
*Kāli* is the row beginning with the letter *ka*, which is indeed the same as *āli*. In the *Vajra Tantra*, they flash forth with the luster of one's own body, covering the entire mandala of space.
The yogi should bring the deities of the chapter on deities into his heart through withdrawal; he shall become one whose nature is aversion. || 12 ||
With a complexion of blue and reddish luster, possessing eyes like the red bandhūka flower, he is adorned with the five mudrās. || 13 ||

Having seen within the sun in the heart of the corpse a row of the fifteen vowels beginning with *a*, formed into a circle and garlanded with rays, one should perceive that [row] transformed into the form of the full autumn moon; that row of vowels (*āli*) having become the moon is called the "moon-row" (*candrālī*), which is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Having likewise seen above that a row of the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka*, one should perceive it transformed into the shape of a solar disc; this transformation into Kālī is the Sun (*mārtaṇḍa*).
"Kālimārtaṇḍa" refers to the gnosis of equality;

"the seed-syllable should be situated in the center" means that because it abides in the midst of the sun (mārtaṇḍa), it is central. Produced by the seed-syllable born from the sun, it is the blue vajra; "gone to" or "situated in" that means it resides within its pericarp—this is the meaning.
Such a seed-syllable, in the form of the syllable *HŪṂ*, should become the mind; it should arise.
They call that very thing "sattva," and they call that same seed, thus arisen, Vajrasattva; of what nature is it?

The wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) has the nature of supreme bliss; it arises from the union of the moon and the sun, which are the natures of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), and it possesses a threefold nature of great bliss according to the divisions of the preliminary (*prayoga*), the main (*maula*), and the concluding (*pṛṣṭha*) stages. || 11 ||

"Visphurantīti" means they flash forth from that very seed-syllable in all directions. "Svadehābhāḥ" means they resemble the body of Hevajra; likewise, they are blue in color, possess the flavor of wrath, are condensed into the forms of the fifteen yoginīs, serve as the means for disciplining the entire world, consist of the bodies of all mantra-deities, and cover the mandala of the sky. "By the method of withdrawal, [they are absorbed] into the heart" means that having withdrawn those very bodies of all the deities, one should cause them to enter into that same seed-syllable.
Thus, this own seed-syllable, unified with all mantras, is the knowledge of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
Then that yogin becomes of the nature of hatred; through the transformation of the moon, sun, and vajra seed-syllables, he becomes the form of the Vajra. || 12 ||

The knowledge of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu consists of the colors, forms, attire, tastes, and signs that will be described hereafter. These mudrās are proclaimed as the purity of the five Buddhas: the crown, the earrings, the necklace, the bracelet on the hand, and the girdle.
With a wrathful gaze and clad in tiger skin, he has the appearance of a sixteen-year-old;
in his left [hands] he holds a vajra and a skull-cup, and also a khaṭvāṅga staff on the left. || 15 ||

On the right is the black vajra, consisting of the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*. The realization of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), which is the nature of a specific transformation, occurs through these five cognitions, such as the mirror-like cognition; this is the fivefold realization of enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*).
As he will state in the eighth [chapter]: "The moon possesses mirror-like cognition; equality [is] the seven-times-seven."
The seed-syllable and the emblem of one’s own deity are called "contemplation" (*pratyavekṣaṇa*).

The performance of all [these] as one is "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*), which is the pure nature of phenomena (*śuddhadharmatā*). Thus, the wise one should meditate upon the forms by means of the fivefold methods that have been taught.
It has been stated that he would be of the nature of hatred;
hatred is Hevajra. Of what kind?
The distinction is that he is either blue and reddish in luster or intensely black.
That eye which is red like the *bandhūka* flower is called "red-*bandhūka*-eyed"; one who possesses such eyes, and whose hair and eyelids are tawny (*piṅga*), is described as such.
By "mudras" is meant the ornaments in the form of seals. || 13 ||

Regarding "cakrī" and so forth: by the elision of the nominative suffix *su* after these four [stems], we have "vajrakapālam," meaning a skull-marked by a vajra; the word "dadhānaḥ" (holding) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
"Consisting of utterance" means having the nature of utterance; these three are the yogas of the solitary hero (*ekavīrayoga*).
In the *Vajratantra*, in the third chapter on the deities, it is said: "The Lord sports in the cremation ground, surrounded by the eight yoginīs."
By this reasoning, that it "breathes," it is called a "cremation ground. || 16 ||
With reference to the fourth yoga, he says "in the charnel ground," and so forth.
There are five stages of yoga: calm abiding (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), both together, the practice of both, and the fifth is delight in both;
the seal (*mudrā*) of that delight is play (*krīḍā*), not distraction (*vikṣepa*).
Therefore he says: "They play";
the eight yoginīs, Gaurī and the others, are the retinue just as they are in the third yoga, so too in the fourth.

As for the body of the yoga (*yogaśarīra*), one should visualize eight cremation grounds in the cardinal and intermediate directions within the fourfold enclosure; in their center, one should contemplate the two-layered foundational mandala to be described. In its center, one should meditate upon Śrī Heruka with two arms exactly as the three meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) will be taught for the sixteen-armed form. This is the fourth yoga of the Blessed One surrounded by the eight yoginīs, and not that of the solitary hero (*naikavīra*).
But why does one play in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*)? To this he says: "breathing," and so forth.

In these words, parts of words (*padaikadeśa*) are used [for the whole], just as *Bhīma* stands for *Bhīmasena*, *Aḥ* for *Acyuta*, and *Uḥ* for *Umāpati*. Likewise here, the letter *śa* signifies a corpse (*śava*). Since they dwell (*vasanti*) in this, it is a dwelling (*vasati*). Thus, by the logic that "the dwelling of corpses (*śāṃ vasatiḥ*)" is "breathing" (*śvasati*), through this application of meaning, it is designated as *śmaśāna*; it is called a cremation ground.

And here, by the word "śvasati" (breathing), the meaning of the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) being stated indicates the actual analysis; for the analysis here is as follows: that in which they dwell is "vasanam," meaning an abode;

"śmaśānam" is the abode (*vasanam*) of corpses (*śavānām*). Through a phonetic modification (*varṇavikāra*) according to etymological rules (*nairukta*), there is the substitution of *m* for the final syllable of the first member (*pūrvapada*) and the substitution of *ś* for the syllable *va* in the second member (*uttarapada*).
What is their mode of dwelling there?
It consists of walking, standing, lying down, and sitting, respectively upon headless trunks, hanging corpses, those lying on beds, and those pierced by stakes.
Although the cemetery is so called by way of its "breathing" (śvasati), why does he sport there?
This is the intended meaning: just as sentient beings are selfless (*nirātman*) in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), so they are everywhere;
thus, the cremation ground is the seal (*mudrā*) of the abode of all selfless sentient beings.

Sentient beings are empty of the intrinsic nature of sentient beings, and the abodes of sentient beings are also empty of the intrinsic nature of the abodes of sentient beings—this is the meaning of "cremation ground."

Therefore, upon that very object of focus, the play of the Blessed One—who is of the nature of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) consisting of non-referential great compassion and great wisdom—is appropriate; [thus it is said: "nāsti" (there is not) – *ka*; "krīḍato" (of one playing) – *kha*; "krīḍante" (they play) – *ga*;
"nātha" (O Lord) – *ka*, *gha*; "pariṇataḥ" (transformed) – *kha*.
Sva—ka.ghaṃ;
yukta—kha, yukta gha;
samarthaḥ—ka.
In this [verse],
there is no mention of the distraction of sporting in manuscripts *ka*, *kha*, *gha*,
and *ṅa*. In manuscript *ṅa*, it does not exist.
The letter *sa* is present in both *ka* and *kha*;
the letter *ka* and *kha* are not present in *ka* and *kha*.
The trident resting upon a pair of headless torsos (kabandha);
[the reading] *sattvabhāvena* [is found in] manuscript Gha;
[the reading] *sattvāvāsya* [is found in] manuscript Ka.
In the *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*:

The four-armed [deity] arises from the *hūṃ* syllable, having the color and form previously described, through the purification of the conquest of the four Māras. In the first left arm is a human skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras; in the first right arm is a vajra. He is embraced by Prajñā with his remaining two arms. Prajñā is Vajravārāhī, who possesses the form of the Blessed One.
He has six arms and three faces; the left is red, the right has the luster of the moon, and the first is blue.
He is naked, possessing the colors and form previously described. The six arms represent the purity of the six perfections (pāramitās).
In the first left arm is a trident, in the first right arm a vajra, and in the second left arm a bell.
Thus, first, the four yogas of the two-armed Hevajra have been explained; and just as there are four for the two-armed one,
so too are there four each for the four-armed, six-armed, and sixteen-armed forms, as well as for Nairātmyā.
For each of the remaining fourteen Yoginīs, there are three yogas; since there is no fourth, they constitute sixty-two yogas through their total unification.
In order to state the specific characteristics of four-armed Hevajra, he says "four-armed" and so forth.
From this point onward, the three words "in the object of accomplishment," "whoever," and "he should meditate upon him" are to be supplied as appropriate.

The Blessed One’s complete conquest of the four Māras is itself the reality of purity; by virtue of that purity and that reality, he has four arms, possesses the previously described form and color, and is the manifestation of the syllable *HŪṂ*.
He states the specific characteristics of the six-armed [deity] with the words "six-armed" and so forth.
"The purity of the perfections" means that the reality of the six perfections is intended. "The bell" refers to the vajra-bell. "Abiding in union" (samāpatti) is the ellipsis for "he remains."
Of him who has four arms and has conquered the four Māras—(variant: *caturbhujaṃ caturmāranirjitaṃ*); of the previously described form and color;
*huṃ*-born, whose nature is compassion—(variant: *huṃ-bhavaḥ*).
First, the left skull-bowl (kapālaka) contains the gods and asuras, [represented by] the syllables ca, gha, kha, and ca.
The first [syllable] is filled; the right [hand]— ka kha ga gha—
with the six arms, ga.
liṅgitam—absent in manuscripts ka, kha, and gha; bhaved—cha; bhavād—ja; bhagavan—jha.
Six-armed and three-faced—[variants: *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *cha*, *ja*]; O [Lord], in the left hands—[variant: *ka*; *dakṣiṇe* (in the right)—*gha*].
Caṇḍā-ka.gha:
the first face—ka kha [describes him as] naked—ka. kha. ga. cha. ja. jha; "nagno" (naked)—gha; "nagno"—ṭa.
The form and color as previously described—(ka, kha, ga, cha, ja, jha); the form and color as previously described—(gha);
"six" is absent—(ka, ga, gha); first—(ga).
In the right [hand]—gha;
in the second left arm—gha; thus it is said—ka.
In the case of the identity of all,
that which is to be proven is [the following]: *ka-kha-tryaṃ* (the triad of *ka*, *kha*, and *ya*)— *ka-kha*.
Of the Māras—ka, kha; [in some versions] it does not exist—gha;
four-armed—gha.
In the *Vajratantro*, [the chapter on deities]: "In the second right arm is a curved knife; with the remaining two arms, he is joined with a vajra-chain.
Just as the Blessed One is, so too is Prajñā."
In his right and left hands he holds a skull-cup filled with blood; he stands treading upon a corpse that embodies the three realms of existence.
The third chapter on the deities of the *Hevajra* of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas;
[regarding] the right and left [hands], there is the flaying knife and skull-cup for the Wisdom Consorts who embrace Hevajra.
Some say that for the two-armed [Heruka], Ḍombī is the wisdom (*prajñā*), because he was previously described as being embraced by her;
we, however, maintain that in this tantra, Ḍombī is simply a goddess of worship (*pūjādevī*), whereas Nairātmyā is the Great Queen (*mahāmahiṣī*) even for the two-armed form.

Because she is thus described in the sixteenth chapter on the *utsarga*, and because there is no statement of an exception (*apavāda*) regarding her in the case of the two-armed [form], the Blessed One is "one who stands upon the corpse of the three realms" (*traidhātukamṛtakākrānta*); that is, he is one by whom the corpse of the three realms—meaning the corpse of Nairātmyā, who is the consort of the three realms—is stepped upon. Thus, the Blessed One is so designated.
The third chapter on the deities;
in the second right hand—*kartṛ* (scalpel)—according to manuscripts *ka*, *ga*, and *gha*. *ṭa*.

With the two remaining arms—[holding] a skull-cup (kapāla) [in one and] a *vajramudgara* (thunderbolt mallet) [in the other], joined in union (*samāpanna*)—[she tramples] the corpse of the three realms (*traidhātukamṛtaka*). (Note: Variants indicate: *samāpannā* in ka; *vajramudgara* in kha, ga, gha, cha, ja, jha, and he; *paṃ mu va ca* in ka; *kapālaiḥ* in ga; *kapālā* in gha; *traidhātukamṛtaka* in ṭa.)
Thus ends the third chapter on the deities in the *Śrī Hevajra Tantra*—ka; the third chapter on the deities in the *Hevajra Tantra*—kha;
[the section on] the right and left—gha; ṅa; [the section on] the female consorts of Hevajra—ṅa.
"Because it was not previously prescribed," say others— [the text "ka kha nāsti" and "ka kha yeneti" are absent in manuscripts ka and kha].
The Fourth Chapter: The Empowerment of the Deities. We shall now explain the chapter on the empowerment of the deities.

Having emitted a ray of light from its own seed-syllable in one’s own heart, which takes the form of a black, blazing hook, one draws in the Buddhas residing throughout the three realms; having honored them with the eight Mothers, one causes them to lead [the disciple] forward, saying:
"Oṃ, may all the Tathāgatas empower me!"
He is consecrated by those five Buddhas, who take the form of Heruka and consist of the essence of the five Tathāgatas, with five vases filled with the five nectars.
While he is being consecrated, a rain of flowers falls, the sound of a drum resounds, and a rain of saffron occurs.

The "Chapter on the Empowerment of the Deity" refers to the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*)—the washing away of all obscurations and stains along with their latent tendencies by means of the waters of gnosis—of a deity such as Hevajra who has been produced through any one of the previously mentioned procedures. The chapter that elucidates this begins with the words "from the seed-syllable in one's own heart.

This means that from the seed-syllable located in the heart of oneself, who has been produced in the form of the deity—whether it be situated in a sun disk, or in a sun-disk-vajra, or in a moon disk, or in a moon-symbol, according to what is appropriate—the [deity emerges].
In the case of the Vajra family, for the goddesses, it is "black and radiant," according to what is appropriate.
Having worshipped with the eight Mothers, namely Gaurī and the others, and having worshipped those Buddhas in the place of space, one is exhorted; that is,
an entreaty is made to them.
He says that very thing: "May they consecrate me," and so forth.
"By those who have assumed the form of Heruka" means by those who have taken on the appearance of Heruka;
"while being consecrated" is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative;
"he becomes the Lord of his own family upon the head" means that Akṣobhya arises upon the crown of the head.
The consecration is the culmination of accomplishment;
now, we shall explain the deities—[as stated in] Ka, Kha, Cha, Ja, Jha. [We shall explain them]—Ka, Kha.
From the seed-syllable in one's own heart—*ka*, *ga*; from the seed-syllable in one's own heart—*kha*; from the seed-syllable in [one's] heart—*he*, *paṃ*, *mu*, *va*;
not present—*gha*; rays—*cha*; rays—*ja*, *jha*;
due to black radiance—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*; due to brilliance—*cha*, *ja*, *jha*.
Those situated within the three realms—ka. gha; "situated" ga;
"eight" not present—ka. ga. he paṃ mu va; "is not spoken of" kha.
Let them consecrate—ka, kha;
in the state of Buddhahood—ka, kha; with the forms of Heruka—ka; with the forms of Heruka—he;
*pañcāmṛtaṃ bhāṇḍa*—ka, gha; *pañcāmṛtaṃbhṛtaḥ*—kha, jha; *pañcāmṛtabhūtaṃ*—ga.

One is consecrated as having the nature of the Tathāgata (Tathāgatātmaka). [Then follow: 19. the corpse-seat (śavāsana), 20. the washing (prakṣālana), 21. the deities (devatān), and 20. thus (iti). In the Vajra-tantra, one is worshipped by Rūpavajrā and the others, and vajra-songs are sung by Locanā and the others.
While being consecrated on the crown of the head, one becomes the Lord of one's own family;
by this, Heruka is perfected.
Having meditated upon the visualization of the empowerment during the three junctions of the day, one should arise.
"One should abide in the form of the deity. || 3 ||
The fourth chapter is the Chapter on Consecration.
Therefore, he says "by this" and so forth;
"at the three junctions" means at the three times of daybreak, noon, and sunset.

Regarding "the meditation on empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhānabhāvanā*): having relied upon oneself as Hevajra—accomplished through the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) during the morning twilight, and accomplished instantaneously (*jhaṭiti*) during the midday and evening twilights—one performs that meditation on empowerment, which is the meditation on his consecration (*abhiṣekabhāvanā*). Having done that, one should arise.
Once arisen, what should be done? To this he says: "The deity," and so forth.
The deity is one's own chosen deity; that itself is the form (mūrti). By means of that [form], one should cultivate resolute conviction at every moment. || 2–3 ||
In the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti, the fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Empowerment of the Deities, is concluded.

1. Is worshipped; 2. Vajra-songs; 3. Is sung by Locanā; 4. Being consecrated; 5. Upon the head; 6. Meditation; 7. That which is to be meditated upon, one meditates, or while meditating; 8. Should remain; 9. Thus, in the glorious *Heruka-tantra*, [the chapter on] the deities; 10. The fifth chapter, the Chapter on Attaining Reality (*tattva*). Now, we shall explain the Chapter on Reality.
In its own nature, there is no form nor a seer; no sound nor a hearer; no smell nor a smeller; no taste nor a taster; no touch nor a toucher; and neither mind nor mental factors. || 1 ||

Two applications of the deity have been stated: the concentrated application during the junctions (saṃdhyā) and the non-concentrated application during the intervals between the junctions. Now, the application of reality (tattva-yoga) must be explained, because without these three there is no swifter awakening; therefore, he says "the application of reality," and so forth. The chapter that illuminates reality is the "Chapter on Reality" (Tattvapaṭala).
Form consists of blue, yellow, and so forth; that does not exist, it is not found.

How is it non-existent? It does not exist by way of its own nature—that nature which is imagined by the foolish to be an entity graspable by vision—because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many.

The deluded intellect of the ignorant merely manifests through various unreal forms, just as in a dream and the like; since there is no form when its appearance is absent, there is no seer either. Therefore he says, "and there is no seer"—meaning that there is no seer.
The "seer" refers both to the visual faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*) and to the person (*puruṣa*); neither exists by way of its own intrinsic nature.
The intrinsic nature of these two, which is imagined by the foolish as a grasper of objects, does not exist at all; likewise,
up to and including neither touch nor the toucher— by this much, the ten sense bases, beginning with form and the eye, [are explained].
It has been stated that the person (*pudgala*), in the form of a seer and so forth, does not exist, but it is not the mind (*citta*) that does not exist.

Mind is characterized by consciousness; it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it cognizes. It consists of the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*), from the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element.
These very [six consciousnesses] that have just passed away constitute the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
These seven consciousness-elements are the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
Furthermore, the person who has cognized by means of the six consciousnesses is also called "consciousness" because he cognizes; therefore, he too is designated by the term "mind" (*citta*).
Neither of those two exists, because they possess the characteristic of being a grasper (*grāhaka*), and since there is no object to be grasped (*grāhya*), a grasper is impossible.
We shall explain: 1. the essential nature (*svarūpa*), 2. the seers (*draṣṭāraḥ*), 3. the hearers (*śrotāraḥ*), 4. [and] the nihilist (*nāstika*).
6. fragrance, 7.
taste, 8. touch—[the one] together with what is touched, [the one] nourished, [and] what is touched.
9. [the mind], 10. mental factors, 11. by these three—
12. From this point onward, the *Gha* manuscript is missing. 13–13. [In the *Vajra-tantra*, the fifth chapter on Reality (*tattva*) ends with:
"The knower of yoga should always worship his mother and his sister."
O you who are devoted to reality, [worship] the actress, the washerwoman, the diamond-worker, the outcaste woman, and likewise the brahmin woman, according to the ritual of wisdom and means.
Why should one worship [it], since there is nothing to be grasped?
This reason is established because of the absence of a nature that is either unitary or manifold; for it applies to the ten bases with parts as well as to partless atoms.

Since a coarse appearance is impossible even in a single atom, the reason [adduced] for the production of a form appearing as partless within those substances that constitute the *dharmāyatana* is unestablished; therefore, the *dharmāyatana* does not exist. To this, he says: "nor mental" (*na caittika*). A mental object (*caittika*) is that which is the object of the mind (*citta*), namely the *dharmāyatana*; that too does not exist.

Since non-momentary things have been refuted elsewhere, and since even momentary things cannot be objects of cognition, and because past and future things lack existence while present things lack causality and thus possess the characteristic of being ungraspable,
if the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the person (*pudgala*) do not exist in a dual form, then in what form do they exist?

In their nature as error appearing as duality, they exist substantially because they are dependently originated; however, that which is their true nature—the emptiness of duality, representation-only, and mere luminosity, which is of one uniform taste everywhere—exists for them in the ultimate sense, for that is the ultimate: the object and domain of the supreme supramundane gnosis.
In this regard, it should be thoroughly understood that form (rūpa) does not exist as comprised of duality,
because the very adherence to its existence is the root of all misfortune;
the form of delusion appearing as duality must be abandoned, since all misfortunes are varieties of delusion.

Furthermore, the nature of the emptiness of duality must be directly perceived (*pratyakṣīkartavya*) by them, because that direct perception itself is the nature of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and because it is the antidote to all delusion, and because it gradually accomplishes great bliss, great liberation, and mastery over all the qualities of a Buddha.
That great liberation is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) because it is the supreme fruit; and that correct knowledge is also the ultimate reality, insofar as its object is the supreme reality.
By this much, suchness (*tathatā*)—the reality (*tattva*)—has been explained. || 1 ||
In order to introduce the reality of the family (kulatattva), he says "the mother," and so forth:
"The mother" refers to one who desires one's welfare;
"the sister" refers to one whose affection is steadfast.
Out of affection for the family of sentient beings,
she is skillful as a dancer; and wisdom, devoted to pure deeds, is like a washerwoman.
She is called Vajrī because she delights in meditation;
Caṇḍālī because she has abandoned pride; and Brāhmaṇī because she is patient by nature and fears reproach.
1. Mother – 2. I worship – 3. In yoga.
4. Naṭī – 5. Vajrī – 6. Caṇḍālī.

7. Brāhmaṇī—The Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī should be studied with diligence so that no breach occurs; if it is not kept secret, suffering is caused by beasts of prey, thieves, fire, and terrestrial spirits. || 3 ||
Mudrā: It is said that there are five families; because one is sealed by means of this vajra for the sake of liberation, it is therefore designated as "mudrā. (4)
O Great Compassionate One, they say that the five families—Vajra, Padma, Karma, Tathāgata, and Ratna—are the most excellent. (5)
In the Vajra [family], the ḍombī shall be the mudrā; likewise, in the Padma [family], the nartī; in the Karma [family], she is called the rajakī; and in the Tathāgata [family], the brāhmaṇī. || 6 ||
Caṇḍālinī is to be known as the Jewel; these are determined to be the five mudrās. This is the Tathāgata family, which is thus described in brief. || 7 ||
"Wisdom," and so forth: wisdom (*prajñā*) is any one of the [insights] such as selflessness (*nairātmya*), while the means (*upāya*) is Hevajra.

Through these very forms, accomplished by means of the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), the seeing, embracing, penetration, and investigation of the two bodies constitute the application of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyavidhāna*); with that, one should worship.
Being "one who loves the truth" means being one who is fond of the realization of reality. || 2 ||

"With effort" (*prayatnena*) refers to the exertion for concealment; he explains that very thing as follows: "so that no disclosure (*bheda*) occurs. Disclosure (*bheda*) means exposure (*udbheda*), which is the inference by others through the power of reasoning on their own part, as well as the leaking of secrets (*mantrabheda*). Leaking of secrets (*mantrabheda*) is the telling of one's counsel to another, either by oneself or with the help of an associate, due to intoxication, arrogance, anger, and so forth.
Regarding non-concealment, the invisible fault (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*) such as falling into hell is indeed well known.

He also states the visible faults with the words beginning "in an unprotected [place]," connecting them with the phrase "suffering is inflicted by beasts of prey and so forth. Here, "beasts of prey" (vyāḍa) refers to snakes, tigers, and the like;
"land-dwelling tormentors" (bhūcara-śāsaka) refers to humans, piśācas, and so on. || 3 ||
That by which one is marked, and from which this family is characterized—such as the vajra, lotus, and so forth—is called a *mudrā*. (4.7)
In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the fifth chapter on Reality]: "The glorious one has gone into suchness and likewise returned from it;
by virtue of this wisdom and logic, he is designated as the Tathāgata. (8)
They say that families are of six kinds, but in brief they are fivefold; subsequently, they become threefold through the division of body, speech, and mind. || 9 ||
Of the families consisting of the five elements, which have the nature of the five aggregates—by means of this [knowledge], one is reckoned or counted; thus it is called "kula. || 10 ||
"Having gone to suchness" means that he abides in the *dharmakāya*, which is of a single flavor with perfectly pure suchness;
"the glorious one" means he is the sovereign of all the qualities of a Buddha, and not like the *śrāvakas* and others.

"And having come" means that from that very suchness, he has come forth by way of its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) as the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* in order to accomplish the welfare of the world.
Thus, there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) of the words *tathā* and *āgata*;
the middle letter *t* is elided according to etymological rules (*nairukta*).
In this way, all are indeed *tathāgatas*.
Their five families consist of the mirror-like wisdom and the others. || 8 ||
[Objection: But surely all Buddhas possess the five gnoses; how then can there be a distinction of families (*kula*)?

[Response: Due to the distinction of lineages (*gotra*). For Bodhisattvas, each of the [five]—the mirror-like [wisdom] and so forth—has its own lineage established from beginningless time. However, the lineage of sentient beings is the sixth, consisting of those who are empty of [such] reflection. Therefore it is said: "They say there are six kinds of families."
In brief, however, it is fivefold; yet because of the predominance of the single radiance even of that which exists in many places, it is threefold—this being its threefold nature.

From the statement "by means of the divisions of body, speech, and mind," it is understood that the yoga of reality consists in the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding one's own body, speech, and mind as the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. || 9 ||
Thus, with reference to the five families (*pañcakula*), he says "of the families," and so forth.

"Five" means a pentad (*pañcaka*). That which is the pentad of the elements (*bhūta*) within one's own body is to be regarded as the [five] families. Because of the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the families within the five elements, [one perceives them] as having the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); likewise, because of the conviction regarding the five families even within the five aggregates of oneself.

The meaning is as follows: because that which is uncountable—the multitude of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—is reckoned and counted by means of each individual lineage (*gotra*), they are therefore called the "five families" (*pañcakula*). || 10 ||
Text: *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: There is no meditator, nor is there an object of meditation; there is no mantra, nor is there a deity.
Both mantra and deity abide in a nature free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). (11)
Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amogha, Ratna, and Āroli, as well as Sāttvika, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Sarva—when awakened, these are called the Tattva. || 12 ||
With reference to the two truths, he says: "There is not," and so forth.

"There is no meditator (bhāvaka) and no object of meditation (bhāva)" means that the object of meditation (*bhāva*) is the act of meditating (*bhāvanā*), and the meditator (*bhāvaka*) is the agent; these two should not be perceived as distinct from the object to be meditated upon.

The meaning is that one should cultivate the conviction in reality (*tattvādhimokṣa*) to the effect that "I am not other than the deity and the mantra," and that even the act of meditation is nothing but the very nature of their manifestation, and nothing else.
*Tattva*, *satya*, and *bhūta* are synonyms;
therefore, in the chapter on reality (*tattvapaṭala*), the two truths must be explained.
Therein, this entire detailed exposition is stated with reference to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) as the means for accomplishing the supreme vastness.
Regarding the means for achieving supreme profundity, he speaks with reference to ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), beginning with the words "the mantra" and so forth:
even those two—the deity and the mantra—do not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth; why?
The intended meaning is that they do not exist in the manner in which they appear.
To the question, "In that case, how do those two exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha)? he says: "They abide," and so forth;
"proliferation" (prapañca), "error" (viparyāsa), and "delusion" (bhrānti) are synonymous.
In that regard, because it is not the domain of any delusions, the *dharmadhātu* is non-conceptual (*niṣprapañca*).
Right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) which takes that as its object consists of great bliss; because all signs of delusion have set, it is non-conceptual.

Through that very right knowledge, because the afflictions along with their seeds are exhausted and the representations (*vijñapti*) appearing as the environment, the body, and enjoyments are abandoned, the untainted *dharmadhātu* is non-conceptual.
This triad, resembling pure space, infinite and free from conceptual proliferation, is the meaning of the *dharmakāya*;
that itself is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); by means of that intrinsic nature.
The meaning is that these two are to be directly realized. || 11 ||

For instance: he himself is Vairocana because he is renowned as mere luminosity; he himself is Akṣobhya because he is free from appearance; he himself is Amoghasiddhi because he accomplishes the welfare of the universe; he himself is Ratnasambhava because of his attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha; and he himself is Ārolika because of his perfect discernment of them within himself.
Thus, because he consists of the five wisdoms, he himself is Sāttvika, meaning Vajrasattva.
[Vajra Tantra, Chapter Five: The Chapter on Reality] Brahmā is the Buddha by virtue of being extinguished (nirvṛti); he is called Viṣṇu by virtue of pervading (viṣaṇa).
Śiva is eternally auspicious; as the All, he abides within the Self of all.
Because reality is awakened through the awakening of bliss (rati) by virtue of its being true happiness,
and because it arises within the body, it is therefore called "Devatā" (the Goddess).
One who possesses such fortune (bhaga) is called "Bhagavān" (the Blessed One).

They say there are six kinds of *bhagas*, consisting of all the qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and so forth; or else, he is called *Bhagavān* because of his shattering (*bhañjana*) of the afflictions (*kleśas*) and other [obstacles] known as the Māras. || 15 ||
"Brahmā," and so forth.
He alone is called Brahmā and the others.
To the question "How so? he says: "Brahmā," and so forth.
Precisely because he is of the nature of perfectly pure awakening (*suviviśuddhabodha*), he is the Buddha; that very [Buddha] is the Supreme Brahman, and therefore he alone is Brahmā.
"By way of cessation" (*nirvṛtitaḥ*) means by way of having the nature of liberation (*mokṣa*).
Cessation (*nirvṛti*), Nirvāṇa, liberation (*mokṣa*), the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), and Buddha are synonyms.
"Because of entering" means because of entering through identity.
Where?
Into the supremely profound *dharmakāya*.
The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *viś* (to enter), with the changes of *ṣatva* and *ṇatva*.
"Always auspicious" (*sadā-sukalyāṇa*) means because of being eternally auspicious and supremely auspicious.
"All," and so forth.
Because he abides as the knower within the *dharmadhātu*, which is the self of all, therefore he is "all. (13)
"By way of being true bliss" means by way of being the untainted, stable, and supreme bliss.
"Because of awakening to delight" means because of experiencing that very unsurpassed bliss; for he who does not experience it is as if merely asleep.
That which was indicated as the state of Brahmā and so forth has thus been explained.
With the words "deha" and so forth, he says something else: the meaning is that he himself is the deity because of his arising from the body (*dehasambhava*).
There is elision of the *hal* (consonant) in the first member of the compound and elision of *sambha* in the second member.
By adding the suffix *tal*, which denotes the same meaning as the base, *deva* itself becomes *devatā*.
This indicates that it is easily accessible because it arises within the body. || 14 ||
"Buddha" means "the perfectly awakened one" (saṃbuddha).
Furthermore, those qualities such as sovereignty (aiśvarya) and so forth are "entire" (akhilā), meaning they are complete in their manifestation. [The variants for the last word are:
viśanāda (ka, kha); visnād (ga); not present (gha); viṣanād (ṅa, ca, cha, ja).
Viṣṇu-Rudra is said [to be] "gha.
"Sarvatra" is "ka. From "kalyāṇāt" is "ka," from "saṃkalpanād" is "kha," and from "sukalyāṇām" is "ga."

The Buddha, he [is] Pañcamī-mukha-vajra.
"Bhagavān"—this is *ka*; "Bhagavant"—this is *kha*.
"Ṣaṣṭhī"—this is *kha*.
They say [it is] "aiśvaryādi" (beginning with sovereignty), etc.; "aiśvaryādiguṇākhilāḥ" (all the qualities beginning with sovereignty)—ka, ga; "akhilaiḥ"—ṅa;
"because it shatters through killing" (*māraṇāt bhañjayati*)—ka, "māraṇām"—ga; "māraṇādbhujaḥ"—gha.

From the *Hevajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*:
Because she gives birth to the world, Wisdom (Prajñā) is called the Mother; likewise, she is called the Sister because Wisdom shows the divisions [of reality]. (16)
She is proclaimed as the Washerwoman because she colors all sentient beings, and as the Daughter because she milks out their qualities;
and O Great Compassionate One, Wisdom is called the Dancer because of its flickering nature.
Because the Blessed Lady is intangible, she is therefore proclaimed as the Ḍombī. || 18 ||
Likewise, she is remembered as Rajaki. || 17 ||
They are complete. And so it has been said: "Sovereignty, knowledge, fame, glory, beauty, and the effort for wealth—these six are remembered as *bhaga*."
Thus. (Se0 Ṭī0, pṛ0) In this view, the analysis of the compound should be made as "one who possesses the bhagas.
The ultimate truth has been stated. || 15 ||
Furthermore, he speaks again regarding conventional truth for the sake of quickly accumulating the provisions: "The mother," and so forth.
The summary is this: by words such as "mother" and so on, mere wisdom (*prajñā*) is expressed; it is not necessarily external particulars.
"The world of beings" refers to the noble world (*āryaloka*), because others are devoid of activity.
"Distinction" refers to the diversity of the objects of knowledge. || 16 ||
The enumeration is given by the words "the dyer" and so forth;
the definition is given by the words "because of coloring" and so forth;
"of sentient beings" refers to those who possess consciousness.
"Of the quality" refers to [the quality of] existence and pleasure (*satsukha*).
"Due to its flickering nature" means because it moves rapidly among the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). || 17-18 ||

Therefore, O Ḍombī—[as found in] Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, Cha, Ja; it will be made manifest in the *Vajra-tantra*: "Recitation (*japa*) is declared to be speech (*jalpana*), because of the continuous speaking of the *mālā* and *akṣara*s."
The footprints are the maṇḍala; it is called a maṇḍala because of its being rubbed [or marked]. || 19 ||
The snapping of the hands is the mudrā, as is the crushing of the fingers;
that which is meditated upon and what is contemplated is dhyāna, because it is a process of reflection. || 20 ||
Whatever happiness was attained by one's father is that very happiness enjoyed by oneself;
the death which occurs with such happiness is called the bliss of meditation.
The Fifth Chapter: On Reality.
"Speech is recitation (*japa*)," says Hevajra; it arises from the heart-mantra of one who possesses the ego-identity of Hevajra. That very speech is recitation—this is the summary.
"The foot-drawing" refers to the reflection of the foot, such as the dust or mud left by the feet; that is the drawing of the mandala—this is the great summary.
"From rubbing" means either being trodden upon by Hevajra or maintaining the dhāraṇī of Hevajra.
The meaning is that "mala" consists of the verbal root *mala*, the suffix *a*, and the augment *ṇḍ*. || 19 ||
*Sphoṭa* is expansion;
*moṭana* is contraction;
these two are the *mudrās*.
"Because it was composed by Hevajra"—this is the great summary.

Regarding the phrase "that is to be meditated upon," and so forth: the meaning is that whatever thought arises for one who possesses the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) of Hevajra, that itself is meditation (*dhyāna*).
The phrase "because" (*yasmāt*) implies that it is derived from the root *dhyai*, meaning "to contemplate," according to the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*).
The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), characterized by the supreme bliss of great liberation (*mahāmokṣasukha*), which is to be directly realized, has been described.
Its direct realization is achieved through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The perfection of cultivation is blissful meditation (dhyāna).
Therefore, it must be stated what its cultivation is, or what its meditation is; hence he says: "In the father," and so forth.
The father is the Guru who holds the Vajra;
the locative case is used in the sense of the ablative.

The meaning is that it was obtained from the father—that great bliss of liberation which was taught by the father using the analogy of worldly happiness. The implication is that even the mere hearing of this is difficult for gods, humans, and others who have not been instructed, let alone its actual experience.

"That bliss is enjoyed by oneself" means that very [bliss] which is without appearance, infinite, unsurpassed, inexhaustible, and immutable. Jāpa... [variant readings: 0kālya (ka), 0kalyāḥ (ga), 0kāli (gha)].
From the visualization—ka, kha, gha;
of the footprint-line—ka, ga;

Not that—*ka*; not we—*kha*; this meditation—*ga*; not duality—*gha*.
This reading is found in the *ka* manuscript; whereas *dhyāyaṃ* is in *kha*, *0dhyayaṃ* in *ga*, and *0dhyeyaṃ* in *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *jha*, and *ṭa*.
Therefore, *kha*.

The Great Reality (mahattat) — ka kha ga gha.
Thus, in the Śrī Hevajra Tantra, the chapter on Reality (tattva) — ka. Foremost — Bhoṭa.
In the *Vajrapañjikā-muktāvalī*,
it is said: "The great bliss of liberation is enjoyed by oneself," meaning as if directly before one's eyes.
Why?

Because while experiencing worldly pleasure, one resolves upon that very pleasure according to its characteristics; and by resolving thus, when that has been made the object of focus, one prevents the mind from shifting or spreading toward other objects. Then, through the continuous, respectful, and sustained application—both with effort and without effort—of a mind that has been rendered steady and subtle, such is the extent of its cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In order to explain meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), he says: "bliss," and so forth;
"death," and so forth.
[This refers to] by means of the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) cultivated for a long time in that very manner.

"By which" means by that state in which death occurs here; "that" refers to that very state, which is called the meditation of great bliss (*mahāsukha-dhyāna*) because of the perfection of cultivation.
What is the meaning of "death occurs here"?

"In this world" (*iha*) means that, apart from that great bliss (*mahāsukha*), death—which is non-perception—occurs with respect to other external or internal objects for one, two, many *praharas*, days, months, or years; even due to the bites of gadflies and mosquitoes, or blows from slaps, fists, and whips, or even by the sounds of sharp cymbals, drums, conchs, kettledrums, and great clouds, there is no awakening during that time.

Alternatively, the cultivation of the innate (*sahaja*) is not tenable, because the illustrative innate (*dṛṣṭānta-sahaja*) is [already] manifest, while the illustrated innate (*dāṣṭantika-sahaja*) has been experienced, and thus it is unfit to be an object of meditation (*dhyeya*).
Therefore, he says: "In the father," and so forth.
That which was obtained from the father is enjoyed along with the [worldly] example; "by oneself" means it is directly experienced.
Death is liberation (mokṣa).
"By means of which bliss" refers to the innate bliss of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntika*).
Here, that bliss is called "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*).
The bliss of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is said to be the bliss of the illustrated case (*dārṣṭāntika*), which is cultivated through identity with the bliss of the illustrative example.
The meaning is that this occurs because one attains a state of single flavor through the bliss of the commonality between that which is being experienced and its opposite.
This concludes the fifth chapter, on Reality, in the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti.

The sixth chapter on Conduct. Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme conduct that has reached the further shore, by which one proceeds to the *siddhānta* (the established conclusion) in the *Hevajra*, which is the cause of accomplishment. (1)
The practitioner should wear divine earrings on his ears,
a discus on his head, and two bracelets on his hands.
A girdle upon the hips, anklets likewise on the feet, armlets at the base of the upper arms, and a garland of bones around the neck. (3)
Wearing a tiger skin as a lower garment, consuming the nectar of the five [senses], the dwelling place of the person engaged in the yoga of Heruka is among the five colors. ||4||

Even through the application of both principles, without the observances (*samaya*), awakening will not be attained more swiftly; therefore, he speaks the chapter on conduct (*caryāpaṭala*) beginning with "hereafter" and so forth.
I shall proclaim that conduct which consists of the performance of difficult vows as taught by all the Buddhas;
"to the further shore" means transcending the world.

"Excellent" (*varām*) means the most superior, because there is no returning again. "By which" (*yena*) refers to that mark (*liṅga*) by which it is known. "The established conclusion" (*siddhāntam*) refers to the proposition (*pratijñā*) of the yogis, which is difficult to transcend.
For what purpose is the pledge?
It means for the sake of the accomplishment taught in the Vajra Tantra, by means of the cause which is the attainment of Hevajra.
It is "divine" because it consists of the partless [rays of light]. (1–3)
The "five-fold nectar" (*pañcāmṛta*) consists of the five ambrosias.
The fifth caste is the lowest. || 4 ||

The *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* states: "That which is endowed with five colors is conceived as a single color, because no distinction is perceived between the many and the single color. (5)
The auspicious meditation is said to be practiced under a solitary tree, or in a cremation ground,
or likewise in a delightful mother-house, or in a lonely wilderness.

If, when some degree of warmth has been attained, one desires to engage in the conduct, or if there is a wish to attain accomplishment through this conduct, then one should practice by means of this very conduct.
The reflection is indeed of a single color, yet it is imagined as being endowed with five colors by the ignorant. Why?
To this he says: "Because no distinction is perceived despite the presence of many colors."
For living beings of different species have different forms, such as elephants, horses, and boars, which are distinct from cows;
whereas those of the same species have similar forms, such as cows among cows and elephants among elephants.
Likewise, the letters have forms distinct from cows and the like, and thus they are of a different species from them, not because of a mutual similarity of form among themselves.
Thus, even by means of the worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), which is extremely manifest, the uniformity of caste is established; how much more so by the convention of the yogis?
For in beginningless saṃsāra, everyone possesses all castes. What need is there to speak of this from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)?
For suchness is the ultimate reality of all things, and it is by its very nature utterly pure.
Having gained resolute conviction in that very [suchness], one dwells in the five colors. (5)
He states the location appropriate for the practice with the words beginning "under a single tree.
The meaning is that this practice, which prioritizes uninterrupted yoga, is suitable only in solitary places. (6)
And to show that this should not be done impulsively out of restlessness, he says "something," and so forth.
When some degree of heat—that is, a slight power of yoga—is properly attained, by which one becomes inclined toward yoga and is no longer negligent;
and when snakes, beasts of prey, humans, non-humans, and the like have no power over him and protect him.
Nor does he fear them;
he is not distressed by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the like;
and he is not perturbed by greed, delusion, fear, or anger. Then, the connection is that "one should practice by means of this conduct."
"If it is desired" means:
if there is a liking for it, then one should practice; otherwise, if regret arises later, there will be a loss of yoga.
"In order to attain accomplishment" means:
The meaning is: "If one possesses such vigor, one attains the state of Hevajra in this very life, without any slackening in the practice of yoga. (7)

Having taken this daughter of Vajra— charming-faced, large-eyed, with limbs dark as the blue lotus, consecrated by herself, compassionate, adorned with beauty and youth— he awakens through the practice in the Vajra Tantra. (8)

Due to the absence of a Vajra family, she is consecrated by means of the family of one’s own chosen deity, or else by the implantation of the seed-syllable of enlightenment (*bodhibīja*) for one born of another family.

Amoghasiddhi resides in the girdle; Prajñā has the form of the *khaṭvāṅga*; and the Yogin, through the purification of hatred, takes the form of the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*). In the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary on the *Hevajra*, it is said: Akṣobhya is in the form of the wheel, and Amitābha is the nature of the earrings.
Ratneśa is in the necklace of the neck, and Vairocana is remembered as being in the hand. || 11 ||
One should take hold [of it].
(9) If song is sung out of joy, then it is supreme when accompanied by the vajra;
if one dances when joy has arisen for the sake of liberation, then the concentrated yogi should perform the dance with vajra-steps. (10)
The meaning is that it is appropriate to say "she awakens" because of her excellence of lineage and because she is more difficult for others to subdue.
[She is] "one's own desired" object to be accomplished.
"Born of another family" means born of a lineage other than that of one's own chosen deity;
"refined" means properly consecrated.
The connection is that "having taken her up, the practice is performed. || 9 ||
"From bliss" means from the bliss born of yoga;
"endowed with the vajra" means endowed with the vajra because of its indivisibility—that is, it is endowed with the two truths and indicates them; this is the meaning of "the Vajra Song.
"By means of vajra-words" means by means of the gestures (*mudrās*) of hand, foot, face, and gaze which illuminate reality. || 10 ||

Established through the purity of mantra, song and dance are known as meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) and mindfulness (smṛti); therefore, the yogi should always, at all times, perform song and dance.
"Medicine should indeed be consumed and water should be drunk constantly; thus, old age and death shall not afflict one, and one shall always be protected. (14)
"In the form of a wheel" means in the form of a discus (*cakra*);
"in the hand" refers to the bracelet (*rucaka*) located on the forearm;
"through the purification of hatred" means in the form of a vajra. || 11-12 ||
"By the purity of mantra" means by the conviction in mantra;
"songs" means singing;
"dances" means dancing.
The connection is as follows: because of the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that "cultivation has been performed" by way of its being cultivation, there is "constant singing and constant dancing";
[the word] *nityatām* means "constantly."
"Death" refers to death itself;
"protective beings" refers to those who have attained protection. || 13-14 ||

And in the Vajra-tantra, one should apply a crown made of stolen hair; therein, one should place the skull-bowls of the five Buddhas arising from the syllable *hūṃ*, and it should be worn according to the practice of yoga-conduct (*caryā*). [Chapter Six: Conduct] 15.

Having fashioned a skull-cup fragment with five protruding fingers, he always wears it upon his crown; likewise, he carries two girdles by nature as wisdom and means. Furthermore, through his conduct, the yogi bears sacred ash and a hair-strainer. (16)

The sound of the hand-drum is the recitation; the meditation on the wisdom-khaṭvāṅga is the visualization. Through the practice of the vajra-skull-cup, this very thing becomes both the object of recitation and the object of visualization. (17)
One should avoid greed, delusion, fear, anger, and shameful actions; therefore, a gift is not given with a calculation of what one has received and what one has not. || 19 ||
One should consume whatever food, whether solid or soft, as well as drink, as it may be obtained; one should not engage in the conceptualization of "liked" versus "disliked. || 20 ||
There is no grasping here.

The practitioner of mantra should not entertain any conceptual discrimination regarding what is fit or unfit to be eaten, likewise what is fit or unfit to be drunk, or what is fit or unfit to be approached. || 21 ||

Even a disciple who has attained accomplishment and is illumined by perfect knowledge must pay homage to the Guru; for if he does not, that accomplished one is destined for the Avīci hell as a result of his abandonment [of the teacher]. 22.
Even attachment to one's body and life is the root of obstacles to yoga; therefore he says "sleep," and so forth.
"The self" refers to attachment to body and life.
"Without doubt" means that no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 18 ||

Having given the gift of the body, from the very beginning to all the Buddhas and to all sentient beings— since this is so— one does not give with a consideration of fortune or misfortune regarding success, because of giving without expectation. || 19 ||
"He pays homage" means that one should pay homage; for if one does not pay homage, one would fall into the Avīci hell.
Therefore he says "from Avīci," and so forth, [using] the phrase "by the cause of abandonment" for the sake of providing a remedy. || 22 ||

There is no giving of the body—one should practice the five [nectars] through discernment; they are given as food and drink. To obtain them, one should consume them, for the mantra of the vessel has not been contrived. Regarding what is edible and inedible, even one who has attained accomplishment speaks only of conceptualization. One should abandon the Avīci hell; by the cause of abandoning Avīci, it is a limb [of the path]. If one abandons it through one's own discernment, disregarding portions and non-portions, one will cook in Avīci. In the *Vajra-tantra*, one who is devoid of training and initiation, as well as shame and activity—such a yogi of great compassion should wander with the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. (23)

Transcending fire-offerings, sacrifices, and ascetic penances, and devoid of mantras and meditations, the true practitioner of yoga performs his conduct, liberated from the rules and vows of the samaya. || 24 ||
Even if a Daitya equal to Śakra should certainly stand before him, he should not feel fear there; he should roam about in the form of a lion.
Compassion is constantly drunk for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings; the yogi, delighting in the drink of yoga, does not immerse himself in any other drink. 26.

The eighth chapter, titled "The Assembly of the Yoginī-cakra," concerning the great yoginīs. Now we shall explain the Yoginī-cakra: Having visualized the *bhaga* within the element of space (*khadhātu*), one should perform the meditation in its center, first [visualizing] the cakra according to the rule, and the deities according to their arising. (1) The cakra is earth, water, and fire according to the rule; for the deities, it is the great wind, according to the arising of the meditator. (2) The cakra-maṇḍala is the city of great liberation, the supreme primordial abode; these are one in meaning.
That [basis] is twofold, due to the distinction between the support (*ādhāra*) and the supported (*ādheya*);
without that, there is no application of the three types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, since this application has not been mentioned in the *Devatāpaṭala*, it must be explained here; therefore, he says: "Now," and so forth.

The Yoginī is Nairātmyā; the circle (cakra) in which she is predominant is the Yoginī-cakra. "In the void" (*khāta*) means that when the universal manifestation within one's own mind has been rendered non-apparent through the meditation on the awakening of emptiness, the infinite space appearing therein is the *khadhātu* (space-element).

Having meditated upon the *bhaga* (the womb/vulva) within that *khadhātu*—because of its similarity to a *bhaga* by virtue of being triangular and because it shatters all obscurations—the great *dharmodaya-mudrā*, white as the autumn moon, is the *bhaga*. This is the meaning of "having contemplated that."
"One should perform the visualization in the center" means that one should perform the visualization of the *ādhāra-cakra* (foundation wheel) in the center of that vulva (*bhaga*).
To explain how this is done, he says: "The wheel first," and so forth;
this is the summary (*uddeśa*). The detailed exposition (*nirdeśa*) of this begins with: "The wheel is the earth," and so forth.
By means of the conventional designation of *dharma*, the mandalas of Indra, Varuṇa, Agni, and Vāyu are expressed by words such as "wheel" (*cakra*) and so forth;
just as the word "arising" (*udaya*) refers to the practitioner (*bhāvaka*), or alternatively, "wheels" (*cakrāṇi*) refers to the mandalas.

But here, the Maheśvara-maṇḍala alone is called the "wheel" (cakra) because of its preeminence; and that is indeed the earth itself, as it has been stated according to the proper method that the wheel is the earth (kṣoṇī).
Before the golden circle (*kāñcana-maṇḍala*) is the water circle (*jala-maṇḍala*); therefore he says, "water first"—this is the rule (*nyāya*).

Just as right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) has the nature of illumination, so too does light; therefore, by virtue of this similarity to the rule, light is according to the rule. Thus he says, "according to the rule, [it is] fire" (*hutāśana*).

The parents of the deities do not emit semen; rather, they are born from the wind (*vāyu*). Therefore, because he transforms the deities, he is called a "deity" (*devatā*). For this reason, it is said: "the great wind of the deities.
Just as the arising of the deities is conceived, so too does the practitioner (*bhāvaka*) achieve success in this manner.
For this reason, it is said: "and the practitioner according to the arising. 2. Now, therefore—ga.

The letter *ga* belongs to the nectar situated at the navel, and likewise for the nectar situated at the navel;
by means of the seed-syllables of the moon and the sun, which subsequently overpower the sun, there arises the great bliss of the union of the two. [Vajratantre, Melāpakapaṭalaḥ Aṣṭamaḥ]
The *āli* (vowels) abide in the form of the moon, and the *kāli* (consonants) in the form of the sun. || 5 ||

From the union of the two, the Moon and the Sun, Gaurī and the others are proclaimed; the Moon possesses the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*), while the Seven-Horsed One (the Sun) possesses the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*).
What kind of seed?

It is "overpowered by the western sun," meaning it is mounted upon that sun which was visualized subsequently over the moon once the latter had been visualized. The union of these two is "great bliss"; the meaning is that the union (*melā*) or meeting of the moon and sun is the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), which is sovereign bliss, the great bliss of liberation common to all the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, that great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is fourfold:
the seed-syllable upon the sun is the bliss of application (*prayogasuka*);
the sign arising from it is the fundamental bliss (*mūlasukha*); and the seed-syllable within the center of the sign is the bliss of discernment (*paricchedasukha*).
Therefore, the emanation and reabsorption of the maṇḍala of infinite yoginīs is the bliss for the sake of others.
Now, as to how the moon and sun arise therein, he says: "sthitā" and so forth.

The form of the fifteen vowels is the *saṃhāra* (withdrawal) of the creative mind (*bhāvakacitta*), which resembles pure crystal and pervades the two cavities; this is the *āli*, whose nature is that of all yoginīs. It abides in the form of the moon, meaning that the moon is its transformation.

Above that very moon, the row of thirty-four consonants has appeared; this is the *kāli*, whose nature is that of all Buddhas. It abides in the form of the sun, meaning that the sun is its transformation. || 5 ||
The union of these two, the moon and the sun, which has been described, consists of Gaurī and the others; the meaning is that these are the fifteen Yoginīs who are the transformations thereof.
By this much, the fact that the Yoginīs have the nature of Vajradhara—by virtue of being composed of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—has been demonstrated.
Now, in order to demonstrate that they have the nature of the five Tathāgatas by virtue of being composed of the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*), he says: "The mirror-like," and so forth.

In brief, the Buddhas possess five types of gnosis: the mirror-like gnosis (ādarśajñāna), the gnosis of equality (samatājñāna), the discerning gnosis (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna), the gnosis of accomplishing activities (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna), and the gnosis of the utterly pure realm of phenomena (suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna).

Here, by way of the mirror-like gnosis as their intrinsic nature, you are the moon; and the "seven-horsed" one is the sun, renowned in the world, who possesses equality—meaning he has the nature of the gnosis of equality. (6)

The syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are not intended for the *piṇḍa* (syllabic cluster) arising from the letters.
One should visualize the Lord of the Maṇḍala arisen from the image of the sentient being (*sattvabimba*).

That which is produced by the seed-syllable and accompanied by the emblem (*cihna*) of one's own deity is the "discernment" (*pratyavekṣaṇa*); the meaning is that its intrinsic nature is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
"By all" means by the assembly of yoginīs emanated from the seed-syllable (bīja) contained within the [central] sign; "by all" because of its omnipresence.
"One" means that very same seed-syllable, which has become unified through those [yoginīs] having been withdrawn [into it].
"Practice" (anuṣṭhāna) means the knowledge of the performance of duties (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna). This is the meaning.
"Accomplishment" means that through the transformation of the seed-syllables marked by the signs of the moon and sun, there is the accomplishment of the form of one's own deity;
this is the state of pure reality (*śuddhadharmatā*), which means the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*).
"The wise one should meditate on the five forms" means that the wise one—the learned one—should meditate on the mirror-like [wisdom] and the others.
19. The union of the vowels and consonants— the seat (*viṣṭara*) or throne consisting of the forms of the moon and sun—
of whom is this seat?
Of Vajrasattva; that is to say, of Sattvavajra.
Who is this Sattvavajra?

He is the "arising from the syllable" (akṣarodbhava) pertaining to the aggregate (piṇḍa) of the aggregate arisen from the syllable; the meaning is the generation of the seed-syllable within the center of the emblem.
For here, the words *vajra* and *piṇḍa* signify the *cihna* (symbol),
while the word *sattva* signifies the *bīja* (seed-syllable),
such as *hūṃ* and so forth.

The syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, as well as the syllable *āḥ* indicated by the word "and" (*ca*), the *praṇava* (oṃ), and the melting of the bodies of wisdom and means, are not intended for the generation of the Lord within the Nairātmyā maṇḍala.

If [one asks], "If there is no arising from the melting of gnosis (*jñānadrava*), how then [does it arise]? he says: "From the image of the being," and so forth. "Image" (*bimba*) refers to the emblem (*cihna*). The "being" (*sattva*) is the seed-syllable within the emblem. The "image of the being" (*sattvabimba*) is the image containing the being; from that, [the Lord] emerges.
"Maṇḍaleśam" means the lord of the maṇḍala; [the word] "nairātmyām" has this meaning. 27.
