54. How is it that [the mandala] has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*)? He says: "The *āli*," and so forth.
The word "iti" indicates the reason. 55. Because *āli* is wisdom and *kāli* is means; this is the meaning.
He asks, "Whence do those *āli* and *kāli* come? and says: "56. Of the moon and sun," and so forth.

The moon and sun have the nature of *āli* and *kāli*. Through their differentiation—that is, through making them manifold—by means of the seed-syllable situated upon the heart-moon symbol of Nairātmyā, one emanates Sattvavajrā and the others. The meaning is that this occurs by placing fourteen moons and fourteen suns within the lotuses that serve as the seats for the fourteen goddesses. 58. Thus is the sense.
59. "From this" means from the moon and sun situated upon their respective seats;
"Gaurī and the others" refers to Vajragaurī and the rest, as follows.
60. Just as the moon and sun are common to them, is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) also common?
He says "no," beginning with "varṇa" and so forth:
*varṇa* is a syllable, that is, a seed-syllable (*bīja*); its differentiation is *bheda*, meaning that each seed-syllable is distinct;
"separately" (*pṛthakpṛthak*) means belonging to one [deity] and another.

Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and the eighth is considered to be Ḍombinī.
88. Adhovatī and Ūrdhvavatī are indeed known as Khecarī and Bhūcarī.
89. These two abide by way of the nature of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; they are the two deities. 90. [End of section.]

He states the distinction of their locations with the words beginning "adhyātma" (inner self) and so forth: the connection is that one should meditate on the Yoginīs as being within the inner enclosure (*adhyātmapuṭa*), because it is the abode of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). || || 91–92 ||
In the eastern direction (Indra), in the southern direction (Yama),
and in the outer enclosure, there are the four [goddesses] beginning with Gaurī.
In the eastern and other gates are Pukkasī and the others; in the corners beginning with the northeast [are the remaining goddesses].
95. Regarding *adhavati* and so forth:

the suffix *ati* is applied to the roots *ava* (in the senses of protection, motion, affection, etc. and *ūrdhva*, just as it is to the root *vas*. Thus, one who moves downward is *adhovati*, and one who moves upward is *ūrdhvavati*.

There is elision of the initial [syllable] of *avataḥ*, and elision of the final syllable of *adhas*. Thus, the connection is: "Adhavatī is the Earth-walker (bhūcarī), and Ūrdhvavatī is the Sky-walker (khecarī). These two remain established. (98) The Earth-walker remains by way of the nature of worldly existence (*bhava*), because she moves downwards; for that very reason, she is downward-facing.
(99) The Sky-walker remains by way of the nature of liberation (*nirvāṇa*), because she moves upwards; for that very reason, she is upward-facing.
1. 2. In the internal casket (*adhyātmasaṃpuṭa*), within the internal chamber (*adhyātmapuṭa*), there are five yoginīs.

3. O Yogin, one should meditate upon the aggregates (*skandhas*) as having the nature of the five [Tathāgatas]; while meditating, [one should do so] always. O Gaurī, you who are like Indra’s thunderbolt (*indravajrā*), you who resemble Indra’s thunderbolt, you who consist of Indra’s thunderbolt!
5. Caurī is in Vāruṇī; Kauverī is in Kauvera; [there is] Vajraḍākinī. 6. The Yoginī Nairātmyā is in Nairātmya; there is no Gaurī in Nairātmya.

10. [These] are known as the Carīs.

A discus on the neck, a necklace on the neck, a hand-bracelet, and a girdle.

in the fifth she is blue-colored, and in the sixth she has a white body. 23.

74. When this six-limbed [yoga] has been attained in such a state of intoxication (*mada*), one should subsequently cultivate the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) alone, ending with the stage of cessation (*virama*).

75. This is the meaning: yoga is [union] with the Blessed Lady Nairātmyā; this very [yoga], in the eighth chapter, constitutes the nature of the three bodies (kāyatraya). 76. It is that wherein the three samādhis reside.

having entered the abode of meditation and sat upon a comfortable seat, and having recited the half [of the mantra] with one's own mantra, [one should visualize] Nairātmyā, who gathers all the Tathāgatas, 80.
as a maṇḍala situated in the expanse of the sky before oneself, and worship her with the eight offering goddesses emerging from the seed-syllable in one's own heart.

98. In the Vajra Tantra.
Chapter 8: The Chapter on the Assembly (Melāpakapaṭala). Gaurī holds the moon; Caurī holds the sun;
Vetālī has water in her hand; Ghasmarī holds medicine;
Pukkasī has a vajra in her hand; and Śavarī likewise holds mercury.
Caṇḍālī should play the hand-drum while embracing the neck of Ḍombī.
In front of him, he should perform the confession of sins and so forth as follows:

"I confess all my own misdeeds; I rejoice in all the virtue of all noble ones and ordinary beings; until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dharma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha. For the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings, and for their attainment of the three types of enlightenment according to their respective capacities, I generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening. Then, one should cultivate loving-kindness that bestows divine happiness upon all sentient beings.
Then, toward those very beings, [one cultivates] compassion, characterized by the removal of all suffering; then, toward those very beings, joy, characterized by the non-separation from happiness;
and then, toward those very beings, equanimity, characterized by the gathering together of all mundane and supramundane virtues.

Then, having generated the mind that reflects all phenomena, and having ascertained that this very mind arises through delusion as a reflection of objects even though no external object exists—just as in a dream—one should abandon all reflections of objects such as blue or yellow in order to relinquish delusion, and perceive one's own mind as a reflection of that [true] image: infinite, mere luminosity, free from appearances, resembling a cloudless sky at midday in autumn.

This is that ultimate *bodhicitta*, this is that primary *prajñāpāramitā*, and this indeed is the supreme gnosis of emptiness; having meditated upon this, one should consecrate it with the mantra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-gnosis of emptiness.
Thereafter, having meditated on a sun [disk] in front by means of the syllable *repha*, one should visualize a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from the syllable *hūṃ* upon that sun.
And with that very same vajra, one should visualize a rampart and a cage-like enclosure.

Then, having visualized the great *dharmodaya* mudrā—standing upright, white as the autumn moon, triangular, and hollow within—one should contemplate within its womb the yellow square *māhendra* maṇḍala; above that, the white circular *vāruṇa* maṇḍala; above that, the red triangular *āgneya* maṇḍala; and above that, the black bow-shaped *vāyavya* maṇḍala. Having transformed these, one should meditate upon the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) resting upon a vajra at the center of the pericarp of a vast reflected lotus, composed of five most brilliantly shining jewels.

The *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* states: "The maṇḍala is square with four gates, adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces by the four goddesses, embellished with four archways, and honored by the worship of the sixteen offering goddesses."
Adorned with vajra-threads,
it resounds with the bells and world-peak banners shaken by the wind.
Within its womb-receptacle, one should visualize an eight-petalled lotus;
upon its pericarp and in the petals of the cardinal directions, one should contemplate five corpse-seats.
On the outer receptacle, there are four in the corners, four at the gates, one below, and one above.

Then, having gathered the meditator’s mind—which was previously cultivated there—into the heart of the corpse upon the central seat as the infinite [syllable *A*], resembling clear crystal, in the form of the series of fifteen vowels; one should visualize that transformed into a full moon.

Above that, one should visualize a sun-maṇḍala transformed from the series of thirty-four consonants, and above that, the syllable *A*. From that [sun] comes a knife, and within its center is the syllable *A*.

From that syllable *A*, having emanated all the Tathāgatas in the form of the fifteen Yoginīs and having reabsorbed them right there, one should visualize the Blessed Lady Nairātmyā as the transformation of the moon, sun, discus, and seed-syllable;
she is black in color, extremely fierce, adorned with the five mudrās, and possesses a wheel on her head, earrings, a necklace, bracelets, and a girdle on her wrists.
Clad in a tiger-skin garment, radiant, with blazing tawny hair standing erect,
she has two arms, one face, knitted brows, and red eyes.
She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff in her left hands and a curved knife in her right,
standing in the ardhaparyaṅka dancing posture upon a moon-seat with the luster of the moon.

Adorned with four syllables within the lotuses of the four wheels, and resplendent with the radiant seed-syllables situated upon the moon and the discus between the breasts—this is the first samādhi, named Ādiyoga, and it is the *svābhāvika-kāya*.

In the *Vajratantre*, in the chapter on the *melāpaka*: "Thereafter, having emanated fourteen moon-maṇḍalas from the seed-syllable situated at the heart-mark, one should place them one by one in the hearts of the corpses serving as seats."
Then, having emanated fourteen solar disks from that very seed-syllable, one should place them upon those moons.
Through the union of moon and sun, the seed-syllables arise above the suns.

There, in the inner circle, upon the suns of the directions starting from the east, the syllables *ā*, *ī*, *u* are placed in sequence. In the outer circle, upon the suns of the corners starting from the northeast, the syllables *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḹ* are placed in sequence. Upon the suns at the gates starting from the east, the syllables *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, *o* are placed in sequence. Upon the sun below is *au*, and upon the sun above is *aṃ*.
Each [deity] arises from a seed-syllable (*bīja*) as a scissor (*kartṛ*), with that very same seed-syllable within its womb; from that follows the process of emanation and reabsorption,
and then the fourteen goddesses arise from the transformation of the moon, sun, scissors, and seed-syllables.
All are exactly like that; in the cardinal directions are Nairātmyayoginī, Vajrā, Gaurī, and Vāriyoginī, while in the intermediate corners are Vajraḍākī, Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī.
At the gates are Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, and Ghasmarī;
these twelve face Nairātmyā,
while below is Bhūcarī, facing downward.
Above, the Khecarī with her face turned upward, within the womb of the heart-moon-sword of all [the goddesses], [one should place] their respective seed-syllables. Thereafter,

having drawn in the circle of gnosis (jñānamaṇḍala) by means of the rays of the *han-mantra*, and having dispelled the obstacles with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should offer the previously consecrated water for honor (*argha*) and water for the feet (*pādya*) to that [deity] stationed in the expanse of the sky, using its own mantra.

Then, with the syllables *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*, one should visualize the wisdom-maṇḍala as being drawn in, entered, bound, and subjugated within the commitment-maṇḍala, becoming of one flavor like milk and water;
thereafter, one should perceive Vajrām established through identity within one's own aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

In the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is Gaurī; in the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is Vāriyoginī; in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is Vajraḍākī; in the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is Nairātmyā. In the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is Pukkasī; in the water element (*ab-dhātu*) is Śavarī; in the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) is Caṇḍālī; in the air element (*vāyu-dhātu*) is Ḍombī. In the sense-field of form (*rūpa-āyatana*) is Gaurī; in the sense-field of sound (*śabda-āyatana*) is Caurī; in the sense-field of odor (*gandha-āyatana*) is Vettālī; in the sense-field of taste (*rasa-āyatana*) is Ghasmarī; in the sense-field of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*) is Bhūcarī; in the sense-field of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) is Khecarī. In the sense-field of the eye (*cakṣus-āyatana*) is Vajrā; in the sense-field of the ear (*śrotra-āyatana*) is Nairātmyā; in the sense-field of the nose (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*) is Gaurī; in the sense-field of the tongue (*jihvā-āyatana*) is Vāriyoginī; in the sense-field of the body (*kāya-āyatana*) is Vajraḍākī; in the sense-field of the mind (*mana-āyatana*) is Nairātmyā. In hatred (*dveṣa*) is Nairātmyā; in delusion (*moha*) is Vajrā; in passion (*rāga*) is Vāriyoginī; in pride (*māna*) is Gaurī; in envy (*īrṣyā*) is Vajraḍākī. For all of them, the empowerment of the body is by means of the syllable *oṃ* at the head; the empowerment of speech is by means of the syllable *āḥ* at the throat; the empowerment of mind is by means of the syllable *hūṃ* at the heart.
In this same way, one should also resolve upon the purification of the other aggregates, elements, sense-bases, afflictions, and secondary afflictions.

Then, having drawn in all the Tathāgatas by means of rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart and established them in the sky, [one meditates on] the seed-syllable in one's own heart...

39. One should request consecration after being fully honored by the eight Mother goddesses who have been emanated. 40. Then, one should visualize them sprinkling the Lord of the Maṇḍala and the Maṇḍala itself with water consisting of the five wisdoms from full jeweled vases.
41. [They are to be visualized] as sprinkling the Lord of the Maṇḍala and the Maṇḍala with full jeweled vases.
42–43. One should seal [the body] with five mudrās produced from the consecration waters by means of the lords of one’s own family:
44. by means of Citta (Akṣobhya), Śāśvata (Vairocana), Ratneśa (Ratnasambhava), Lokeśa (Amitābha), and Amoghasiddhi;
45. [or alternatively] by means of Citta, Śāśvata, Ratneśa, and Lokeśa.
46. Likewise, the Gatekeepers (dvārapālī); 47. the Dwellers in the Corners (koṇavāsinī);
48–49. [placed] above and below by means of Delusion (moha) and Passion (rāga).
50. Then, having emanated the eight offering goddesses from the mantra of one’s own heart, having expanded them, and having worshipped them, one should reabsorb them.
51. Therein:
52. Because of worshipping with vessels held in the hands that are slightly bent, the substances for worship [are placed] in the hand-cupped palms (*karakapāla*).
53. They should produce [them] through their own power;
54. and they should enjoy them;
55. on the eighth day, she should embrace the neck of the Lord of the Wheel.
56. In this [mandala], the other yoginīs belonging to the seven mandalas should enter by means of the yoga of radiating light.
57. And all of them—58. having generated vajras from their own lotus-abodes—the Blessed Lady should enjoy.
59. Black, red, then yellow, green, blue, and white in sequence;
60. one should meditate upon the wheel together with its leader as consisting solely of innate bliss.
61. Thus is the second samādhi, named Maṇḍalarājāgri, which is the saṃbhogakāya.

62. Thereafter, impelled by the Lord of the Mandala, all the goddesses, in due order, having accomplished the welfare of the world in a manner appropriate to them through clouds of emanations from their own bodies, 63. should reabsorb those clouds of their own bodies into the root body.
64. In that regard, the female gatekeepers and the earth-dwelling goddesses [place] sentient beings, in due order, within the faculties of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
65. They establish [the practitioner] in the powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; 66. Khecarī is established in these powers;
67. Pukkasī is joyful.
68. Vimalā and Prabhākarī;
69. Śavarī, Arciṣmatī, Sudurjayā, and Abhimukhī; 70. Caṇḍālī and Dūraṅgamā.
71. [The stage] of *cala* [is associated with the two bodhisattvas];
72. *Ḍombī* [is associated] with Sādhumati and Dharmamegha;
73. the remaining [stages] are on the five Buddha-bhūmis.
74. 75. One should pray [to her].
(ga. ca) 76. [She is] filled with the five wisdoms. (ga. ca)
77. by the wholesome ones;
78. the resident woman;
79. in Madhumattarā and Ca.

81. *Ṣaḍādyā* is *ka kha*. 82. *Pūjyamānām* is *ga*. *ca*.
83. And from the intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
84. Of Vajrādhipati, *ka*; 85. His other [consort] is *ga*.
86. Māṇḍalopaka; 87. Sphuraṇayoginyaśca Ga;
88. Sphuraṇayoginyaśca Ca.
89. Should they consume [it]?
(ka kha) 90. Black and red (ga); black and red (ca) 91. White (śitaṃ ka)
92. King Śrī Ka 93. The Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogika-svakāya) Ka 94. Pervasion (spharaṇa) Ga
95. One's own body;
96. faith, mindfulness, vigor, mindfulness, and concentration; 97. and [the remaining factors].

98. In the *Hevajratantra*, 99. the chapter on the assembly (*melāpakapaṭala*): movement is meditative union; that is cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The fruit of cultivation is the two-fold innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which is indicated by the second half of the verse.
This is its meaning:

That which is happiness according to the proper method—because it is supreme and because it is non-delusory—and because it is the primary cause, that is the *cakra*; the meaning is that it is the *yoginī-cakra*, its very nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, that which is the *bodhicitta* produced by the power of the cause according to its arising, it is called "name" (*nāma*) because it causes all [the qualities] of the deities to incline toward it; the meaning is that it is the deity who is most exalted. "The Blessed One Vajradhara"—this is the explanation of this very point, beginning with the words "that" (*tat*), and so forth.

The bliss produced by that meditation is called "the wheel" (*cakra*); it is designated as the "wheel of yoginīs" (*yoginīcakra*) because they are gathered together through the nature of supreme wisdom (*paramaprajñā*).
In the Vajra Tantra, [the eighth chapter, the Melāpaka]: "The deities are the bodhicitta that is to be personally realized according to the proper method;
as it arises, the semen becomes twofold, and from that, the innate (sahaja)."
Wisdom is indeed the woman, while skillful means is remembered as the man;
subsequently, these two are divided into a twofold nature through the distinction between the ultimate and the conventional.
For in the male there is indeed a twofold nature: either semen or his pleasure;
and in the female, as in the male, it is either semen or her pleasure.
He asks, "What kind of happiness is that? and says: "According to the rule" (*yathānyāyam*), which means it is non-erroneous and supreme.
He explains this very point by saying "to be personally experienced" (*svasaṃvedyam*); here, by the word "to be experienced," the manifestation of the bliss to be accomplished is indicated.

Because that which has not become manifest cannot be an object of cognition; by the word "saṃ" (in *saṃvedya*), excellence is intended in the sense of "perfectly," and by the word "sva" (in *svavedya*), non-delusion is intended,
meaning that it is cognized in its own form and not through the superimposition of error.

The term "deity" is a restatement of the phrase "of the deities," and its meaning is explained as follows: "enlightenment" (bodhi) is that very bodhicitta which is self-cognized and has the nature of the dharmakāya.
The mind that is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of awakening is *bodhicitta*;
its intrinsic nature is that of the *sāmbhogika-kāya*. Because it is joined with a subtle form, it means the embodiment of Vajradhara.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "according to its arising" (*yathodayam*).
Because it has arisen in accordance with the object, even though it possesses an aspect (*sākāra*), it is not attached to that object;
as to what that [consciousness] is, he says: "the pure" (*śukra*), for that very reason.
There is a twofold nature; innate bliss is of two kinds.
If this [bliss] is innate (*sahaja*), then what will become of the woman and the man? To this he says "the woman," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of these two," the locative case indicates that the bliss is twofold; as to how this is so, he says: "by way of the distinction between the open (*vivṛti*) and the concealed (*saṃvṛti*)."
Self-awareness is the manifestation [of reality] because it is unobscured by virtue of being free from appearances;
conventional reality is according to its arising because it is slightly obscured by a trace of form.
In this very *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*, there is indeed the differentiation of the four joys; for the innate joy is fourfold according to the perspective of the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*).
Bliss is the first hero; supreme bliss is the Yoginī;
the bliss of sexual union is the totality. He who knows all is the means to that happiness.
Through Ānanda there is some pleasure; Paramānanda is greater than that;
through Virama there would be dispassion (virāga); and Sahajānanda remains as the remainder.
"Therefore" means because of the twofold nature of each of the two;
"of the four" means of the fourfold division;
"division" refers to the division within the generality of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).

But surely, the four joys are recited quite differently—as *ānanda*, *paramānanda*, *viramānanda*, and *sahajānanda*—yet here they are described differently; how then is there no contradiction? To this he says, "The innate," and so forth: the four, beginning with *ānanda* and *paramānanda*, are cultivated in the context of the stage of generation (*utpattipakṣa*).
However, in the context of the stage of generation (*utpannakrama*), the meaning is that only the single innate (*sahaja*) is cultivated in its fourfold form;
thus, the twofold and fourfold nature of the innate has been demonstrated.
He states the threefold nature in its entirety with the words beginning "bliss" (*ānanda*):

the "hero" (*vīra*) is the practitioner (*sādhaka*), so called because he has initiated heroic vigor (*vīrya*) for the sake of reaching the further shore of the accomplishments for his own and others' benefit; he himself is bliss.
Since no one other than Ānanda can be the enjoyer of bliss,
and because the Yoginī seeks the supreme bliss for the sake of the bliss of union (*suratānanda*), the bliss of union is the third.
By counting them as one through their commonality of *surata*,
"the whole indeed" (*samastam vai*) means all three together; he states that very point with the words beginning with "that" (*tad*).
The bliss born of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is that bliss; cultivation is the means.
In the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the four joys (*ānanda*) are cultivated because they arise sequentially as those whose intrinsic nature is joy. Thus, this is logical.

Regarding the generation stage (*utpannakrama*), however, only innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is to be cultivated; he states the three-fold reasoning for this in three verses beginning with "by means of bliss" (*ānandena*).
This is the summarized meaning of these [verses]: here, the goal to be accomplished is bliss that is self-cognizable, equal to space, and identical to that [space].
But what, then, is that?
In the Vajra Tantra, the first [initiation] is for the desire of touch; the second is for the longing for bliss;
the third is for the destruction of passion; and by that, the fourth is cultivated. (Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Assembly) 33.
Existence is said to be supreme bliss, and nirvāṇa is from the absence of passion;
but the innate (sahaja) is merely the intermediate bliss, devoid of these two.
That which is real, supreme, and manifest—indicated respectively by the words *sva* (self), *saṃ* (together), and *vedya* (the object of knowledge)—these three belong only to the Innate (*sahaja*);
therefore, that alone is to be cultivated constantly and not the others, because they are distinct from the goal (*sādhya*).
In this regard, the lack of supremacy, the state of being delusive, and the non-manifestation of the desired [object] of the three types of bliss are explained in sequence by means of three verses.
"Something slight" (*kiñcit*) means a little; because it is inferior, it is not excellent—this is the meaning.

"Excessive" (*adhika*) means indeed excessive; that is, more than that bliss (*ānanda*), but not more than the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Because it is middling, it is not excellent—this is the meaning. "Dispassion" (*virāga*) means turning away; therefore, the bliss of cessation (*virama-sukha*) is indeed inferior, because it is intermingled with suffering—this is the meaning.

"By way of remainder" (*śeṣataḥ*) means, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), that innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is indeed to be cultivated as innate bliss itself; this is the connection with what follows.
"Expectation," "desire," and "longing" are synonyms.
And because it is conceptual, it is an error;
therefore, due to its state of expectancy, the first two are errors:
[the thought] "touch" and "with the desire for the lotus."
The word "proper" (*yuktam*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

According to the sequence indicated in the first verse, the third is *viramānanda* (the joy of cessation) and the fourth is *sahajānanda* (innate joy). Here, by the word "passion" (*rāga*), the supreme bliss is meant—not in the sense of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*)—because it is the locus of attachment; its destruction is [the state of] its non-existence, which is the reality (*tattva*); from that, [the fourth joy] arises.
By that, it is characterized; this is the meaning of "having that as its characteristic.

Since the *viramānanda* (bliss of cessation) is characterized by the destruction of superior bliss—[expressed] as "I have experienced true bliss"—it is, therefore, erroneous because it consists of the conceptual construction of recollecting past pleasure.
"Bhava" means that from which something comes into being;
the meaning is the immediate cause.
"Nirvāṇa" means destruction.

"Middle" (*madhyama*) means the middle interval; that which possesses this is "middle" (*madhya*), with the suffix *-ac* in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). It is "with an interval" because its causality is mediated—this is the meaning.
(From the *Hevajrapañjikā-muktāvalī*) There is neither passion nor dispassion, and no "middle" is perceived;
herein there is neither wisdom (*prajñā*) nor means (*upāya*), due to the perfect awakening to reality (*tattva*). (35)
The innate state is not described by another, nor is it found in anyone else;
it is known by oneself through merit and by attending upon the Guru at the sacred occasions.
The meaning is this: even at the time of *paramānanda* (supreme bliss), there is no manifestation of the most excellent pleasure, because that [pleasure] is its cause;

nor is it manifested at the time of *viramānanda* (cessation-bliss), because it has already perished; and at the time of *ānanda* (bliss), there is certainly no manifestation, because it is the cause of the cause.

By these three causes of non-manifestation, since it arises precisely in the form of supreme bliss, one might ask: "If this is so, why are four [blisses] cultivated even in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), given that only this bliss becomes manifest?
This is because each [subsequent bliss] serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the preceding one.
If that is so, why is there only one [deity] in the stage of completion (utpannakrama)?
Because this stage is characterized primarily by resolute conviction (adhimukti), since it consists in the constant manifestation of the innate (sahaja) alone. || 34 ||

When innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) has been taught in this way, some might have the apprehension that they have already accomplished their purpose and that further meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is useless; therefore, he says "not by another," and so forth.
"Not by another" means not even by [such figures as] the Buddha-Vajradhara;

"in no one whatsoever" means even in a lord of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*). The underlying sense is that because it is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*), it transcends the conceptualization of speech.
How, then, is its teaching or its hearing possible?

It occurs through the conventionality of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*) and not by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), just like the experience of pleasure and pain by gods and hell-beings.
However, when that [nirvāṇa] becomes manifest, it is experienced by way of its own intrinsic nature; and at that time, it is experienced by oneself alone, not through the words of another.
He says this very thing: it is known by oneself;
therefore, cultivation is not at all useless, because it is impossible to directly realize that [reality] without the perfection of cultivation.
And so it has been said: "The path that cuts the thorn of craving has been taught by me to you; you yourselves must practice it; the Tathāgatas are merely proclaimers."
—In the *Vajra-tantra*, in the chapter on the *melāpaka* (the gathering), it says: "From merit," and so forth.

It is thought thus: here, the mundane innate joy (*sahajānanda*) is not the goal to be accomplished, because it has already been realized; and because, in comparison with the ever-increasing happiness of the celestial realms and so forth, it is inferior, being tainted by outflows (*sāsrava*) and thus impure; and because it is the very root of the defects belonging to cyclic existence.

What, then, is it? It is that which is to be personally realized by the Tathāgatas alone; it is co-nate with the attainment of the *dharmakāya* and equal to space; it is the co-nate *saṃbhogakāya*, being its natural outflow; it is characterized by supreme excellence, utter purity, and eternal bliss—this is the *sahajānanda* (innate joy) that is to be accomplished here.

Since there is no other way to reach it, one should cultivate it by resolving upon this very worldly *sahajānanda* according to the instructions. Upon the perfection of that cultivation, it becomes manifest and is known directly by oneself, not previously.

Therefore, since hearing, reflection, and meditation are not in vain here, the "means" (*upāya*) is the path; its "service" (*sevā*) is correct cultivation. It has many "stages" (*parvāṇi*), meaning many modes.
A stage obtained from a teacher is a "teacher-stage" (*guruparva*); that which is bestowed according to rule by a teacher upon a worthy disciple is what is meant by "instruction" (*avavāda*).
Instruction (*avavāda*) is discourse for the sake of comprehension;

comprehension (*avagama*) is realization (*adhigama*); discourse is teaching through the lineage of gurus (*guruparva*). Service to the means (*upāyasevā*) refers to service toward the lineage of gurus as the means. By this [service], it is known that there are four causes for realization:
dwelling in a suitable place, reliance upon virtuous persons, right application of the mind, and having performed merit in the past. These four causes of realization have been stated.
In this context, by the mention of "relying on a guru" (guruparva), taking refuge in a virtuous person is stated;
by the mention of "practicing the means" (upāyasevā), the correct mental application (samyak-praṇidhāna) is explicitly stated;
and by implication, dwelling in a suitable locality (pratirūpa-deśavāsa) is stated, because that [correct application] is impossible without it.
By the mention of "merit" (*puṇya*), the state of having performed merit was expressed;
however, here it is said "from merit" (*puṇyāt*), not "from previously performed merit.
What is the reason for this?
For even through merit accumulated in this life, realization is desired in the system of Mantra; and what is that specific method?

It is that specific method which consists of the repeated purification, in accordance with the occasion and in accordance with realization, of the worlds of oneself, sentient beings, and the vessel-world every day by means of the meditation on the wheel of the support and the supported, and so forth. // 36 //
[Chapter] Eight: *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī* One should perceive that all these other things—whether inferior, middling, or superior—are equal, by means of the meditations on reality (*tattva*). (37)
The inferior is the subtle object, while the superior is said to be the state of being; the middle is devoid of both, and "others" refers to the six sense faculties. || 38 ||
Whatever things there are, whether stable or moving—all these are indeed myself; they are equal and possess identical activity through the contemplation of reality in its state of equilibrium.

But surely this specific method exists in the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) and not in the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*), because in the latter there is meditation on mere innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) alone;
therefore, he says: "inferior, middling," and so forth. (37)
The explanation of this very point begins with "inferior" and so forth,
up to "subtle object"; [it refers to] one's own body, which is the state of the self’s mind and mental factors.
"Excluded from two" means excluded from the two parts of one's own body;
"the six faculties" refers to the eyes and so forth, which are the presiding deities over one's own body. || 38 ||
"Stable and moving" refers to external things, both sentient and insentient;
"not at all 'I'" means that I alone am not the sole Vajradhara;
"equal in activity" means they possess non-differentiated consciousness.

He asks, "How? and says: "By means of the meditations on reality. This is explained by the term "of equal flavor" (*samarasaiḥ*), which means "by means of meditations on the state of equal flavor" (*samarasabhāvanaiḥ*). || 39 ||
"Equal" (sama) is said to mean "the same" (tulya); its wheel is known as "flavor" (rasa), and for this reason it is called "single-natured" (ekabhāva). || 40 ||
For the entire world is of equal essence with me; the three worlds have originated from me.
All this is pervaded by me; no world is seen to consist of anything else.
The explanation of this [term] is also "equal" (*sama*) and so forth; "tulya" means "similar," and by this,
the meaning of the first member of the compound is stated.
Regarding the phrase "of that": *rasa*, *sāra*, *tattva*, and *bhāva* are synonyms for the inferior, middling, and so forth.
What is this *rasa*?
"Cakra" means the circle of yoginīs characterized by self-cognizable bliss;
by this, the meaning of the latter member of the compound is stated.
He states the collective meaning [of the term *samājā*]: "But the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) is the single nature (*ekabhāva*)."

"One whose taste is equal" (sam-rasa) means one who has an equal flavor; "one whose state is singular" (eka-bhāva) means one who has a single nature—by this meaning, that is, by the aforementioned meaning of the individual components. || 40 ||
Regarding how one should cultivate that state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*), he says "mad" and so forth:
"the entire world" refers to all mobile beings;
for they are indeed born from me (*madbhava*), since there is no such thing as a self other than the mind.

And since all things arise from the mind, the three worlds are thus born of me alone; all stationary beings are likewise born of me as previously described— this refers to both the stationary and the moving.
Because it has the nature of mind, [the thought] "it is pervaded by me" does not mean it is of another nature, nor does it lack the nature of mind;
yet, if the universe has the nature of mind, how can it have the nature of great bliss?

For one whose mind is self-awareness and for whom the emptiness of duality is the very nature of the mind, all minds are thus permeated by the knowledge equal to space, which consists of great bliss; because of this commonality of experiencing the emptiness of duality, the yoga of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣayoga*) is described by this. || 41 ||

In the Vajra Tantra, [the eighth chapter, the Melāpaka-paṭala]: "Having understood this, the yogi who is well-composed in practice achieves accomplishment; of this there is no doubt, even if he is a man of little merit. (42)
Whether eating, drinking, bathing, awake, or even asleep, one should contemplate this constantly; then the seeker of Mahāmudrā attains it. || 43 ||
For the entire world is indeed conceptualized by the mind; since it is not conceptualized, the thorough knowledge of all phenomena is cultivation, yet it is not cultivation at all. // 44 //
He states its benefit with the words beginning "In this way," etc., up to "even one of little merit.
"Even one of little merit" means even one who has performed no meritorious deeds in previous births. "Is accomplished" means that through this very yoga, there is an accumulation of merit. || 42 ||
"Khāne" means in eating;
"even while asleep" means that through respectful practice, one sees [the object] exactly so even in dreams;
"sātatya" (continuity) refers to the spontaneous flow of this very yoga.
To the question "What is the use of this continuity? he says: "For the sake of accomplishing Mahāmudrā," and so forth; the meaning is that it is for the purpose of attaining Mahāmudrā. || 43 ||
Thus, having explained the state of having performed merit through the section on resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*),
he says "For they are cultivated," and so forth, in order to explain the correct aspiration (*samyak-praṇidhāna*) of the mind;
"the entire world" refers to the worlds of sentient beings and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
All of these are indeed cultivated;
however, he asks why there is this restriction and says "by the mind" and so forth.
The meaning is that because they are not conceptualized by the mind—that is, by the conceptualizing consciousness (vikalpavijñāna)—for that very reason this restriction is established.
If they are not conceptualized, then they are not cultivated; thus he says, "All phenomena," and so forth.

The meaning is that the thorough knowledge of phenomena itself is their cultivation, and there is no cultivation other than this, which is to say, no conceptualization, because conceptualizations are by nature deluded. || 44 ||

In the Vajra Tantra, whatever stable and moving entities are meditated upon—be they grasses, shrubs, creepers, and so forth—by those [practitioners], that indeed is the supreme chapter on the gathering (*melāpaka*).
Reality is the very nature of one's own being.
Among those [states], there is no other supreme [state] than this great bliss which is self-cognized.
Accomplishment is to be self-cognized, for meditative cultivation is indeed self-cognized.
Regarding the passage beginning with "stable" (*sthira*),

the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes trees, mountains, oceans, and so forth, as well as living beings; all of these should be meditated upon as the supreme reality (*parameva tattvam*), not as the reality of mere resolute conviction (*adhimuktitattvam*), though they are conceptually constructed through various discursive expressions and diverse forms.
Furthermore, as to what that supreme reality (tattva) is, he says: "The self," and so forth.
The state of the self—that is, of one's own mind—is the reality; this [reality] has that very thing as its essential nature (svarūpa). || 45 ||
Thus it has been said: "Of these, one is reality"—this connects with what precedes; "there is no other" means that there is no second reality.
To the question, "What then is that one?", he says: "to be self-cognized," and so forth.
Is it not the case that emptiness alone is the supreme reality? For it is called the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*);
since "realities" (*bhūtāni*) means "truths" (*tattvāni*), the "limit" (*koṭi*) refers to their pinnacle or summit, meaning that there is no reality beyond this.
But here, is there not a contradiction in saying that the supreme reality is self-cognizable?
There is no contradiction;

for emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not something other than phenomena (*dharma*), since *dharmatā* has no separate body from them. Rather, emptiness is that very state of being devoid of duality, the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), which belongs to the reality of all phenomena—that very reality which is self-cognizable.
If that [consciousness] is the supreme reality, then it is stated that the supreme reality is indeed self-cognizable;
so how could there be any contradiction?
And [it applies to] all things, both stable and moving—ga.
Ya-kha, yai ga bhāvante— ka. Ga gha valaṃ ga.
To be experienced (saṃvedya) – ka; self-experienced (svayaṃ vedyaṃ) – ga; experienced (vedya) – cha; in the experienced (vedye) – ja;
great bliss (mahāsukham) – ga;
from that which is self-experienced (svasaṃvedyād) – ṭa. O Pāṇḍaravāsinī (he paṃ yo ra mā).
Bhavaṃ is *ka*; bhavaga is *gha*; bhavo is *siddhi-ka*. *Ga* is *svasaṃvedya-ka*; *gha* is *svasaṃvedyaṃ-kha*. *He* is *paṃ*; *yo* is *mā*; *svayaṃvedya* is *ga*.
The meditations— gha;
the second reality is "ka"—
ga, ca.
That suchness is the state of being devoid of duality—ka. kha. This much of the reading does not exist in the Pāṇḍulipi manuscript.

The *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* states: Action consists of that which is self-cognized; from affliction, action arises. One is oneself the destroyer, oneself the doer, oneself the king, and oneself the lord. (47)

Moreover, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the supreme reality only of the objects of cognition (*ālambana-tattva*), not of the subjects of cognition (*ālambaka-tattva*) and so forth; self-cognition (*svasaṃvedya*), however, consists of the ultimate reality of all phenomena. For indeed, self-cognition is also the supreme [reality] of the objects of cognition, because by the vision of emptiness, one's own nature is also seen.
But the subject of cognition is supreme only as self-cognition, not as emptiness, because it is insentient (*jaḍatvāt*).

Furthermore, regarding the other seven supreme principles (*paramatattva*) that are accepted—namely, the principle of the fruit (*phalatattva*), the principle of the cause (*hetutattva*), the principle of the path (*mārgatattva*), the principle of action (*karmatattva*), the principle of the agent (*kārakatattva*), the principle of the Lord (*īśvaratattva*), and the principle of sovereignty (*prabhutattva*)—he says "great bliss" (*mahat sukham*) and so forth in order to demonstrate that these too are precisely that which is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*).
For Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*), characterized by incomparable, perfectly pure, and eternal bliss, is the supreme principle of the fruit;
its designation is "great bliss," and the term "self-cognized" applies here as well.
The meaning is that it is indeed self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*), because its characteristic is existence (*bhāva*).
"Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is awakening (*bodhi*); that arises from self-cognition alone.
That itself is the supreme reality of the cause (*hetutattva*), because existence alone is the generator; such is the meaning.
The word "hi" (indeed) is used for emphasis; [the meaning is: meditation is indeed self-cognizable, therefore that alone is the supreme reality of the path. || 46 ||
"Consisting of self-awareness" means that action has the nature of self-awareness; the meaning is that this alone is the supreme reality of action (*karmatattva*).
To explain how that is action, he says "because of affliction," and so forth.
For action is indeed twofold: knowledge and abandonment.

The destruction of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable is abandonment (*prahāṇa*); knowledge (*jñāna*) consists of all the qualities of a Buddha, which have awakening as their intrinsic nature. In this context, by the phrase "because of [the act of] piercing" (*bādhanāt*), abandonment is explicitly stated, while knowledge is stated by implication. In some readings, it is "because of awakening" (*bodhanāt*); by that, knowledge is explicitly stated, and abandonment is stated by implication.

"Karma is born" means that karma comes into being; it is indeed self-cognized, for there is no operation of the path other than the path itself, nor is there a separate instrument of the path; the agent is the Bodhisattva.

He who is the remover of those two obscurations and the producer of gnosis—therefore, the Bodhisattva who has reached the supreme state of agency—is himself self-cognizable; thus he says, "He is himself the remover, he is himself the producer," because there is no agent distinct from him. This is the sense: for whomsoever those perfections of gnosis and abandonment exist.

Because he is the supreme among all the world, he is the highest lord in the world; and that [lordship] is precisely that, as it says: "He is himself the king," meaning that by virtue of that perfection of his own welfare, he is always capable of performing the welfare of others in every possible way.
He is the supreme lord of sentient beings, and he himself is that very same thing; thus it is said: "The self-effulgent lord. (47)
Consisting of self-awareness because of awakening—kha. cha. jha.
ña. ṭa. O, he who is himself the agent and himself the destroyer—ga.
There is none— *ga*—
the supreme of all—
*ka kha*— *‘ga’*— this much of the reading does not exist in the palm-leaf manuscript (*pāṇḍulipī*).
And there are no noble practices— ka, kha—
from the very perception of the eternal— ka.
The meditation on *ka* and *kha* is supreme;
there is no *ga*.
This sentence "bodhanāditya - ka kha" does not exist in the 'ga' recension; it is found in the 'ga' and 'ca' readings.
That which belongs to those two—ākha. ga. ca;
supreme—ga. ca;
by that—ka.
In the Vajra Tantra, passion, hatred, and likewise envy, delusion, and pride—all these do not equal even a sixteenth part of that delightful state. (Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Assembly)
Who, then, is this? Is he one among the five Tathāgatas?
No; he says: "Passion," and so forth.
Passion is Amitābha, hatred is Akṣobhya, envy is Amoghasiddhi, delusion is Vairocana, and pride is Ratnasambhava.
The locative case in the phrase "in that state" (*tatpade*) is used in the sense of the genitive;

it means that they do not equal even a sixteenth part (*kalām nārghanti ṣoḍaśīm*) of that self-cognizable, delightful state—the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the state of the Great Vajradhara. The meaning is that they do not attain even the sixteenth limb, because [that state] is included within the perfection of all the Tathāgatas; such is the intended sense.

And here, by the verse beginning with "bhāvyante hi," the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is stated; by the half-verse beginning with "sthiracalāśca," its object (*ālambana*) is stated for the purpose of avoiding erroneous cultivation;
and by the verse beginning with "bhāvyante vai param," its aspect (*ākāra*) is stated for the purpose of avoiding other aspects.
The greatness of that form has been explained by three verses beginning with "Of these, one... [and so forth]. This is for the purpose of generating respect;
respect means honor or devotion (*ruci*).
For cultivation accompanied by devotion is "cultivation with honor" (*satkṛtya-bhāvanā*), and through the power of such devotion, there also arises continuous cultivation (*sātatyabhāvanā*).
Realization comes from those two;
thus, the correct cultivation of the means has been described, which is the right application of the mind. || 48 ||

Now the occasion for the teacher must be explained, for which purpose one relies upon a virtuous person; a "virtuous person" means a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and a "teacher" (*guru*) means one capable of giving correct instruction.
[The variants read: *rāgadveṣa tathā śyyaṃ* (ka), *rāgadveṣaṃ* (kha, ga), *rāgadveṣa tathā īṣyā* (gha), and likewise *tathaiverṣyā ca*.
*moha mānam*—ka, kha, gha; *mauha mānam*—ga.
*sarva tatra pade*—ka; *sarva tatraḥ padasya*—gha;
*nāsti*—gha.
kalā—ka, kha, gha;

[the author] also discusses *bhāvanā*. Ka.Kha.

The meaning of the words:
What is that which relies upon the *tatpuruṣa* compound?

[It is] the knowledge (*jñāna*) arising from the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), equal to space, endowed with its means (*sopāya*), and within it the three worlds are born, by virtue of having wisdom and means as their intrinsic nature. (49)
Therefore, he speaks of the "Guru-parva" (the festival of the Guru) with two verses, beginning with "Dharmodaya":

*dharmāḥ* refers to the noble qualities (*āryadharma*); that in which these arise is the *dharmodaya*, meaning the *dharmadhātu*. Its seal (*mudrā*) is also called *dharmodaya*, meaning the *dharmadhātu*.

In this context, however, it is called a "lotus" (padma) because of its similarity to that [actual lotus], for the purpose of generating in the yogins a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding it;
since knowledge arises within that [source of phenomena], it is the "knowledge arising from the source of phenomena" (*dharmodayodbhava*).
Of what nature is it? It is equal to space (*khasama*). Why is it equal to space? Because, being free from appearance (*nirābhāsa*), it culminates in the emptiness of duality.
Why is it free from appearance? Because an experience that has proceeded toward a most excellent and beloved object of cognition does not extend to other objects of cognition.

Nevertheless, it would not be equal to space (*khasama*) if it were produced by the mind; yet this is not the case, because it is self-arisen (*svayambhū*), arising in that manner even when the mind’s activity has ceased. For this very reason, it is called "innate" (*sahaja*).

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "endowed with means" (*sopāyānvita*). It is "similar" (*samāna*) because there is only a slight difference from that [space], and it is "with means" (*upāya*) because it accomplishes the welfare of others.
Thus, the state of being similar is its "essence" (*sa-bhāva*), like a similar class (*sapakṣa*).
The meaning is that it is the pure mundane knowledge obtained subsequent to that;
moreover, it is indeed innate because of its self-arisen nature,
and it is "endowed with" or accompanied by that.

If one asks, "What should he do with that? the answer is: "He should meditate upon it"—this is the ellipsis. But [an objector might say]: "In that case, only two types of cognition have arisen there, not some deity; and in the system of mantra, it is the deity itself that must be meditated upon, not mere cognition. To this, he says: "In the three worlds," and so forth. The secrets of body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas residing in the ten directions and three times are each infinite. The three worlds are the three realms; the collection of these three worlds is the "three worlds" (*trailokya*). Mahāvajradhara has arisen therein. Because of that—since that is the case—one should meditate upon that cognition.
In what form was he born? It means in the form of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), that is, by way of the nature of wisdom and skillful means.
Wisdom is supreme knowledge; it means the *dharmakāya*.
The non-dual form consists of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, which arise from that [wisdom].
The meaning is that he is born from those two forms, which constitute the universal means for accomplishing the welfare of the world in all its aspects without limit.
[In the *Vajra-tantra*, Chapter Eight, the *Melāpaka-paṭala*: "The Blessed One should take the form of semen; that bliss is known as the *kāminī*."
The separation of the one and the many is non-solar; from that moment, there is another supreme delight.
To explain how he is born therein even from those two, he says "śukra" and so forth;
"Bhagavān" refers to the means (*upāya*) which encompasses the two bodies.

Regarding the phrase "having the form of semen" (*śukrākāra*): that which is called the second, the *sahaja*, is "semen" (*śukra*) because it is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of space-like gnosis (*khasamajñāna*). Since that [gnosis] is its form, it is "having that form" (*tadākāra*); the meaning is that the Blessed One has arisen in that very form. Why is that? Because of their non-difference due to being the outflow of space-like gnosis. Regarding "that bliss": that which was called space-like gnosis is the "passionate woman" (*kāminī*), who is Prajñā; this is because of their non-difference through the commonality of space-like gnosis.

If it is argued that "let there be wisdom alone and not means, because [means] are conceptual due to having a form," he says: "It is one... He states this because it has as its object the freedom from being one or many; thus, it is the freedom from being one or many.
Why is that? He says: "Precisely because of the moment."
That very knowledge, which is equal to space, is a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) because it is a festival of bliss;

since he has arisen from that very moment and not through the power of ignorance, therefore this is the intended meaning: that these mental aspects (*ākāra*) are non-existent because they lack both a single and a manifold nature.

Therefore, the very non-existence of all phenomena—which possess a body of consciousness—according to their respective forms, is the emptiness of duality. And that [emptiness] is directly perceived by means of a cognition equal to space (*khasama-jñāna*) through its movement toward the supreme state.
Subsequently, it is determined by that very same [cognition] through a cognition possessing form (*sākāra-jñāna*) which arises by the power of the former;

for even though it possesses form, it appears as if it were like an illusion (*māyā*) and so forth because of its non-existence according to its form. This is due to the intensity with which the foolish cling to objects, just as the appearance of forms such as blue and so forth is seen as being the object itself.

As it is said in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*: "One perceives all phenomena as equal to space through a gnosis that is non-distinct from the object of knowledge; subsequently, one perceives all phenomena as being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an echo, a mirror-image, the moon in water, or a magical creation. Therefore, because its means (*upāya*) also consists of the vision of ultimate reality, it is composed of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

This very point is stated: "The other delight" (*aparā ratiḥ*); the meaning is that this second [delight] is wisdom (*prajñā*) itself, because it is supreme gnosis and because of its great bliss. (50)
The *Vajrapañjikā-muktāvalī* states: This gnosis is to be personally realized; its domain transcends the path of speech.
For this is the stage of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānakrama*), consisting of the gnosis of the Omniscient One.
Earth, water, wind, fire, and space—
In an instant, none can obstruct the awareness of one's own and others' consciousness;
in an instant, one may become a single form consisting of heavens and underworlds,
and cannot be obstructed by the conceptualization of self and other.

Moreover, how could there be for the Buddhas the enjoyment of all Buddha-qualities—such as the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) characterized by the vision of all phenomena in all their aspects—as well as the performance of the welfare of the world in all its modes, if the means did not exist? The concluding verse beginning with "to be self-cognized" (*svasaṃvedyam*) summarizes everything that was stated in the preceding passage starting with "it is known by oneself" (*ātmanā jñāyate*). It summarizes the statement that "this gnosis is to be self-cognized and is not described by another," and the statement that "the innate (*sahaja*) is not found in anything."
"Beyond the range of the path of speech" means that the path of speech is the activity of words; "beyond its range" means it has transcended that domain.
This is the summary of the entire sequence of arising;

for this is indeed the sequence of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānakrama*). By the Blessed One Vajradhara, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*) which subsumes the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, there was an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) established through identity with oneself, sentient beings, and the vessel-world. The mode of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakāra*) which takes that as its object is the sequence of empowerment.
He says this very thing: "consisting of the omniscient wisdom" (*sarvajñajñānatanmayam*).

The "omniscient wisdom" (*sarvajñajñāna*) is the realization within oneself through identity with all the wisdoms of all the Tathāgatas; that indeed is the state of Vajradhara. The entire universe, both moving and unmoving, has that very nature and consists of it;
and since both the omniscient wisdom and [the universe] consist of it, there is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) in the sense of a collective whole. || 51 ||
With these two verses beginning with "The earth" (*pṛthivī*), he describes the benefits pertaining to the present life:

"How could there not be accomplishment through the earth and so forth, according to the *Vajra-tantra*, the entire range of Vedic doctrines, and the expansion of ritual actions? [This is from] the eighth chapter, the Chapter on Assemblage. Through purity, however, there will be rebirth in another existence. (54)
Without that, there is no accomplishment in this world or the next;

it is not known by whomsoever that for one who has not realized Hevajra, all effort is in vain. [He] is not obstructed, because through his desire he sinks into the earth and emerges from it; he passes through walls and even through mountains without impediment; he is not afflicted by poisons, weapons, and the like; he sleeps, sits, stands, and walks upon water, both above and below its surface, and is not afflicted (or moistened) by rain and so forth, likewise with fire, wind, and space as appropriate.
"Perceiving the consciousness of oneself and others" means that one thoroughly knows the minds of oneself and others, whether past, future, or present;
the verse beginning with "He goes to heaven," etc., has its meaning already explained.
[Verses 52–53] To demonstrate the superiority of this tantra over other scriptures, there are two verses beginning with "All," etc.

The Vedas, the external treatises, the established doctrines, and the sūtras of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka— because one considers rebirth to be within these, the extensions of karma such as rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth prescribed by the system of mantras (Mantranīti)—
through all of these, there would be no accomplishment; the meaning is that perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) does not arise.
He says whether or not [enlightenment] occurs according to the system of the *pāramitās*: "It may be," and so forth.

"Purification" (*śuddhi*) refers to that by which one is purified through the exhaustion of the obscurations of afflictions and the known (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*); this is the path characterized by the six *pāramitās*. By means of that, enlightenment (*bodhi*) certainly comes to be; however, "in another existence of rebirth" (*punarjanma-bhavāntare*) means in a subsequent birth, a continuity of births—that itself is "existence" (*bhava*), which is *saṃsāra*, because like *saṃsāra* it is long-lasting; the meaning is a succession of births over three incalculable eons (*kalpāsaṅkhyeya*).
Thus, the meaning is that it comes to be when there is an interval (*antare*) or separation [from that path].
In the Yoga Tantras, enlightenment is said to be attained in this very life.
To the question, "What is its superiority over those [other systems]? he says: "And not... and so forth.
Even in other tantras, that supreme enlightenment occurs either in this very life or in a proximate future birth; yet that does not occur without this innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
This *Hevajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* should be maintained day and night through constant application to reality, like the flow of a river’s current or the continuous flame of a lamp. (56)
The eighth chapter, titled "The Assembly of the Yoginī-cakra," concerning the great yoginīs.
If one asks, "In that case, what is the distinction between these [other tantras]? he says, "Hevajra," and so forth.
The meaning is that for the sake of the correct thorough understanding of that [teaching] indicated by other tantras, the Hevajra itself must be known by practitioners;
the sense is that this is their *uttaratantra* (subsequent or explanatory tantra). || 55 ||
If it is asked, "Enlightenment is difficult to attain; how can it be accomplished in a single lifetime even through the cultivation of innate bliss?
he says: "Like a river," and so forth.
The stream of a river is its current; likewise, the flow is a continuous, uninterrupted succession. By that—
The light of a lamp is the flame of a lamp; its continuity is likewise the constant and uninterrupted yoga of reality, which is the yoga of innate bliss (sahajānanda). By means of that—
One must remain thus for a day and night;
the meaning is that in this way, awakening (*bodhi*) will necessarily be accomplished in this very life.

The *melāpaka*—the gathering—of the great Yoginīs such as Nairātmyā and others occurs in the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) within innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). A chapter (*paṭala*) is so named because it illuminates that [gathering]; therefore, it is called by the name *Yoginīcakra*, meaning it is renowned by this term. || 56 ||
In the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti, this is the eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Assembly (*melāpaka*).
The Ninth Chapter on Purity. Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter on purity: "Indeed, the purity of all things is known as suchness (tathatā);
subsequently, it is described according to the individual distinctions of the deities. (1)
The six sense-faculties, the five aggregates, the six bases, and the five elements, though pure by their very nature, are veiled by ignorance and the afflictions. (2)

Regarding the "Chapter on Purity" (*viśuddhipaṭalam*): it is called purity (*viśuddhi*) because by means of it things are purified; that nature (*prakṛti*) through which, when fully understood, phenomena become pure and free from defects—that is their purity, because it bestows accomplishment upon the practitioner who understands it.
The chapter that elucidates this is the "Chapter on Purity.
In this context, pervasive purity is suchness (*tathatā*).
The localized [forms] are Vajragaurī and so forth;
this is what is stated by the words "of all" and so on, meaning that the deities are "exalted. || 1 ||
Now, what is pure, or how is it pure?
To this he says: "The six sense-faculties," and so forth;
"by nature" means by their very essence (*prakṛtyā*).

If everything were pure by its very nature, then effort for the sake of purification would be useless; to this he replies with the words beginning "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). Non-afflicted ignorance is the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), while the afflictions such as attachment and so forth are the obscuration of the afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). That which is veiled and defiled by these is purified, because of the removal of those very adventitious stains. The meaning is that effort is for the purpose of removing stains, not for the purpose of producing a previously non-existent intrinsic nature. || 2 ||

Ninth: *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*. Purity is of the nature of self-awareness; one is not liberated by means of [external] purity, because the object is of a pure nature. Self-awareness is supreme bliss. (3)
If it is asked, "What is the nature of that purity of things which has been described as having the essence of suchness (tathatā) and the essence of the deity?
he says: "To be personally experienced," and so forth.
"To be personally experienced" (svasaṃvedya) has been explained in the eighth chapter; the meaning is that purity is precisely that very form.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Not [by another]," and so forth;

for one is not liberated specifically by a purification other than self-cognition (*svasaṃvedya*). The meaning is that one is not purified by a purification of all obscurations together with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*).
Then, what is that purification which is the result and is obtained through a path cultivated over a long period of time?
How is it that "it was not so before"?
Because [the mind] is by its very nature entirely pure;
therefore, he says: "of objects," and so forth.

The objects are the senses and so forth, because they serve as the objective supports for their respective cognitions; the meaning is that the supreme bliss, which is self-evident to them, is the ultimate reality (paramārtha).
Why is this so? He says: "Because of its pure nature."

And they are pure because they consist of the experience of emptiness, by virtue of being the self-awareness of the nature of the emptiness of duality; and they are entities because they consist of the arising of the mind. Thus, their nature is purity. Their reality (*tattva*) is that state [of purity]; therefore, because all objects of knowledge are non-different from the self-cognizable bliss which is the fruit consisting of the commonality of the experience of emptiness, the meaning is that, through the aspect of emptiness, suchness itself is the reality of all entities.
Through the aspect of the experience of emptiness, there is the circle of Yoginīs;
the variety of experiences of the distinctions among objects of focus is the variety of Yoginīs; the reality of each of these objects of focus is as follows. (3)

in the internal enclosure (adhyātmapuṭa), the limbs of the hyāsa are always present—sadā hyāsāṅga; with the external [enclosure]—śāṃ—gha;
it is accomplished—sidhyate—ka; they are accomplished—sidhyante—kha, gha; they are perfected—siddhante—ga.
Cha: each [of these] attains purity; Gha:
subsequently, the outer enclosure.

Bhūcarīkā—ga.

Khecarī is known as *ka*; it is also known as *gha*. It is called *prokṣata* in *ga*, and *pakṣata* in *gha*.
These two are established—*sthitāvaitau* (kha), *sthitāvet* (ga).
*Dvidevatī* (ka, ga, gha, jha), *devatiḥ* (kha), *devatīḥ* (cha), *devati* (ja).
*Gorī* (ka, gha), *gori* (kha, ga).
Always explained—ka, gha; always renowned—ga. Caurya—ga;
proclaimed—ga, gha.
They are proclaimed as "ga," and so forth; regarding this "ga," he says "ga."
Dvidevatī is known as Sparśavajrā; Bhūcarī is proclaimed from the element of touch, while Khecarī arises from the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Indeed, through the constant purification of these, the practitioners of reality (tattvayogins) attain accomplishment.
The emptiness of the arms is purity; the feet are pure through the conquest of Māra;
the faces are purified by the eight liberations; and the eyes of the holders of the three vajras are pure.
Earth is known as Pukkasī, the water element is remembered as Śavarī;
fire should be known as Caṇḍālinī, and wind is proclaimed as Ḍombī.
With the words beginning "of the arms," [the author] explains the purification of the arms and other features of sixteen-armed Hevajra:
the reality that is the purification of the sixteen arms consists of the sixteen emptinesses (*śūnyatā*).

Namely: internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātmabahirdhā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-dispersal (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*). The meaning is that these very [emptinesses] are made into arms.

"From the purification of Māra" means the four feet, which signify the destruction of the four Māras. "Of the faces" refers to *mukhānām*. "By the three-vajra-holder" means by the vajras of body, speech, and mind;
the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used here because of the intended sense of distinction (*bhedavivakṣāyām*).
"Earth," and so forth; the meaning is that the purification of earth and the other elements consists of Pukkasī and the others.
Sparśya—ka. gha;
Bhūcarī—ka. kha. ga; Khecarī—ka. gha.
*sabāhyāsām* — *ka*, *gha*;
*sidhyante* — *ka*, *ga*, *gha*, *cha*, *jha*; *sidhyate* — *kha*; *stānyatā* — *gha*.
*visuddhi*—kha;
*caraṇo*—ka, *caraṇau*—jha;
*māravisudhi*—kha, *māraviśuddhitaḥ*—ga.
*mukhāṣṭāpimukhena*—ka; *mukheneṣṭavimokṣa*—kha; *mukhanyaṣṭā*—ga; *sukhāṣṭāvimokṣa*—gha. *śuddhitri*—ka; *sudhitrivajrināṃ*—kha; *vajrīnāṃ*—ga; *śuddhitrivajrināṃ*—gha. *pṛthivi*—kha.
Pukkasi-ga;

Ḍombī—ka, ga;
Prakṛttitā—ka; Prakīrtitā—kha, ga; Prakīrtitāḥ—gha.
Of the purifications—ga; great emptiness—ga;
emptiness of emptiness—ga.
Emptiness of characteristics—ga;
emptiness of intrinsic nature and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—ka kha;
as bliss—ga.
The source of all pleasures.
In the *Vajratantre*, [the ninth chapter on purification], the *Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī* states: Nairātmyā is designated as hatred; Rāgavajrī is passion; Vajraḍākinī is envy; Vāriyoginī is slander;
and Guptagaurikā is greed.
Moha-vajrā is likewise said to be the purification of hatred and the other afflictions;
by means of her, the aggregates are purified from the perspective of the generation stage.
By whatever means the world is bound, by those very same means one should release that bondage.
The world is deluded; it does not know reality. Deprived of reality, it shall not attain accomplishment.
"Hatred," and so forth; "the one with the wheel" (cakrī) refers to the lord of the wheel.
The meaning is that the fivefold [set] beginning with selflessness is the purification of the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as hatred and the rest.
For this very reason, he says: "the purification of hatred and the rest.
By this [phrase], "by the pentad beginning with selflessness" is meant.
"The aggregate" refers to the remaining aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which means the pentad beginning with the eye.
The purity of the mental faculty (*manas*) is also non-self (*nairātmya*);
thus, in the context of the theory of origination,
the purification of the various [perceptions] and so forth has been explained.
Regarding the stage of the arisen (*utpannakrama*), he states that [the practice] has a single flavor with the words "by which, however" (*yena tu*).

The meaning is: by means of whatever form and so forth the world is bound, by those very same means I release the bondage; it is not through the cultivation of the forms of deities and the like. He explains how the world is bound with the words "the world," and so forth.
He is deluded; he conceptualizes a non-existent duality.
He does not perceive reality; he does not know the true, non-dual state.
Devoid of reality, he is lacking in the cultivation of the ultimate truth.
One does not attain accomplishment or liberation.
- I am known as Vajrī out of hatred—ka. gha; Vajri—kha; Vajrā—ga. cha. ja. bho; Cakrī—jha. hepaṃmuva;
Rāga—ṅaca. ṭa; Yoginī—ka. kha. gha.
