*paiśunyā*—ka. ga. gha; *paisunyā*—kha; *paiśūnyaṃ*—ṭa;
*guptigaurikā*—ka; *guptigaurikāḥ*—gha.
Mogha—ṅaca. ṭa. Tathatā—ga. Viśodhanam—ga.
It is purified—*ka*; they are purified—*ga*.
By this, the aggregate (*skandha*) is purified; the arising of the aggregate—*ka*.
But by which—*ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*.
The three worlds are oppressed—ka, ga; the world is bound—kha; it binds the world—gha.
There is none—ka;
there is none—gha.
Release from bondage—ka, kha, ga, gha; release, release—ka, kha; release—ga; you are released—gha; O world—ka.
*mucyati*—ka, kha, gha;
*vartinas tattva*—ka; *vetti na tvaṃ*—kha; *vettir na*—gha;
*vivarjita*—ka, kha; *tattvamukhaṃ vivarjita*—gha.
I shall not obtain success—ka; I shall not obtain success—kha, gha; I shall not obtain success—ga; I shall obtain [it]—cha, jha. End of the cycle—ga.
Mistress of the cycle—bho.
In the case of the gradual method— O!
[the purity is] manifold, etc.— Ga and Ca.

Therefore, I consider the world to be of a pure nature, neither smell, nor sound, nor form, nor taste, nor purity of mind; neither touch, nor mental objects (dharmas), but pure by virtue of the purity of all things.

The Ninth Chapter on Purity: Smell, sound, and form are neither *ka* nor *kha*; taste is *ka kha ga gha*. The purity of the mind—[it is] pure (*viśuddhā*)—*ka*, *gha*; [it is] pure (*viśuddhām*)—*kha*. I contemplate the world as the pure Great Vajra Gaurī—*ka*; I contemplate the world as the nature of Vajragaurī—*kha*; I contemplate the world as the pure nature of Vajrarāga—*ga*; I contemplate the world as Mahāvajragaurī—*gha*.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Purity," in the *Śrīvajranairātmyatantra*—(ka); the ninth chapter on purity—(kha); the ninth chapter—(ga, gha). (Regarding the variants: "How, O Noble One?"—(ga); "Mind-consciousness is the grasper of the six"—(ga, ca).
Bhava-ga; naibhāvatāpi-ga; sarvaviśuddhi-ga.
The two principal ones—ga;
the reality—ka;
there is not—ka, kha, ga, ca.
The Chapter on Consecration: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mandala in its proper sequence;
I shall also explain the procedure by which the disciple is consecrated. (1)
The yogi, first identifying himself with the deity, should purify the earth;
having diligently transformed it into a vajra with the syllable *hūṃ*, he should thereafter draw the maṇḍala.
In a garden, in a secluded place, in the dwellings of Bodhisattvas, or in the center of a maṇḍala hall, one should draw the excellent maṇḍala. (3)
Either with a divine streak of powder, or with a medium one, or with powders made of the five precious gems, or with rice and so forth. || 4 ||
And so forth.
"Yathā" means without error; "krama" means the procedure (*vidhi*).
That by which the disciple is consecrated is also a procedure; this is to be connected with the phrase "it shall be explained. || 1 ||
"Consisting of the deity" means being established in union with one's own deity.
"Having made [them] vajra with *hūṃ*" refers to the Bodhisattvas, such as Hevajra and others, according to the sequence taught in the Chapter on Deities. (2)
*Āgāra* means a house. That by which something is written is a *lekha*; it is both dust (*rajas*) and a *lekha*, hence *rajo-lekha*.
Furthermore, that [dust] is divine for superior jewels, while it is middling for inferior ones.
"By means of rice and so forth" refers to items such as śāli rice and chalk. || 3-4 ||
Tenth: A mandala measuring three cubits should be constructed; according to the *Vajrapañjikā*, it should be made three thumb-breadths larger than that.
Therein, the divine Vidyā born of the five families should be introduced.
Alternatively, whatever [mudrā] is obtained, even one sixteen years old, that mudrā should be served for as long as she remains possessed of *śukra*. (6)
Having covered the mouth of the mudrā as well as the mouth of the means (upāya),
one should pour into the mouth of the disciple that which has arisen there through their union.
And in that very state, one should act with equal flavor within the sphere of the disciple;
from self-reflexive awareness, knowledge arises, devoid of the cognition of self and other. (8)
"Three," and so forth; the meaning is that it exceeds [the previous measurement] by three thumb-breadths.
This concludes the brief indication of the mandala.
Its detailed description will follow later.
Introducing the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), he says: "The vidyās," and so forth.
"To be entered" means they are to be caused to enter.
"Divine" means supreme.
Alternatively, "if" he is unable [to do so], then he should introduce another woman as she may be obtained.
"Sixteen years old" is specified because of the preeminence of youth.
And "in the same way," even if he is unable, [he may introduce] one who is twenty years old.
The binding of the mouth is for the purpose of preventing both from seeing. 6-7.
"Within the range of the disciple" means that which is to be personally experienced by the disciple.
If one asks, "What is the point of that?
he replies: "Because it is self-experienced."

From that very cultivation of the equality of self and others arises "knowledge"—that is, the result denoted by the term *mahābodhi* (Great Enlightenment). The underlying sense is that since it is impossible to cultivate what has not been previously perceived, its accomplishment would otherwise be untenable.
That very knowledge, which constitutes the result, is further qualified by the words "one's own and others," and so forth.
Apprehension through the distinction of self and other; that which is devoid of this. || 8 ||
In the Vajra Tantra, it is equal to space, stainless, empty, and supreme, consisting of both existence and non-existence;
it is the perfect union of wisdom and means, and the blending of passion and the absence of passion. (9)
He alone is the life-breath of living beings; He alone is the supreme syllable.
He alone is all-pervading; He alone is established within every body. (10)

"Equal to space" (*khasama*) means that it is manifested as having a single flavor (*samarasa*), through the appearance of both self and other in the form of a luminosity that is non-manifesting like space.
"Stainless" (*viraja*) is due to the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Empty" (*śūnya*) is due to the setting of the appearances of the grasped object (*grāhya*).

Existence (*bhāva*) is the body of the yogin, while non-existence (*abhāva*) consists of his very sensations and so forth, which are the forms of the subject; he is described as such because these two [existence and non-existence] have him as their self, since even they are manifested by that very same nature of light (*prakāśa*), due to the subsiding of internal distinctions of form.

"Supreme" (*param*) means absolute (*kevala*), because only that [light] is manifested. Alternatively, "supreme" means the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not the ultimate reality.
Skillful means is the experience of the equality of oneself with all sentient beings, which is compassion;

wisdom is the vision of the emptiness of duality regarding all phenomena. These two are intermingled, because they manifest as a single flavor—the nature of luminosity—whether toward sentient beings or non-sentient things. They are likewise intermingled in passion and non-passion, for they manifest in that very same way.
In that regard, non-dual gnosis and its co-emergent great bliss are passion; suchness is the absence of passion. || 9 ||
"Prāṇa" means the living soul (jīva), because it is devoid of life when separated from that [breath].
He is the supreme syllable (paramākṣara) because he is without beginning or end.
He is all-pervading (vyāpī) because all phenomena are mere cognition (vijñaptimātra).
"He is established in all bodies" because living bodies are presided over by consciousness. || 10 ||

The Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī states: "He alone is that Great Vital Breath; he alone is that which consists of the world. Existence and non-existence arise from him, as do all other things whatsoever. (11)
The ancient Lord Puruṣa is everything—consciousness and form;
he is the Self, the individual soul, existence, time, and indeed the person (pudgala). He is the intrinsic nature of all beings, abiding in the form of Māyā. || 12 ||
"Existence" refers to the body; "non-existence" refers to sensation and so forth. "The others" refers to the six sense-faculties.
"Those which are" refers to external existents, both stable and moving. (11)

The followers of the Upaniṣads [maintain] that everything is consciousness; the Sāṃkhyas [hold] that the person (puruṣa) is of the nature of consciousness; some Proponents of the Person (pudgalavādins) say that it is the "person" (pudgala) because of its repeated dissolution into the various states of existence; the Proponents of God (īśvaravādins) say that the person is the Lord (īśvara), whose knowledge is both eternal and non-eternal; and the Proponents of the Self (ātmavādins) say that it is the self alone that is born, lives, dies, is bound, and is liberated.

Thus, the Digambaras say "it is the *jīva*"; the proponents of *sattva* say "it is *sattva*"; the proponents of time (*kālavādins*) say "time destroys all beings"; others, the proponents of *pudgala*, say "it is the *pudgala*—it is filled by *karmas* and it dissolves precisely through their exhaustion.
All entities are established both by worldly consensus and by scripture.
Their intrinsic nature is well-established; they exist conventionally, appearing in various ways according to the distinctions of conceptual construction.
And "having an illusory form" means as if creating various forms for oneself. || 12 ||

In the Vajra Tantra, the first is mere bliss (ānanda), supreme bliss (paramānanda) is from the second; the third is called the cessation-bliss (viramānanda), and the fourth is known as the innate (sahaja). || 13 ||
Having heard this, all the wise ones, beginning with Vajragarbha, were struck with supreme amazement; they fainted and fell to the ground. (14)

The world is the joy of initial bliss (*prathamānanda*), and the world is likewise the supreme joy (*paramānanda*); the world is also the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), yet the innate joy (*sahajānanda*) does not exist within these three. (15)
Thus [it is said].
"First, mere bliss" means bliss without distinction.
"From the number two" means the second.
"Named cessation" means the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*); the short vowel is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

Thus, that which is to be made the object of the disciple's experience is innate bliss (sahajānanda) itself, designated by such terms as "of equal flavor" (samarasa) and so forth, and distinguished by its various moments. || 13 ||
Astonishment and doubt. || 14 ||
To the question "How, then, has it been attained?", he says "The first," and so forth.
The world-form (*jagadrūpa*) is so called because it is the object of worldly cognition; its connection is with "and indeed supreme bliss" (*paramānandaścaiva*).
The particle *eva* (indeed) serves the purpose of restriction.
Bliss alone, of three kinds, is to be known by the world in its successive order;

beyond that, because there is an absence of bliss, the innate (*sahaja*) does not exist. This means that the innate neither exists nor is it experienced within these very three, because it is of a different character.
The word "iti" belongs to the compiler; the meaning is that they had thus fallen into doubt. || 15 ||
The Lord Hevajra, the singular embodiment of all Buddhas, spoke this divine commentary on the *Hevajratantra* in order to dispel the doubts of Vajragarbha for the sake of his enlightenment. (16)
Neither passion nor dispassion, and no middle state is perceived;
by the very avoidance of these three, it is called innate awakening (sahajabodhi). || 17 ||
The verse beginning with "Bhagavān" refers to the compiler [of the text], who is of one body with all Buddhas— meaning his physical form is undivided—
and is called *apanaya* because by means of this [verse], [the obstacles] are removed (*apanīyate*).
Because it is supreme, it is "divine";
"for enlightenment" means for the sake of certainty. || 16 ||
What does he say?
"No," and so forth.
Passion (*rāga*) is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), because it is the longing for the fruit about to arise; therefore, it is not perceived in the form of full awakening (*sambodhi*).
Dispassion (*virāga*) is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), because it involves the destruction of the fruit; therefore, even that is not perceived in the form of perfect awakening (*sambodhi*).
The intermediate state of bliss (*madhyamā sukhāvasthā*) is the first bliss (*prathamānanda*);
however, it is merely the intermediate bliss (*madhyamānanda*) alone, according to the statement in the *Hevajratantra* (8th chapter).
How is it middling?

Because of its inferiority; for in the world, even that which is devoid of longing is called "middling," such as "middling news" or a "middling body. That [first bliss] also, though consisting of the first bliss, is not perceived as the form of middling awakening (*sambodhi*), because passion and dispassion are [the nature of] awakening due to having the fruit as their object, but it is not middling awakening because it has contact as its object.
And so, it will be stated in the sixteenth [chapter]: "Neither beginning, nor end, nor middle"—the meaning is that there is no beginning, no end, and no middle.
Precisely by the exclusion of these three moments, the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is fully realized as being distinct from them;
for it arises eternally as its own inherent fruit, and that is called enlightenment (*sambodhi*).
Since "perfect awakening" (*sambodhi*) is defined as the correct and direct realization of the fruit, how can it be considered fully understood by this much alone?
For there is the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), which is the longing for the fruit about to arise, and the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*), characterized by the destruction of the fruit.
Therefore, it is well known that he resides precisely between these two;

however, as for his definition, it is said to be "well-explained by the very words 'innate' (*sahaja*) and so forth, through the avoidance of the three"—but that is incorrect. For in the *Vajra-tantra* it says: "Alternatively, he is the essence of all, or else he is devoid of all [the others]; in the beginning of the *virama*, he is characterized by being devoid of the three joys (*ānanda*). (10th chapter, verse 18)
For the Dharmakāya is indeed without beginning or end; it is perfect enlightenment, and that itself is innate bliss. || 17 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "Alternatively" (*athavā*):

"Alternatively" means that by one way of explanation, it is "of the nature of all" (*sarvātmaka*); "that very [state]" means that innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is indeed of the nature of all, for it is present throughout the three joys (*ānanda*), in the sense that it is common to them through its generic quality of bliss and through its generic experience of the emptiness of duality.

"Alternatively" means that by another way of explanation, it is "devoid of all," being excluded from the three joys because it does not conform to them by virtue of its own self-cognizable specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
Relying precisely upon this qualification, it was stated that "by the avoidance of three";
therefore, this which was said, beginning with "virama," is not incorrect.
Is that which precedes *viramānanda* indeed *paramānanda*? No; he says: "devoid of the three joys."
The meaning is effectively stated as "above supreme bliss" (*paramānandād ūrdhvam*).
For it will be said in the sixteenth [chapter]: "The end of the supreme is the middle *virama*.
This means that what follows supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) is the "middle" in relation to *viramānanda*.

In the thirteenth [chapter], however, he will state quite clearly: "I am of the nature of innate bliss (sahajānanda), beginning with the cessation (virama) and ending with the supreme (parama). By all of this, the following is meant: supreme bliss (paramānanda) is the preparatory stage of that [innate bliss]; cessation-bliss (viramānanda), on the other hand, is a conceptual construction (vikalpa) belonging to the subsequent recollection; between those two is the fundamental, objectless, non-conceptual (niṣprapañca) happiness, which is innate bliss (sahajānanda).
In the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*, first it appears like a cloud; once accomplished, it suddenly becomes like an illusion;
it appears like a dream, as if there were no distinction between sleeping and waking.
He says that when the characteristic of non-duality is established, the practitioner of mudrā-yoga attains accomplishment:
"The Teacher [describes] the mandala as four-cornered and brilliantly radiant."

When innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) has been thus correctly identified, for one who meditates upon that very state, there gradually arise four meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) known as "cloud-like," "illusion-like," "dream-like," and "dream-awakened. He describes these very states in a verse beginning with "firstly," and so on:

as long as the innate [bliss] being cultivated together with the cultivation of union does not become manifest, it appears as if covered by clouds; the meaning here is that it shines like the full moon obscured by clouds.
But when it becomes manifest, then it is perfected.
Once it is accomplished, it becomes like an illusion; because it manifests directly through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*) created by the mind, thereafter it suddenly appears like a dream.

For the yogi who has entered the sleep of yoga (*yoganidrā*), having abandoned the conceptualization of union and meditating upon that alone according to the instruction, it manifests suddenly before his very eyes.
Thereafter, it appears as if there is no distinction between sleep and waking; the meaning is that it is not differentiated from sleep and waking.
How is it not differentiated from waking?
Because [phenomena] such as the embrace of the two bodies and the perception [of objects] are possible.
How is it not different from a dream?
Because even though those [objects] exist, they are not perceived; rather, that [reality] becomes manifest through mere innate cultivation (*sahaja-bhāvanā*).
Thus, regarding how the yogi achieves perfection through the accomplishment of the four concentrations, he says: "Non-differentiation," and so forth.

Non-differentiation (*abheda*) is the lack of distinction between dream and waking; by that, there is the characteristic of innate cultivation (*sahaja-bhāvanā*). Through that, there is accomplishment (*siddhi*), which is the direct realization of the innate (*sahaja-sākṣātkriyā*). Established in that state, the yogi achieves perfection through the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. Of what sort is he?
The practitioner of mudrā (mudrā-yogin), being endowed with the external vidyā that has been mastered,

is the primary cause for the attainment of the characteristics [of] Mahāmudrā-siddhi; and since the yoga of mudrā is its auxiliary cause, this indeed constitutes the commitment (samaya) in this context.
The accomplishment of the Knowledge-Man (*vidyāpuruṣa*) and the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) cannot occur without the Family-Knowledge (*kulavidyā*).
[The Tenth Chapter: The Consecration] The great, blazing four-gated [palace], adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces.
It was adorned with variegated garlands and yak-tail fans, beautified by eight pillars, secured with diamond threads, and graced with various flowers.
Incense, a lamp, and likewise perfume, together with the eight jars and other such items.
And they should have sprouting tips with their necks covered by cloth;
one should offer the Vijaya [vessel], encircled by the five jewels, in the east.

The wise practitioner should mark out [the mandala] with a new, well-prepared, correctly measured, and beautiful thread, according to the form of his own chosen deity. He should recite one hundred thousand mantras for the Lord of the Mandala and ten thousand for the deities of the retinue. With the very mantra previously mentioned, the learned one should purify the ground.
However, she is not desired in the first three samādhis, because at that time she is a cause of distraction; thus,
the consecrations must be bestowed in this manner,
and in this way the practitioner of the mudrā-yoga attains accomplishment.

For this purpose—meaning for the consecration of disciples and for the accomplishment of attainments—he said "the mandala"; that is to say, he taught both the commitment mandala (*samaya-maṇḍala*) and the practice mandala (*sādhana-maṇḍala*). The qualifiers of the mandala are "four-cornered" and so forth.
Everything is easily understood.
One should place [the syllable] "dadyāt" [therein].
With the words "of the Lord of the Mandala" and so forth, he describes the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*).
"Of the mandala-deities" means for each of the mandala-deities individually;
"by the previously mentioned [mantra]" refers to *rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
One should cause the offering (*bali*) to be presented there with the mantra beginning with the letter *A*,
as well as the protection (*rakṣā*) as previously instructed, just as it was in the meditative visualization (*dhyāna*).
The initiations that have been revealed should be bestowed according to the rule within one's own maṇḍala;
and the worship and veneration are exactly as they have been described here.
Having drawn a pure double-layered circle, one should likewise draw the [deities] beginning with Gaurī; furthermore, one should draw a curved knife (kartrikā) in the east, the south, and the west.
In the north, the southeast, the southwest, and likewise the northwest, as well as in the northeast, below, and above, according to what has been described.
Assuming the majestic posture of Vajrasattva and placing the feet in the *ālīḍha* stance, the Maṇḍala Master should enter [the maṇḍala] through the yoga of the two-armed Hevajra.

"Previously" means before the purification. "From the mantra beginning with the letter A" refers to [the visualization of] the enclosure, the cage, and so forth, according to the rule "The letter A is the mouth. And "here" means even in the case of what is to be drawn.
26 || "And the request for worship" refers to the Guru; "here" means in the written support-maṇḍala.

27. "Firm mind" refers to Vajrasattva; "made manifest" (*kṛtāṭopa*) means made manifest by him. "Assumed the *ālīḍha* posture" means he has taken up the *ālīḍha* stance. "Of the feet" means by means of the shanks. "Maṇḍala" means a circle.

30. Just as it was ignited and just as it was instructed, for the sake of sharpening, one should draw two circles and within that well-defined mandala, having drawn two circles, one should not [draw] Gaurī and the others; rather, one should then draw Sugaurī and the others. Then, in the south, west, northwest, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, and likewise in the upper and lower directions—just as they were described, both above and below, just as they were described above and below—one should indeed [place] Vajrasattva with feet in the *mālinī* (striding) posture and [the consort] in the *pratyālīḍha* posture. Having entered the conduct of the Maṇḍalācārya, possessing the yoga of the two-armed Heruka, from the purification of the ground, the syllable OṂ is [the seed]. In the *Vajratantro* [Abhiṣekapaṭala, Tenth]: Having bathed, pure, with limbs scented with fragrance, adorned with variegated ornaments, assuming a majestic display through the sound of "HŪṂ-HŪṂ," and terrifying through the sound of "HĪ-HĪ."

31. Afterwards, the reality (tattva) was fully explained as pure and consisting of the nature of gnosis (jñāna). Through the purification of saṃsāra, there is no distinction whatsoever in supreme bliss; there is neither an entity (bhāva) nor a subject of existence (bhāvaka).
There is neither conflict, nor the grasped, nor the grasper; there is no flesh, no blood, no excrement, no urine, no vomit, no delusion, and no purity or sanctity.

33. Subsequently, the term "Reality" (tattva) refers to that which is comprised within the meditative absorption (samādhi) beyond syllables for those practicing the generation stage (utpattikrama). For those practicing the completion stage (utpannakrama), however, that very body of yoga is merely the conventional rule (samaya); it is pure because the stains of causal signs have set. It is "consisting of gnosis" (jñānarūpin), meaning its form is non-dual gnosis. Regarding the phrase "by means of the purification of cyclic existence" (saṃsāravyavadānena): the sense is that where there is gnosis, there is no distinction between affliction and purification; this is because the diversity of appearances that create differentiation has subsided.

32 || To clarify this very point, he states two verses beginning with *parama* and so forth. *Paramarati* (supreme delight) is supreme wisdom (*paramā prajñā*), which is non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*). Within that, the object of meditation (*bhāvya*)—non-dual representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*)—does not appear as something other than the meditating mind (*bhāvaka*). Nor does the meditating mind appear as something other than that object of meditation, because both manifest without distinction. Furthermore, there is no "body" (*vigraha*); for the yogin, even his own body does not appear. There is no "graspable" (*grāhya*), meaning external bodies, sense-faculties, and stationary objects do not appear. There is no "grasper" (*grāhaka*), meaning his own sense-faculties do not appear. When these do not appear, the self (*ātman*) and so forth certainly do not appear either. Consequently, there is no disgust toward things such as excrement, nor is there delusion regarding the self or what belongs to the self. "Neither purity nor holiness" means that there is no sprinkling with water and the like, nor indeed does water and such appear at all. This is the meaning.

33. Pure, pure, with fragrant limbs, adorned with various and wonderful ornaments, having performed the non-dual, assuming a majestic and terrifying form, proclaiming the reality (*tattva*) through the sounds *hī*, *hīṃ*, *hīḥ*, and *hīḥ*. It is the embodiment of knowledge, beyond even the mind and the mental. It is neither non-existence nor existence; it is neither the state of being (*bhāva*) nor the agent of being (*bhāvaka*); it is neither the object of meditation (*bhāvya*) nor the meditator (*bhāvaka*); it is neither existence (*bhāva*) nor the agent of existence (*bhāvaka*). There is no physical body (*vigraha*), nor is there a grasper (*grāhaka*), nor an object of grasping (*grāhya*), nor a grasper; there is no object of grasping, nor a grasper. There is no blood, no blood, no urine, no excrement; no urine, no excrement, no urine, and no ghee. No delusion (*moha*), no ghee, no delusion; again, no woman, no water, no delusion, and no disgust (*ghṛṇa*). No purity, no limb, no disgust, no delusion, no vomiting, no delusion—this is the pure activity. [This is] the *Vajrapañjikā-muktāvalī*: no passion (*rāga*), no hatred (*dveṣa*), no delusion (*moha*), no envy (*īrṣyā*), no slander (*paiśunya*), no pride (*māna*), and nothing visible. Thus spoke the one named Vajragarbha: "Why would the body, which consists of the elements, be [real] by its own nature? For from the very beginning, it is pure and devoid of intrinsic nature."

35. Passion and the other afflictions do not exist for them, because their basis (*āśraya*), their object (*ālambana*), and their improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) are not perceived. Having thus explained the antidote to the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), he speaks of the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) with the words beginning "the visible" (*na dṛśyam*). The visible, which is the knowable, does not appear. Since there is neither an entity (*bhāva*) nor an agent of existence (*bhāvaka*), neither conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) nor the word that is the cause of conceptual construction appears. There is no enemy and no friend; that is to say, neither a bad friend (*pāpamitra*)—such as a non-Buddhist teacher (*tīrthika*) and so forth—nor a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)—such as the Guru, the Buddha, and so forth—appears. To the question "What is this?", he says: "waveless" (*nistaraṅga*), and so forth. Waves are conceptual constructions because of their instability; due to their cessation, it is waveless. It is called "innate" (*sahaja*) because the innate is the nature (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena. However, in this context, because it has the innate as its object, it is infinite gnosis (*jñāna*) free from the appearance of the innate. It is "variegated" (*citra*) in the sense of being of various kinds—the manifestation of names and signs—and because that has set, it is "of a single flavor" (*ekarasa*).
34. From touch, by way of the property of solidity, earth arises there; and from the liquid form of the bodhicitta, the water element itself is born.
38. Origin: From friction, fire (tejas) is produced; from movement, wind (vāyu) is proclaimed [to arise].

39 || The meaning of the latter part [of the verse] is that the body is pure in its form as waveless radiance (*nistaraṅga-prakāśa-rūpa*), not in its form as perceived by the ignorant (*bāla-grāhya*). Some maintain that even in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), the body is the supreme reality (*paramaṃ tattva*) because it consists of the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) subsumed within the four joys (*catur-ānanda*).
36 To refute that, he asks again: "O Blessed One," and so forth.

The aggregate (skandha) is the body; in what manner is it composed of the great elements? The intended meaning is that it is precisely by way of consisting of the four joys. "The Blessed One"—having understood this intention—the Vajra-holder [acts] "from touch," such as from embracing and so forth.
That which is being touched, namely hardness itself, is the property (*dharma*), the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*);
by that [characteristic], "therein" means in the moment of bliss (*ānandakṣaṇa*).
And "from non-existence" refers to the moment of innate bliss (*sahajānandakṣaṇa*).
"From friction" refers to the moment of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*);
"from going" refers to the moment of cessation-bliss (*viramānanda*). In the *Hevajra-pañjikā Muktāvalī*: "Bliss is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), moving and surrounded by the five."
Therefore, that bliss which is called reality is not a great element, since bliss [arises] from it.
That which is produced in co-nascence is proclaimed as "co-nate" (sahaja);
its intrinsic nature is declared to be the co-nate, the single vow of all aspects.
Regarding "bliss": among the four types of bliss, how is space the element of bliss? Because it is formless;
[the body] is a mass enveloped and constructed by these five great elements.
Therefore, the phrase "consisting of the great elements" (*mahābhautika*) is for the sake of what follows.

When this has been said, others might think: "The Blessed One has stated our own position; by the use of the word 'great' (*maha*), the meaning is that the Great Being (*mahad-bhūta*) is the Great Element (*mahā-bhūta*), the supreme reality. To refute that, the Blessed One himself says: "Therefore," and so forth.

"It is not called reality" means that this is not the primary reality; it is said that even the [four] blisses (*ānanda*) are not reality, so how much less so their innate [bliss] (*sahaja*)? Why is this? He says: "Because bliss is a great element (*mahābhūta*)."

This is the intended meaning: here the word *bhūta* does not have the sense of "reality" (*tattva*); what then? It means "arisen" (*utpanna*). And arising is neither causeless nor from a single cause; thus, the word *bhūta* has the sense of "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*), for that which is produced by causes and conditions coming together is "conditioned. And whatever is conditioned is impermanent. Furthermore, the prefix *mahā-* has the sense of excellence (*prakarṣa*).
Therefore, because it is accomplished with extreme effort and is extremely impermanent, this is the meaning of the term "great element" (*mahābhūta*) in this context.
And since this pleasure is a great element, for that very reason it is not the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Is it then the case that innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is also being censured by this? True, it is censured.
If that is so, why was it previously described at length? It was previously described as a general "innate" (*sahaja*) by way of being a counter-example to the "supreme innate" (*paramasahaja*).
For there are two kinds of innate: the occasional and the eternal;
that which is eternal is the supreme.
That alone is the supreme reality because of its inexhaustibility and immutability.
To explain this, he says "by the two innate," and so forth;
that is, by the two innate wisdom and means, and not by external ones.
"That which is bliss" means that innate [bliss]; "that" refers to the supreme innate [state].
The yogi becomes the means of compassion through the separation from causes, by means of the mudrā.
"Bodhicitta is defined as the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion.
To the question "Why so?", he says: "Its own nature," and so forth.

It is called "its own nature" (*svabhāvam*) because its arising occurs from itself—that is, from the very moment of the mind that serves as the material cause (*upādāna*), independently of any subsequent moment.

That which is such is the innate (*sahaja*); because it arises together with each successive moment of consciousness until the end of space, he asks "Which one? and says "of all phenomena," and so forth. It is "possessing all aspects" (*sarvākāra*) because all phenomena appear within it as mere appearances. It is "one" and "of a single flavor" because appearances subsumed under duality have set. It is "face-to-face," "excellent," and "supreme. As it has been said: "The bliss that is tranquil, immovable, supreme, sovereign, equal to the unequaled, and free from conceptual construction."
It is true that it is both excellent and singular, and it is both restraint and restraint in every aspect; thus it is called "the single restraint in all its aspects.
Furthermore, as for what wisdom and method are, he says they are "innate," beginning with the word "compassion" (kṛpā).

The contemplation of the equality of oneself with all sentient beings is compassion (*karuṇā*); that is the skillful means (*upāya*). And that practitioner (*yogin*), because he possesses the nature of a yogi, is the seal (*mudrā*), which is wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, that practitioner’s contemplation of the mere manifestation of all phenomena as they truly are is wisdom (*prajñā*), as previously described.

How is that? Through separation from causes; "causes" refers to the conditions, namely the appearances comprised within duality. By their separation—that is, by their disappearance—the meaning is "having rendered them appearanceless.

These two, wisdom and means, are innate (*sahaja*), being perfected through the power of cultivation; furthermore, they do not depend on further effort. From these two arises the innate *sarvākāraikasaṃvara* (the single vow of all aspects).
To clarify that very non-referential *bodhicitta*, he says: "Emptiness," and so forth.

The experience of the emptiness of duality regarding all phenomena is non-appearance, which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Through emptiness itself is the experience of the equality of self in all sentient beings; compassion (*karuṇā*) is the union with innate bliss. The mind that is distinct from, mixed with, or conjoined with these two is the *bodhicitta*.

This is that supreme reality, pure, having the nature of gnosis, the essence of Mahāvajradhara, and the object of realization. Just as it is in the case of the [ultimate] meaning, so too should devotion be practiced toward the illustrative example, because it is the means for its accomplishment and because it is the pledge (*samaya*). || 42 ||
In the *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*: "There is no recitation of mantra, no austerity, no fire-oblation, no mandala-substance, and no mandala;

yet that is the recitation of mantra, that is the austerity, that is the fire-oblation, that is the mandala-substance, and that is the mandala. In brief, it consists of the assembly of the mind. (43–44)

The tenth chapter on consecration. Now, as to whether one who practices the yoga of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*) should perform mantra recitation and so forth while meditating upon this [mandala], or not—it is said: "Not by mantra," and so on.
"Mantra" refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) and others; its "recitation" (*japa*) is the muttering [of it].
"Austerity" (*tapas*) consists of abstaining from what is blameworthy, such as changing one's clothes three times [a day] and so forth.
The offering of clarified butter and other substances into the fire is *homa*;
the deities such as Hevajra and Vajragaurī are the members of the mandala (*maṇḍaleyāḥ*);
and the mandala is the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*).
If it is argued that, in that case, the fruit of mantra-recitation and so forth would not belong to that yogin, he says "sa" and so on.

"Sa" refers to that very *bodhicitta*. For it is as follows: because it contemplates the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*) and protects the world, it is *mantra*; because it is continuous, it is *jāpa* (recitation); because of its union with meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*), untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*), and compassion, there is the cessation of faults; for this very reason, the changing of the three garments constitutes the "threefold bathing," due to the removal of the stains of afflictions, conceptual constructions, and signs.

Because it has the nature of the fire of non-conceptual wisdom (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*) and because it burns away the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), that very thing is the *homa*.

Bodhicitta itself is Hevajra; that same [Bodhicitta], because its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*), is the circle of Yoginīs (*yoginīcakra*). Therefore, those are the deities of the maṇḍala (*maṇḍaleya*);
their support is meditative absorption (*samādhi*), since it is the cause of their stability, and that is a property of the mind (*cittadharma*). Therefore, that is also the maṇḍala. (43)
The verse beginning with "In brief" (*samāsataḥ*) consists of a single line; by means of it, he concludes the meaning of the preceding verse.

"In brief" means that, according to the principle already stated, through the inclusion of all practices such as the recitation of mantras, one should become the embodiment of the mental assembly (*cittasamāja*); this is the remainder [of the sense].

The "mind" (*citta*) as previously described is the *bodhicitta*; that itself is the "assembly" (*samāja*), the merging into a single flavor of all phenomena. The yogi should become of that very nature, because no self apart from it is perceived.
This is his supreme consecration (*abhiṣeka*), since by means of this, the stains of afflictions, conceptual constructions, and signs are directly washed away.
The chapter indicating the consecration is the "Consecration Chapter. 44.

The tenth chapter, on Initiation, in the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti. The eleventh chapter: On Vision and the Manifest Enlightenment of Vajragarbha. The gaze directed toward the forehead is said to always cause falling [into a swoon]; the gaze resting on the left is for subjugation. The gaze is like a doll, with two [fingers] on the left.
Attraction is on the right side, with two [fingers] indeed pointing upward.

The middle gaze is for immobilization; it is directed between the two nostrils. Pātana (causing to fall) is achieved by means of *recaka* (exhalation), while *vaśīkarana* (subjugation) is achieved by *kumbhaka* (retention).

*Ākṛṣṭi* (attraction) is achieved by *pūraka* (inhalation), and *stambhana* (immobilization) by *praśāntaka* (the tranquilized state). *Pātana* is proclaimed for oily trees, *vaśya* for flowers, *ākṛṣṭi* for diamond-like trees (*vajravṛkṣa*), and *stambhana* for moving grass.
In order to lead sentient beings into the teaching, there are four [magical] powers: causing to fall, subjugation, summoning, and paralyzing;
their characteristics are defined respectively by the meanings of the four verses.

In that regard, the one which rests on the forehead with the two female figures looking straight ahead and possessing the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of wrath is *pātanā* (the rite of casting down); the one resting on the left side with the two figures looking to the left is *vaśyā* (subjugation); the one resting on the upper part with the two figures looking to the right is *ākṛṣṭiḥ* (attraction); and the one resting on the bridge of the nose with the two figures looking straight ahead is *stambhanā* (paralysis).

The breath exiting through the nose is *recaka* (exhalation); entering, it is *pūraka* (inhalation); when the interior is filled, it is *kumbhaka* (retention); and having entered and become motionless, it is *praśānta* (tranquility). For the practice of these [mudrās], there are four characteristics in their respective order.
A sap-bearing tree [produces] a flower, and the *snuhī* plant [produces] swaying grass.
[Chapter] Eleven: *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*. Through the yoga of six months of practice, one attains accomplishment; there is no doubt about this.
One must not entertain delusion regarding this, for the miraculous powers of the Buddhas are inconceivable.
Having accomplished the four visions, the wise one should deliver sentient beings;
there should be no act of killing here, for that would result in the supreme breach of the samaya.
Every improper act must be performed, setting aside the deception of sentient beings;
for the accomplishment of the mudrā is not attained merely by harming sentient beings. || 7 ||

There, with a concentrated mind, one should consume the *samaya* while it is blazing—whether it be that which begins with *na*, *ga*, *ha*, or *antaśva*. Likewise, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are to be consumed in the Hevajra system for the sake of accomplishment.

Then, one should observe the seven-fold revolution according to the characteristics taught in the Hevajra; when there is a seven-fold revolution, there will be a beautiful voice and clear vision, and accomplishment which transcends the defilement of the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*).
The great-bodied one possesses a fragrant body. || 10 ||
Error, doubt, the superknowledges of a Buddha, and the empowerments of a Buddha. || 5 ||
One who exists at the end of seven consecutive human births is called a "seven-turner" (saptāvarta). || 9 ||
The five characteristics, such as having a beautiful voice and so forth, are the detractors and obstructors of the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*). || 10 ||

In the *Vajra-tantra* [the eleventh chapter, titled "The Manifest Enlightenment of Vajragarbha," concerning the section on Vision]: If a yogin perceives its seven shadows, then by merely consuming it, he shall attain the state of a sky-walker (*khecaratva*) in an instant. (11)
Now I shall describe the sādhana of Kurukullā, by which all sentient beings are brought under control;
it was previously indicated in brief, but here it is set forth in detail according to the twelve kalpas.
The goddess born from the syllable *hrīḥ* is red in color and has four arms; she holds an arrow and a bow in her hands, and she bears a lotus and a goad. || 13 ||
By the mere cultivation of this [meditation], one may bring the three worlds under control;
by one hundred thousand [recitations], kings; and by ten thousand, the common people.
In the Hevajra Tantra, [chapter] 12.
The arrow is *iṣu*, the bow is *kārmuka*; all are red in color. || 13 ||
The Eleventh Chapter: On Views. In the *Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*: the beasts, yakṣas, and so forth [are subdued] by ten million; the asuras by seven hundred thousand;
the gods by two hundred thousand; and the mantra-practitioners by one hundred. || 15 ||
The first king of manuals, titled "The Perfect Enlightenment of Vajragarbha" within the *Śrī Hevajra-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, is completed.
Vajra is the Holder of the Vajra; his embryo, or heart, is Hevajra. The King of Rituals (Kalparāja) which elucidates his perfect enlightenment [is concluded].

In the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti, the eleventh chapter, the Chapter on Vision, and the first King of Rituals, the Perfect Enlightenment of Vajragarbha, are completed.

The Second King of Rituals: The First Chapter on the Establishment of the Determination of Fire Offerings (Homa). Then Vajragarbha said: The Blessed One said: "May the Blessed One, whose essence is the diamond-core (*vajrasāra*) and who is the singular synthesis of all Buddhas, teach according to the proper method the auspicious characteristics of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). || 1 ||
Having performed the fire sacrifice as prescribed and having prepared the mandala, one should, at the time of dusk, consecrate the image by performing the preliminary rites such as the adhivāsana.
One who is united with one's chosen deity and has mastered the direct application of mantras should cause all the Buddhas residing in the sky to enter the heart of the image. (3)
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe āḥ hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajradhūpe āḥ svāhā | Oṃ vajradīpe āḥ svāhā | Oṃ vajragandhe āḥ svāhā | Oṃ vajranaivedye āḥ hūṃ svāhā || 4 ||
The "installation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) refers to the abiding of deities within images;
its "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is its essential nature.
"Vajras" are the three secrets of all Buddhas; their "essence" (*sāra*) is that which constitutes their self (*ātman*), and thus it is so described. (1)

"Homa" means for the purpose of destroying obstacles; "at dusk" means at the beginning of the night; "having performed" refers to the ritual procedure beginning with the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*). || 2 ||
With "Oṃ" and so forth, he states the mantras for worship. || 4 ||

First: One should offer flowers and so forth produced from the syllable *HŪṂ* with the Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī; the water for honor (*argha*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*), etc., are as before, according to the sequence of procedures in the previous tantra. (5)
For pacification (śāntika), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is circular; for nourishment (pauṣṭika), it is square;
one should accomplish the remaining rites right here [in these two]. || 6 ||

A triangle is prescribed for the rite of killing (māraṇa), measuring either one cubit or half a cubit; for pacification (śāntika), it should be two cubits above and one cubit below; and for nourishment (pauṣṭika), it is considered to be one cubit above and one cubit below.
Twenty-one finger-breadths in length, it is used for killing (māraṇa) when directed downward or upward;
it should be white in color for pacification (śānti), and likewise yellow for nourishment (pauṣṭika).
For killing, the color is black; for subjugation, it is proclaimed to be red.
As it is for subjugation, so it is for summoning; as it is for killing, so it is for hatred and the like.
The word "various" (nānā) means "of various kinds," because this [work] is a subsequent treatise (*uttaratantra*) to the *Pūrvatantra*. || 5 ||
By way of incidental discussion, he states all the fire-offerings (homas) with the words "for pacification" and so forth;
"in this very [context]" means within these three [sections] as appropriate. || 6 ||
One cubit above, and half a cubit below. || 7 ||
"White-colored" means entirely white.
"In [rites such as] hatred and so forth" refers to cruel rites such as causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*). (8–9)

In the Vajra Tantra, [the chapter on the determination of fire-offerings and consecration]: For pacification, sesame; for nourishment, curd; for killing, thorns; likewise, thorns are prescribed for hatred and the like; and for subjugation and attraction, the utpala lotus. (10)

Oṃ! To Agni, the one of great splendor, the accomplisher of all desires, who effects the welfare of sentient beings through compassion; be present here! This is the mantra for the invocation of Agni. || 11 ||
O Goddess, worshipped by the wrathful Hevajra, you are the witness;
O Mother who wears various jewels, I, [name], shall draw the mandala. (12)
"O Consumer of Oblations, go forth to accomplish both your own purpose and that of others;
you shall return at the proper time—grant me all success.
This is the mantra for propitiating Agni. (13)
Oṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hāḥ khaṃ raṃ is the half-mantra;
nī rī hūṃ khaḥ is the mantra for the water for the feet (pādya); dhvaṃ dhvaṃ is the mantra for the food offering (naivedya).
Oṃ oṃ. Regarding what is to be offered, he says "sesame" and so forth.
"O Goddess," this is the invocation mantra for the Earth, stated here because of the introduction of the mantras.
The mantra for the *argha* and other offerings belongs to Agni.

In the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti, this is the first chapter of the second section, concerning the determination of the fire sacrifice (*homa*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Just as a gourd [floats] upon the ocean, so too, amidst all phenomena which are like the sky, how do sentient beings achieve accomplishment? [They do so] by means of the form of their own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).
One whose self is disciplined in the yoga of selflessness, or through the yoga of Heruka,
should not remain for even a moment with a mind directed elsewhere if they desire spiritual accomplishment.
A beautiful and auspicious place has indeed been prescribed for the time of initial practice, where the mantra-practitioner, with a single-pointed and concentrated mind, attains success. || 3 ||
Vajragarbha said, thus he asked: "Like the sky," and so forth.

For just as space is beginningless, even so are the unwholesome and indeterminate dharmas of all sentient beings, which are comprised within the obscurations; their antidote is the cultivation of one's own tutelary deity.
Therefore, [the antidote] is like a gourd compared to the ocean-like mass of opposing factors.
The meaning of the question is: "Since the antidote is not sufficient for the deliverance of sentient beings, how can they achieve success in its cultivation?
To this, the Blessed One gives the answer beginning with "selflessness" (*nairātmya*), and so forth.

For just as a lamp made of oil, lit once within a mountain cave, instantly dispels a mass of darkness accumulated over a long period of time, so too this untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), having arisen but once, destroys in that very moment the heap of opposing factors (*vipakṣa-rāśi*) accumulated since beginningless time; such is the meaning.
If it is asked, "How then does that supramundane path arise so quickly?", [the answer is:
from a specific excellence of yoga (*yoga-viśeṣāt*).
In that regard, the specific object of focus for yoga is the self itself; the specific mental aspect is either Nairātmyā or Heruka. (1–2)
The distinction of cultivation consists in the uninterrupted succession of moments.
If it is asked how there is an uninterrupted succession of moments at the outset, he says: "At first," and so forth.

In the *Vajra-tantra*, the chapter titled "The Determination of Siddhi": At night in one's own home, the wise practitioner should, with the thought "I am a siddha," visualize a Yoginī or else the form of Śrī Heruka.
Washing his feet, eating, sipping water for purification, chewing betel nut,
rubbing his hands with sandalwood paste, and covering his loins with a loincloth;
Whether departing, speaking words, walking, standing, being angry, or laughing, the wise practitioner, observing his vow, should serve the Blessed Lady and meditate upon the Yoginī.
Those wise ones who desire accomplishment should strive with effort not to remain even for a moment in another form with a mind defiled by ignorance, for the sake of attaining success.
"Vajragarbha, I have explained this meditation which destroys all defilements;
for the sake of accomplishment, you should examine it even out of curiosity for one fortnight.
"At night-time" means at the time when people are asleep;
"I am accomplished" refers to a specific form of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*);
"the Yoginī" refers to Nairātmyā.
Thus, the yoga of meditative concentration at midnight has been described. || 4 ||
Regarding the time when people are awake, he speaks of uninterrupted yoga that is not yet fully concentrated: "The feet," and so forth.
The vowel *ā* in *ācaman* has not been lengthened;
[the form] *pūga* is used because of the elision of the case ending (*vibhakti-luk*).
"One should serve" means one should propitiate.
To the question "How?", he says: "The Yoginī," and so forth.
The meaning of the passage beginning with "even for a moment" is as follows:
one's own nature, which is non-different from selflessness, must not be viewed even for a moment;
and one's own mind, free from the notion of "I," must not be allowed to exist even for a moment.

The conclusion is provided by the passage beginning with "O Vajragarbha. He speaks the words beginning with "out of curiosity" in order to generate firmness regarding the power of yoga, [addressing] "sin," which is the mass of opposing factors (*vipakṣa*).
"Both sides" refers to the practice of yoga in both the concentrated and the unconcentrated states.
In the manuscripts Ka and Kha,
there is the elision of *vibhadeḥ*;
furthermore, the portion beginning with "ṇamapi" and so forth is not to be recited here in the manuscripts Ka and Kha.
*Svacitta-ka* and *kartavya-ka-kha*: a few portions here have been omitted;
in the *ka* and *kha* manuscripts, a few portions after the words "hitāsamāhitā yogābhyām" are not to be read.

Having abandoned all discursive thought, you should examine [the reality] by meditating for one day without interruption with a mind focused on the form of the deity, according to the *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*.
In this world of saṃsāra, there is no other means for the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others than this science (vidyā), which,
when practiced even once, produces immediate conviction.
The practitioner is never afflicted by fears or madness, nor by sufferings, nor by calamities such as grief and pain, nor by passion, hatred, and great delusion.
Reflecting thus upon the arising of the fruits of what is beneficial and what is harmful,
how could those yogis remain in Raurava even for a single moment?

Even those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, those who take life, as well as those of low birth, the foolish, and those who perform cruel deeds— [even they shall attain liberation].
It is "day" precisely through yoga in a state of meditative absorption, because of the uninterrupted teaching on the abandonment of all thought.
"Once" means for one fortnight or one day, as previously described.
With the verse beginning with "fear" (bhaya), he demonstrates the cause [of the affliction];
"unmāda" means lack of discipline.
"Thus," and so forth;
"reflecting" means observing that from that yoga arises the emergence of welfare, whereas from worldly conduct arises the emergence of harm.
"Raurava" refers to the conduct of the world.
If it is asked, "What place is there for the most wicked and others?
he says: "Five," and so forth.
By means of examination—ka; exhaustion—kha, ga, gha; examine—cha, jha; examine yourself—ja; you should examine—ṭa;
for the sake of oneself and others—ka; state of cultivation—ka.
When the practitioner is averse, pride [arises]; that which is said to be in the middle of the *ga* and *kṣaṇa* is *ka*, and that which is in the middle of *kṣaṇa* is *gha*.
One who performs non-mantric rites—
(a) one who kills (ka), (b) one who binds living beings (kha), (c) one who kills living beings (gha),
and those of low birth (janmahīna)— (ka).
A portion is missing from both the Ka and Kha manuscripts—from this conjunction, a few parts have been lost here in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.
[In the Vajratantre, the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Siddhis": Even those who are ugly and deformed in limb attain accomplishment through meditation.
He should practice the ten wholesome actions, be devoted to his guru, and have his senses subdued.
Freed from pride and anger, he certainly attains perfection through the yoga of constant practice; having attained perfection, he remains composed in meditative absorption.
One should practice in seclusion for one month until the mudrā is obtained;
once the mantra-practitioner receives the instruction, he is directed by the yoginīs.
"O Vajradhṛk, having taken this such-and-such mudrā, who is wide-eyed and adorned with beauty and youth, perform the welfare of sentient beings! || ||
One should consecrate [the consort] joined with camphor and musk by means of the *bodhicitta*,
and should proclaim the Dharma to her, beginning with the ten wholesome actions.
The mind in the form of the deity and the commitment (samaya) should be cultivated as a single state of mind for one month; there is no doubt that it will become so.
Thinking, "In that case, practitioners of the Dharma would not achieve success through the meditation on selflessness," he says: "The ten," and so forth.
Now, he asks whether there is anything further to be accomplished after the stabilization of the mind; he says "sātatya" and so forth.

Accomplishment (*siddhi*) is the stabilization of the mind, which is the natural, spontaneous flow day after day of the manifestation of the deity’s form as one's own self and the sense of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) [identical with it]; having attained that...
[the rest follows].

"Secretly" means that one should perform the secret worship by means of the forms of Hevajra and Nairātmyā for the sake of obtaining the prophecy. "By means of the bodhicitta" refers to [the practice] preceded by going for refuge and so forth.
The deity-yoga is the mind in the form of the deity.
One-pointedness of mind is the preparation for meditative concentration, or it is the state of having a single intention;
when cultivated, one becomes a vessel for accomplishment. It is accomplished—O Ka!—by means of reflection upon those [objects]. O Ka!
kāmakrodha— ka, kha, gha; siddhiṃ labdhāḥ— kha.
Guhyam—He Paṃ Mu Va. Ādeyam—Ka. Mantritam—Gha.
The conjunct *ga-gha*;
from that, *ka*;
the potential *ka*.
And here [the reading] "bhavenna cātra - ga" occurs;
the text is missing from this point as "ātmatmyābhāvanayā" in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.
Furthermore, a few portions are missing from this point as "siddhisthairyam" in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.
—“care lābhārtham” (in order to obtain [something] while wandering); a few portions are missing in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.
“devarūpa”;
a portion is missing here in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.
Since the woman who has obtained the excellent Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī is free from all conceptual constructions,
or else, by means of her own power, one should draw forth and fashion the mudrā.
Having taken up that practice from among gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, and even kinnaras, one should carry out the conduct out of confidence in one's own fortitude.
The conduct that is proclaimed as having a terrifying form is not said to be for the sake of enjoyment;
rather, it is for the purpose of examining one's own mind: whether the mind is stable or wavering. Therefore, a yogi must always abide in the form of the deity.
Vajragarbha asked: "The Blessed One has said that for one engaged in the yoga of selflessness, how is the purpose of the mudrā distinguished?
How can there be the accomplishment of the mudrā through both the mudrā and the mudrā?"
Having abandoned the female form, one should assume another form of the Blessed One;
having discarded the breast, it becomes the *bola*, situated within the *kakkola*.
"By power" means by the majesty born of meditative concentration; "having drawn forth" means having attracted [it].
"And her" means one who has obtained a boon or has been drawn [to him].
"On account of confidence in steadfastness" means relying upon the stability of the mind.
He asks "Why? and says: "Not," and so forth.
"For the sake of enjoyment" means for the purpose of enjoyment.
She has a terrifying form because she is extremely difficult [to endure].
"Mudrā" refers here to the external *prajñā* who is sought after.
"How? means for what purpose is she sought? "Mudrāsiddhi" means the accomplishment of sealing (*mudraṇa*).
The woman is selflessness; the Blessed One is Hevajra. "The breast" refers to the two breasts on the chest.
How is the excellent *bola* obtained? [It is] *ka*.
And "nārī" [is found] in manuscripts ka and kha;
"varjitam" in manuscript gha; and "yakṣe" in manuscript ka.
*cale*—*gha*.
This reading does not exist—*ka. gha. cha. ja. ṭa*.
*nairātmā*—*ka kha ga gha*.
Regarding "having taken" (*hṛtvā*): *he paṃ yo ra mā*.
*Saṃsthitām*: *kha*.
A portion is missing here in both the *ka* and *kha* manuscripts.
In this passage as well, something appears to be missing from the Ka and Kha manuscripts.
In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Accomplishment"]: "The two banks are the bell (*ghaṇṭā*); the filaments are the *bola*.
The remaining form belongs to the Great Soul, the Heruka of the Heruka-yoga. For the man, masculinity is attained effortlessly."
For this reason, the accomplishment of mudrās occurs for the yogin whose power has become manifest. || 26 ||
Through both arising and dissolution, wisdom and means are not obstructed;
for means is origination, while wisdom is the end of existence. (27)
The shore is the side;
the bell is the testicle;
the filament is the nose.
"Of the one who delights" means of the one whose nature is great delight (*mahārata*). Then, how can there be masculinity for the *Heruka* yogin? To this he says: "Heruka," and so forth.
"Accomplishment of the *mudrā*" refers to the accomplishment of the *mahāmudrā*.
"Power" (*śakti*) itself is "the powerful" (*śakta*), meaning efficacy. || 26 ||
"Arising," and so forth.
"Wisdom and means" refers to the body of one's own vidyā, that is, one's own body.
"Is not obstructed" means it is not touched.
To the question "Why?", he says: "The means," and so forth.
"Occurrence" (*sambhava*) means continuous existence.

The means is the continuous arising of the mind—which appears as a body and so on—in order to accomplish the welfare of the world throughout the extent of space, by virtue of the momentum of the accumulations (*sambhāra*).
Therefore, when the cultivation of the fruit of the means is perfected, how could there be dissolution?
Dissolution (*laya*) is non-perception. It is the manifestation of even the appearing body as unreal, like the moon and stars reflected in the water of a lake.
That very dissolution is wisdom;
therefore, it is the ender of existence.
It brings an end to existence, which has its root in the dogmatic clinging to objects. (27)
*kiñjalkena*—ṭa;
*mahātmanaḥ*—kha; *mahārate*—ga, *mahākṛte*—gha, *mahātmāno*—cha, jha, ṭa;
the portion marked by *-* and *-* does not exist in the manuscript 'ka'.
In *ga* and *kha*, it becomes "puruṣatvamāyā"; in *ga*, "puṃstvamāyāti"; in *gha*, "puṃsamāyāti".
Therefore, [the reading] is *ga* and *jha*;
but *tu* is *ga*.
*Prajñopāya*—ka kha ga gha jha. *He0paṃ0mu0va0*. [This is] in the manuscripts ka and kha. *Saṃbhāgavedha*—ka.

(.... the ender of [existence])—this is found in the Ka and Kha manuscripts. From the *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*: "In reality, there is neither dissolution nor origination for this; because there is no dissolution, nothing whatsoever dissolves, and because there is an absence of dissolution, there is no destruction. (28)
The practitioner, by means of the yoga of the generation stage, should cultivate the manifold world;
having made the manifold world like a dream, he should transcend the manifold through the very manifold.

For that very reason, there is neither dissolution nor origination for this [Mahāmudrā-body], because it is without end; moreover, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), there is no origination even following dissolution.
For this Mahāmudrā-body is itself false, and it is known as being false;
even in its manifestation, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is only dissolution and no origination.
Now, one might object that dissolution (*pralaya*) is indeed just cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); to this he says: "It dissolves," and so forth.
The meaning is this: among those who have attained the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), who is it that dissolves—that is, who is it that becomes absorbed within their own body?
None at all.
And because there is no dissolution (*laya*), there is no destruction or *pralaya*.
This is the thought: even for those beginning with Brahmā, the body is indeed non-existent; it appears as existent only due to attachment to existence (*bhāvābhiniveśa*).
If existence were real, then even *pralaya* would not occur; however, this is not so for one who has attained the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), because of his lack of attachment to existence.

Thus, it is established that the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā has non-abiding nirvāṇa as its nature, because it transcends both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; and that [accomplishment] is obtainable only through meditative cultivation. 28.
As for the nature of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), he says: "In arising," and so forth.
"The manifold" (*prapañca*) refers to the expansion [of phenomena] due to their various forms.

"Having made it like a dream" means having contemplated it as being similar to a dream; for just as in a dream the mind appears in the form of unreal objects, so too is this [world] determined through discourse that is of a single flavor.
"By means of conceptual proliferations" means by means of various discursive elaborations. "One should not proliferate" means one should not conceptualize. || 29 ||
For him there is no arising—ka; for him there is no destruction—kha, ṅa, ca, ṭa; for him there is no [existence]—jha; existence is brought to an end—bhāvam—ka.
kṣayam—ka. ga. gha;
prapañca—ka. ga. gha; svabhāva—ga.
*prapañcaniṣpra0* — Ka, Ga; *prapañcaṃ niṣpra0* — Gha; *na prapañcayet* — He, Paṃ, Mu, Va.
(*...mudrādehaḥ*) — in the Ka and Kha manuscripts. (*...nā tu*) — in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.

In this regard as well, according to the *Vajra-tantra* [Chapter Two, titled "The Determination of Siddhis"] found in the manuscripts Ka and Kha: "Just as an illusion, just as a dream, and just as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) may be, so too does the maṇḍala appear through the yoga of constant practice. (30)
In the empowerments of Mahāmudrā, there is great bliss as it is known;
its power is that very maṇḍala itself, and not something arising from another. (31)
Bliss is black, bliss is yellow, bliss is red, bliss is white;
bliss is dark-brown, bliss is blue, and bliss is the entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
To the question, "What would happen for one who practices in this way? he says: "Just as," and so forth.
"In that very way" means it appears precisely as suchness; thus, one attains a continuous, wordless certainty, whereas for the ignorant, it appears as a mere object. (30)
Having thus explained the manifestation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he speaks of the manifestation of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) with the words beginning "Mahāmudrā" and so forth.
*Mudrā* is wisdom (*prajñā*); the *mudrā-empowerment* is the knowledge of wisdom; and the *mahāmudrā-empowerment* is the fourth empowerment.
The plural form is used due to the distinction between individual instances.
"According to knowledge" means as it has been understood through the teacher's instruction.

"Great bliss" refers to the bliss that is to be accomplished, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). The connection is that this maṇḍala is the very power (*prabhāva*) of that [bliss]; its majesty (*audārya*) consists in being the means for the welfare of the world.
The mandala is the circle of yoginīs together with its leader;
it does not arise from anything else, nor is it composed of any other intrinsic nature. || 31 ||

He speaks again in detail with the words beginning "sukham" (bliss). "Śyāma" means green; "nīla" means dark blue like the sky. The meaning is that although [the world] is divided by differences of color and so forth, it is pervaded by the nature of the bliss of the maṇḍala.
"Moving" refers to the bodies of the deities; "non-moving" refers to garments, ornaments, and the like. || 32 ||

Thus (tathā): kha, ga, jha; *gandharvanagaraṃ*: he, paṃ, yo, ra, mā. It would be "thus-arisen" (*tathābhava*): kha; "it would be internal" (*syād antaro*): gha; "arising from itself" (*ātmasambhavaṃ*): cha; "not thus-arisen" (*astathābhavaṃ*): jha. *Maṇḍala*: ga.
*Satatābhyāsa*—Ṭa;
*mudrābhiṣeke tu*—Ga; *yathājñānam*—Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, He, Paṃ, Mu, Va.
tatprabhāva—ka. ga. gha;
sukha—ka kha ga;
kṛtsna-carācalaṃ—ka. ga. gha.
(vastutvena...lānām) in the Ka and Kha manuscripts;
(sukha...tim āha) in the Ka and Kha manuscripts;
(...va prabhāva) in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.
(nā....mayaṃ) is found in the Ka and Kha manuscripts.
The reading "vyāptam arthaḥ" is missing in both manuscripts. "calaṃ" is in Ka.

Immovable, [consisting of] garments, coverings, and so forth—(ka), 0 garments, veils, and so forth—(bho). The *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* states: Bliss is wisdom (*prajñā*), bliss is the means (*upāya*), and likewise bliss is that which arises from *kunduru*.
Bliss is existence (*bhāva*), bliss is non-existence (*abhāva*); Vajrasattva is remembered as bliss. (33)
Vajragarbha said: This is the yoga of the completion stage; its bliss is considered the great bliss.
For one devoid of the meditation on the completion stage, what is the purpose of the generation stage? (34)
How can there be the arising of a mandala whose nature is bliss from a cause whose nature is non-bliss? To this he says: "Bliss is wisdom," and so forth.
Wisdom and method are bliss, because they are the source of the various joys (*ānanda*) and because they are the support.
"Bliss is likewise born of *kunduru*" means that the bliss of their own meditative union (*svasamāpatti*) is exactly like that; the meaning is that it is bliss itself directly.

"Existence" (*bhāva*) is the bliss consisting of the five Buddhas, having the form of the Seal-holder (*mudrāvajradhara*), because it consists of supreme bliss. "Non-existence" (*abhāva*) is the fluidity of that very [bliss]; it too is bliss, because its nature is non-conceptual bliss (*niṣprapañcasukha*). Therefore, even the cause of the maṇḍala is essentially blissful. [An objection: "Granted that the cause of the Śrī Heruka maṇḍala is essentially blissful, how is it so for the Nairātmyā maṇḍala? To this he says: "Vajrasattva is known as bliss."

The seed-syllable arising from the union of the moon and sun, whose natures are wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), is the deity’s emblem, the vajra. The being (*sattva*) born from its center is the seed-syllable; that being together with the vajra is Vajrasattva. He too is known as bliss; he is said by the Buddhas to have the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). And the mandala of Nairātmyā arises from that;
therefore, it too is essentially of the nature of bliss. (33)
Vajragarbha said: For what purpose did he say this?
It was for the sake of praising even the generation stage by the Blessed One himself.
"True bliss" is supreme bliss; that very great bliss is the single flavor of all existence.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Once arisen," and so forth.
*Bhāvanā* is the mental production of the bodies of deities and the like; one who is *hīna*, meaning devoid or lacking this, [attains] nothing at all. || 34 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that what is to be accomplished here is great bliss (*mahāsukha*) as comprised within the *dharmakāya*, and since in the *dharmakāya* the consciousnesses that manifest as body, enjoyments, and abode have completely ceased, how can there be a body and so forth? Therefore, when that [bliss] is to be accomplished, the cultivation of a body is not logical; to this he says: "I am existence, yet I am not existence. If, then, the appearances of the body and so forth belong to the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, they would be erroneous because they appear as if possessing real existence; consequently, the Buddha too would not be a Buddha by virtue of those two [bodies]. To this he says: "I am a Buddha because of the awakening to reality (*vastu*).
This is the meaning: "reality" refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*); "awakening" to them is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*). Therefore, I am a Buddha.

Furthermore, by means of non-apparent knowledge (*nirābhāsajñāna*), only the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena—known as suchness (*tathatā*)—is perceived, and not their particular characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
Those [objects] are infinite, yet they are seen through the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) by means of their reflection;
and they are discerned through the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) which analyzes them. Both of these wisdoms constitute the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Therefore, I am a Buddha by means of three bodies, not by one alone, because without both the enjoyment body and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), there would be no fulfillment of the perfections of one's own and others' welfare. Furthermore, they are not ultimately delusive, because they appear as being like illusions and so forth, due to their non-existence in accordance with how they appear.
For this very reason, the pure mundane conceptualization is said to be the *saṃbhogakāya* and the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *dharmakāya*.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that "I am supremely profound," he says "mām" and so forth.
"The deluded" refers to those who are devoid of the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Afflicted by indolence" means they are devoid of the wisdom consisting of reflection and the wisdom consisting of cultivation. || 37 ||
Thus, in order to analyze this profundity, he says: "I dwell," and so forth.

"I dwell with the *sāmbhogika-kāya* due to the supreme wonder of the Buddha's perfections.

And so, O son, the realization is like a lamp in the darkness. (40)
To illuminate the majesty of the Self as it has thus come to be, he says: "The expounder," and so forth.

The Dharma—such as the *Hevajra-tantra* and others—which reveals such [a state], the one who explains it, and the listener endowed with the qualities of a disciple—all three of these are "I"; the meaning is that they are to be worshipped just like me.
To the question "Who are you? he replies primarily: "I am the one to be realized.

That which is primarily to be realized—the Great Bliss Dharmakāya—that is I in the primary sense. Furthermore, by saying "the Teacher of the world," he refers to the Saṃbhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya as well.
Thus it has been established that the conception of the body is indeed appropriate.
Furthermore, "I am the world" means: the world is the being born of sexual union;
and that which is the intermediate state body of that very same [being] is also the "world," because its purpose (*loka*) is directed toward that [world]. Therefore, I am both of those as well.

Just as I am indeed the *saṃbhogakāya* because it is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the great bliss of the *dharmakāya*, so too am I the world because it is the outflow of the great bliss of the parents and the *gandharva*; and I am also the *gandharva* due to the coalescence (*saṃmūrcchana*) of great bliss. || 39 ||

"What is the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) in the world of which you are the primary [embodiment]? To this he says: "Innate" (*sahaja*), and so forth. [Objection: Is it not the case that the great bliss to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is what you are primarily? However, the innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) established since beginningless saṃsāra is not something to be accomplished; why then do you say that you are its primary [embodiment]? To this he says: "And thus," and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason.

Since that very [innate bliss] is the means for establishing the cognition of the primary [bliss] by way of an analogy through its similarity, therefore that alone is the metaphorical designation "I am the primary. It is like a lamp in the dark; just as a lamp is the means for perceiving jars and other objects in the dark by way of manifesting them, so too is innate bliss the means for the bliss to be realized, as shown by the verse beginning with "I sport" (*vihare 'ham*). || 40 ||
The Teacher, the Lord, who possesses the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor signs,
is established as the one named Śukra within the womb of the woman in Sukhāvatī.
Without him there would be no bliss, and without bliss he would not exist.
Because it is dependent and lacks independent power, [the self] experiences happiness through its connection with the deity.
Therefore, the Buddha would not be an existent thing, nor indeed would he be of the nature of non-existence;
for while he possesses the form of arms and faces, he is also formless due to his supreme bliss.
To clarify what was stated obscurely, he says: "The thirty-two," and so forth.

I am the lord of those Bodhisattvas born there whose bodies are radiant with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), and I am their sustainer through the enjoyments of the Dharma. Being such as this, I abide in Sukhāvatī.
"Woman" (*yoṣit*) refers both to the Vajra-woman (*vajrayoṣit*) and to the illustrative woman (*dṛṣṭāntayoṣit*). I am situated within her *bhaga* as that which is named "semen" (*śukra*).

"Semen" is the seminal fluid of gnosis (*jñānaretaḥ*), while in the illustrative context it is the external seminal fluid. "By that" means by what is named "semen. "He" refers to the one named "semen."
Therefore, great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is dependent upon semen and physical union;
in their absence, because other causes for it lack efficacy, it arises from the yoga with the deity alone.
Consequently, the essential meaning is that one who desires the bliss to be accomplished must necessarily cultivate the yoga with the deity.

And thus, because the path is neither existence nor non-existence, for that reason the Buddha as the fruit would also not be existence, since by means of the *dharmakāya* he is characterized by the total exhaustion of all afflictions (*saṃkleśa*).
"He" refers to the Buddha.
Nor is he of the nature of non-existence, because the *dharmakāya* is of the nature of perfectly pure, equal-taste gnosis (*samarasa-jñāna*).
And "having the form of arms and faces" refers to the *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*;
and "formless" (*arūpī*), why? Because of supreme bliss—that is to say, by means of the *dharmakāya* and the bliss of the enjoyment of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃbhoga*).
