[The second chapter, titled "The Determination of Siddhi"]: Therefore, the entire world is innate; the innate is said to be one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). That very true nature is *nirvāṇa* through a mind characterized by purity.
The form of the deity-yoga is established as soon as one is born; however, the latent impressions of the material world persist through the positions of the arms, faces, and colors.

Thus, since the fruit is neither existence nor non-existence, therefore the entire world is innate (*sahaja*). It is "innate" because of its union with innate Buddhahood (*buddhatva*). "The entire world" refers to all sentient beings.
What is the meaning of "Buddhahood is innate"?
Thus he says: "Innate," and so forth. "Essential nature" (*svarūpa*) means primordial matter (*prakṛti*). The sense is that the word "innate" (*sahaja*) is a synonym for "primordial matter."
And Buddhahood is primarily the *dharmakāya*.
With reference to that, it says: "Nirvāṇa is one's very own nature.
To the question "How so?", it says: "Purified," and so forth.

Purity (*viśuddhi*) is the absence of stains (*malābhāva*), which is luminosity (*prabhāsvaratā*); it is so described because that [luminosity] is its aspect (*ākāra*) and its nature (*prakṛti*). And because that mind has purity as its aspect, for that reason [it is not an entity]. Since purity is nirvāṇa, therefore it is not an entity (*bhāva*).
Since the mind itself has the aspect of purity, it is therefore not non-existent; this is the meaning.
By this much, it is stated that the natural luminosity of the mind itself is the seed for Buddhahood, established as beginningless.
"In that case, there would be no seed for the *sambhogakāya* at all;
for the ordinary body is the seed of that very [body], not of the deity-body, because they are of a different nature.
To this, he says: "The deity," and so forth.
And here, by the term "form of the deity," its seed-syllable alone is meant.
That [seed-syllable] resides in the embodied being as soon as they are born.
Why is this so? He says: "by the arms," and so forth; the meaning is "because of the commonality of the body."
Just as natural purity is the seed for the purification of adventitious impurities, so too the very natural body is the seed for the body of the deity; this is the intended meaning.
If it is then asked, "In that case, is the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the deity's body useless?", he replies with the words beginning "But rather" (*kiṃ tu*).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "it is also the cause of the natural body."

Therefore, the sense is that the cultivation of the deity's body is not in vain, as it serves both to abandon that [dualistic perception] and to establish and nourish one's own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Just as all living beings die from a piece of poison by means of which the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* [was composed],
so too one who knows the true nature of poison may expel the poison by means of that very same piece of poison.
Just as one seized by wind is given a meal of black gram (*māṣa*),
whereby the wind is destroyed by wind through the application of contrary medicine,
so too does pure existence become [pure] through the counteracting of conceptual construction by means of [conceptual] construction itself.
Just as water that has entered the ear is drawn out by means of water,
so indeed is the conceptual construction of existence purified by means of mental forms.
"It is difficult to accept that the abandonment of the ordinary body occurs through the very cultivation of [the idea of] the body.
Therefore, he says 'by that very [means]' and so forth, in order to prove this with many examples.
How so?"
Māṣa is wind (vāta).
Because it promotes the expulsion of wind, urine, and feces, it is a medicine contrary [to those conditions], owing to its being of the same nature as them. Its preparation is the method (vidhi).
Existence (*bhava*) is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); that becomes purified and exhausted.
"By existence itself" means by the mundane path alone.

For instance—the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, and the five powers; these twenty-two factors constitute the mundane path.
Without that, there is no supramundane path;
it consists of fifteen factors: the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight factors of the path.
Without that, there is no destruction of existence.
Therefore, through a gradual process, the destruction of existence occurs by means of existence itself;
and conceptual construction becomes purified from conceptual construction through a gradual process.
For instance, even the analytical investigation of reality is itself a conceptual construction.
And that very cultivation, through the mediation of the acquisition of the power of meditation, generates non-conceptual knowledge;
and by means of that, conceptual constructions are extinguished.
"Possessed" (*āviṣṭa*) means entered (*praviṣṭa*).
"Dragged" (*kṛṣyate*) means pulled down (*nikṛṣyate*).
"Conceptualization of existence" (*bhāvavikalpa*) refers to the conceptualization of the five aggregates and so forth.
"By means of forms" means by means of the forms of deities such as Śāśvata and Ratneśa;
it is purified, that is, it is destroyed.

In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Siddhis"]: Just as things burnt by fire are again heated by fire.
Likewise, those scorched by the fire of passion perspire from the flame of passion. (49)
For by whatever terrible deed living beings are bound, by that very same means, when applied with skillful method, they are liberated from the bondage of existence. 50.
The world is bound by passion, and by passion alone it is liberated; this is indeed a paradoxical realization that has not been understood by the followers of the Buddha or other teachers. 51.
In the sexual unions (kunduras), there are five according to the nature of the five elements;
that which is the one Great Bliss undergoes a state of fivefold division through various distinctions.

Passion (*rāga*) is the passion of the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is itself the fire, for by it they are burned and tormented, due to its production of the sufferings of the miserable destinies and so forth. Passion is the passion for reality (*tattva*); it is itself the flame, because it burns the fuel of the conceptualizations of the afflictions.
By that [flame], they are not scorched; rather, they are fully ripened. 49.
Fierce action is that born of hatred, such as the taking of life and so forth.
Expedient means is great compassion, such as the protection of the Buddha's teaching and so forth. || 50 ||
"By passion" means by the passion of the afflictions (*kleśa-rāga*).
"By passion alone" means by the passion for reality (*tattva-rāga*) itself.
"Contrary" means being of the same class (*sapakṣa-bhūta*), because it appears as if it were of the same class.
In the ultimate sense, however, they are indeed the very opposites.
"Heretics of the Buddha" refers to heretics who [claim to be] Buddhists. How can they be [considered] Buddhists?
Because they have accepted only the Buddha as their teacher. How [are they] non-Buddhists?
Because of their hostility toward the Vajrayāna, which is the very essence of the Buddha’s teaching. 51.
By all of this, it has been established that the enjoyment (*sambhoga*) of the Vajra Goddess must necessarily be meditated upon.
To further establish that very same point as the cause of the infinite families (*anantakula*), he says: "In the *kunduras*, etc.
The form [with *-e*] is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
In those *kunduras*, which are sexual unions arising from the lotus of Vajradevī—
[the word] "bhavet" means "they occur.
"Five" refers to the five touches (*sparśa*), which consist of the five elements.

"By way of the nature of the five elements" means by way of the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space. What, then, are those elements? He says: "The one alone," and so forth. "Great Bliss" (*mahānanda*) is the bliss of sexual union (*suratānanda*). According to the *Vajrapañjikā-muktāvalī*, from the touch resulting from the union of the *bola* (male organ) and *kakkola* (female organ), there arises the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of solidity. Since that which is solid has the nature of delusion (*moha*), delusion is considered to be Vairocana. (53)

Since the bodhicitta is fluid, and the fluid element is considered to be the water element, and because water has the nature of Akṣobhya, hatred is indeed the leader Akṣobhya. (54) From the conjunction of the friction of two [substances], fire is always produced; thus, passion is Amitavajra, for passion arises from fire. (55)
The mind that resides within the *kakkola* is of the nature of wind;
for envy is Amoghasiddhi, and Amogha arises from wind. || 56 ||
Vajradhara;
"into the state of five" means into the form of the five families;
"by means of divisions" means by the division of the elements.
The meaning is that the reality (*bhūta-tattva*) is precisely that [which consists of] delusion and so forth, as well as Vairocana and so forth; this is the summary verse (*uddeśa-śloka*). || 52 ||
He states a verse of explanation for this very point, beginning with "boil" (bola) and so forth.
The latent tendency toward solidity (*kāṭhinyavāsanā*) is the cognition of solidity (*kāṭhinyapratyaya*), for solidity is indeed the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).

Heat is warmth.

Regarding *kakkolaka*: it refers to that which moves within the *kakkolaka*.

for this very reason, it is called *īrṣyā*, according to the root list (*dhātupāṭha*) where the root *īr* means "to move. In the *Vajratantro* [the second chapter, titled "The Determination of Siddhis"]: Bliss is passion (*rāga*); passion becomes red (*rakta*). Attachment (*rakti*) has the characteristic of space (*ākāśa*).
Space is Piśunavajra; slander arises from space. || 57 ||
The one great mind alone exists in five forms;
from it, thousands upon thousands arise within the five families.
Therefore, this single-natured supreme eternal Great Bliss undergoes a fivefold state through the differentiation of the five mental states, beginning with passion. (59)
In each single family, there are assemblies of Tathāgatas equal in number to the sands of ten Gaṅgā rivers;
indeed, within those families there are many families, and within those families there are hundreds of families.
(60) Bliss is the joy of *surata*; that itself is passion (*rāga*) because it is the locus of attachment. That itself is the "red" (*rakta*), because the mind attached to it is non-different from it.

which is the experience of its own nature alone,
is characterized by space; for it consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the nature of which is the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
It is called "space" because of its similarity to space.
That very Piśunavajra is Ratnasambhava; he is Piśuna because he reveals the ultimate truth (paramārtha). 57.
The Great Mind is Vajradhara, whose nature is great bliss.

How [is it] "by way of division"?
By the fivefold mind, namely, by the five types of mental states such as passion, hatred, envy, and so forth. || 59 ||

By this much, the divisions of great bliss have been established as the five families. To establish that even their further subdivisions are innumerable families, he says in two verses, beginning with "ten," and so forth.

Within those families, there are innumerable families born from the family of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). (61)
The second chapter, titled "The Determination of Siddhis," in the *Hevajra-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
They are equal in number to the grains of sand.

Then the Vajra-holder spoke of the means for the Yoginīs, named "The Introduction to All Tantras," [including] the vow (*saṃvara*), the initiation (*abhiṣeka*), as well as the intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*);
the divisions of bliss and moments (*ānanda-kṣaṇa*), and likewise other matters such as the ritual meal (*bhojana*).
Regarding that, he speaks of the vow: "The vow of all the Buddhas is established in the Evam-kāra;
through initiation, the Evam-kāra, which is great bliss, is correctly known."
Third: The Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī. Then the Yoginīs spoke thus to the Blessed One Vajrasattva: "What is this 'Evam' called, which is the *saṃvara* of the Ḍākinīs?
May the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Guru of the World, explain it according to the proper method."
The Blessed One said:
"That which is divine, shaped like the letter E, adorned in its center with the syllable Vaṃ, is the abode of all pleasures; therein, blisses arise, distinguished by their various moments."
The jewel-casket of the Buddha.
From the knowledge of the moments, the knowledge of bliss is established in the syllable E-VAM.
Likewise, it is characterized by distinct features.
Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth:
"Vajrī" refers to the Holder of the Vajra (Vajradhara).
The "entire tantra" refers to the complete *Hevajratantra*.
Its "nidāna" is the root cause, because the tantra was taught with reference to that. "By name" means it is renowned by this very name.
The means is the teaching of enlightenment; its summary verse begins with "the vow" (*saṃvaram*), and so forth. In that context, "the vow" is the supreme bliss.
"Consecration" refers to the four consecrations.
Speech by way of intentional terminology is "intentional speech" (*sandhyābhāṣa*).
Ānanda, there are four joys (*ānanda*).
The distinction of moments refers to the four moments.
The connection between the first and last words is: "restraint is great bliss.
For whom is it great bliss? For all the Buddhas.
"Correctly" means consisting of non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*).
Why?
Because it is of a single form for all Buddhas, due to having dissolved and become one with suchness (*tathatā*).
Where is it situated?
It is established in the syllable *Evaṃ*.
Because of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), all the stains of the signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) are washed away.
It is known and experienced by all Buddhas who have dissolved [into the absolute] through both wisdom and skillful means.
The yogins know that the four moments—the variegated (*vicitra*), the ripening (*vipāka*), and the crushing (*vimarda*)—are attained together as one.

Regarding the term *ḍākinī*: from the root *ḍai*, meaning "to move through the air," *ḍā* refers to the supernormal power (*ṛddhyabhijñā*) of movement; those whose nature (*śīla*) is to be marked (*aṅkitum*) by that are *ḍākinīs*. Marking (*aṅkanam*) here means a curved or swift motion; thus, the meaning is that the accomplished yoginīs (*siddhayoginīs*) who possess the nature of moving simultaneously in the ten directions by means of supernatural power are *ḍākinīs*. *Saṃvara* is the support (*ādhāra*) for their commitment (*saṃvara*).
The form of the letter *e* is for the purpose of indicating that there is oneness and equality among all the secrets of the Tathāgatas.
It is "divine" (*divya*) because one plays (*divyanti*) therein.
To the question "How is it a *ālaya*? he says: "Blisses," and so forth.
The time of momentary joys;
the knowledge of happiness is the knowledge of bliss and so forth.
He explains this through four verses beginning with "The names, numbers, characteristics, and the various divisions of bliss of the moments.
What do they know? They know the four joys (*ānanda*).

It is "bliss" because it is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and it is "knowledge" because it is perfect knowledge; thus, "bliss-knowledge" is coemergent joy (*sahajānanda*). Its "enjoyment" is the perception of one who wishes to emerge from that state. "Its reversal" means the opposite of that, because it possesses an objective support (*sālambana*). Regarding "observation": in the *Vajra-tantra*, the third chapter titled "The Sandhyā-bhāṣā," it is said: "The manifold (*vicitra*) is known as the various [acts] such as embracing, kissing, and so forth."
The maturation is the opposite of that; it is the enjoyment of the knowledge of bliss.
Vimarda is said to be reflection, such as thinking, "I have experienced pleasure";
Vilakṣaṇa is other than these three, being devoid of both passion and dispassion.

In the *vicitra* stage there is the first joy (*prathamānanda*); in the *vipāka* stage, the supreme joy (*paramānanda*); in the *vimarda* stage, the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*); and in the *vilakṣaṇa* stage, the innate joy (*sahajānanda*). || 9 ||
The Master, the Secret, the Wisdom, and likewise the Fourth;
these are to be known as the joys in sequence, corresponding to the number of the four consecrations. (10)
It is the recollection of that which has just perished.

"Bliss" refers to Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Attachment is the longing for future bliss, occurring during the stages of *ānanda* and *paramānanda*; non-attachment is the lack of longing in one who is satiated by experienced bliss, occurring during *viramānanda*. It is free from both of these, because at that moment there is the direct realization of that very [bliss] which was longed for for a long time. (6–8)
"First bliss" means merely bliss. By this much, the vow (saṃvara) and, in connection with it, the distinctions between the moments of bliss have been indicated. || 9 ||
He speaks of the consecrations with the words beginning "as the master" (*ācārya*).
The consecration that occurs through the master, the secret, and the wisdom is, respectively, the master-consecration, the secret-consecration, and the wisdom-consecration.

Furthermore, "that again likewise" means that which is the bliss to be accomplished (*sādhya-sukha*) should be explained later, after that bliss of the example has been correctly understood; "likewise" means according to the instruction, by way of its similarity to the bliss of the example.
The third among these is called wisdom (*prajñā*); its subdivisions are also four empowerments (*abhiṣeka*), which exist sequentially in two types.
He states them in a half-verse beginning with "Bliss" (*ānanda*) and so forth.
*Saṃkhyā* means enumeration; *saṃjñā* means designation.

The meaning of the half-verse is that there are four joys in their respective order, and four consecrations [named] because of the beginning of practice, because of going far, because of excellent knowledge, and because of the ultimate reality. || 10 ||
Through the purification by laughter, the Ācārya [is purified] in gazing; likewise, the Guhya in the attainment of the hands; and that again, in the practice of the union of the couple.
The consecration (seka) is known to be fourfold for the sake of the accomplishment of sentient beings;
it is called "consecration" because by means of it one is sprinkled or bathed. || 12 ||
Embracing with both hands the Prajñā who is sixteen years of age,
the sprinkling by the Ācārya is considered to arise from the union of the bell and the vajra.
She has a beautiful face, large eyes, and is adorned with beauty and youth.
And with the thumb and the ring finger, one should cause [the substance] to fall into the mouth of the disciple.
The purification of laughter arises from the four eyes; that which is the desire for sexual union on both sides is the "Teacher" (*ācārya*), because it initiates the practice.

"Gazing" (*īkṣaṇa*) is the conjunction of signs. "Attainment of the hand" (*pāṇyāpti*) is the embrace; that is "Wisdom" (*prajñā*), because through the touch of all [parts], there is supreme knowledge.
The system of pairs (*dvandvatantra*) is dependent upon the couple; the meaning is "sexual union" (*rata*). || 11 ||
In order to show the meaning of the word *abhiṣeka*, he says "sekam" and so forth.
"Is bathed" (*snāpyate*) means it is washed, that is, it is made stainless. || 12 ||
The union of the bell and vajra in the two hands; "sprinkling" refers to the master according to the oral instruction; the intermediate consecration is the secret consecration. || 13 ||
[The Third Chapter, titled "The Sandhyābhāṣā"] "I am submerged in the mire of saṃsāra; save me, who have no refuge!
With sweet food, drink, and edibles, with intoxicants, incense, offerings, garlands, and oblations, along with bells, banners, and ointments—this is the most excellent [practice]. (20)

But in that very place, the teacher should perform the ritual of equal flavor within the sphere of the disciple; he should worship Prajñā, and having honored her, he should offer her [to the disciple]. || 15 ||
The Teacher should say: "O Great Being, take this seal which brings happiness, having recognized the disciple as one of great nature, free from longing and devoid of anger. (16)
The Teacher commands him: "O Vajradhṛk, perform the *kunduru*!
I shall explain the duties of the disciple; one should lead him through the consecration. (17)
Having seen the Guru endowed with the mudrā, one should perform praise and worship as follows:
"O Blessed One, Great Peaceful One, solely intent upon Vajrayoga! (18)"
O you who arise from the indivisible vajra-yoga that perfects the mudrās, O Great Beings, just as you [are], O Lord, perform that for me as well! 19.
The Teacher, the Guru— what would he say? "O Mahāsattva," and so forth.
Having done what should one speak?
Having known the disciple to be "mahadbhūta," meaning a great-souled one (mahātman) or one of noble disposition (mahāśaya). || 15-16 ||
*Kundaru* means sexual union; *Vajradhrk* refers to the Holder of Hevajra.
*Anunāthayet* means one should entreat him. || 17 ||

Because he abides in the unions of the two deities, he is the yoga and the practice of the Great Peaceful Vajra; he is single-mindedly devoted to that, being utterly intent upon it. (18) "The accomplisher of the mudrā" means the one who brings satisfaction to the vidyās.
The "Vajras" are all the Buddhas; their "yoga" is equanimity, which is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and he is the source of its arising.
He is thus described as "one whose continuity is indivisible.
"Just as" means by which great bliss they are endowed, O All-pervading Lord! (19) With these [offerings], such as worship and the rest, the disciple should worship the Holder of the Vajra. (21)
When supreme bliss, devoid of all diversity, has been attained in that moment, the Teacher should say: "O Mahāsattva, this great happiness is to be maintained. (22)
"Act for the benefit of sentient beings until the end of enlightenment," thus does the Vajra-holder speak to the disciple during the sequence of initiation rites. (23)
Samsara itself is a mass of mud, a heap of mire.
"Save me! means "Protect me! The word "me" is understood from the phrase "without refuge."
"Sweet" means delicious;
"strength" means great strength, that is to say, great honey. || 20 ||
The remainder:
*vilepana* is anointing (*samālabhana*).
"With these offerings" means with those as previously described. The connection is that "the disciple should worship.
"The Vajra-holder" refers to the guru. || 21 ||

When supreme bliss has arisen by its power and the innate bliss characterized as the present moment is attained, it is "devoid of multiplicity" because the mind abides in that alone. It is "to be held" (dhāraṇīya), meaning this very state must be made firm within the mind. || 22 ||
He asks, "What is the use of that? and replies with the words beginning "as far as" (*yāvat*).

Thus, having initiated [the disciple].
Having thus consecrated [the disciple] according to the rule with the three empowerments,
the Guru, the Vajra-holder,
speaks to the disciple.
One should tell the disciple of the "accumulation of rites," meaning the multitude of duties to be performed;
and by saying "thus," one should explain this fourth consecration which is about to be described. || 23 ||
In the Vajra Tantra, the chapter titled "The Esoteric Language" states: This very great gnosis is established within all bodies;
it is the non-dual Lord who possesses a dual form and whose nature consists of both existence and non-existence. (24)
Pervading the stable and the moving, it remains present and shines forth in the form of Māyā;
through the means of the maṇḍala, the cakra, and so forth, it attains constant certainty.

Then, having obtained the forgiveness of all the yoginīs and sisters, Vajragarbha addressed the Blessed One in this way: “What is called the mandala-circle, the city consisting of the essence of all Buddhas?
May the Blessed Ones teach it according to the proper method; an error has occurred to me. (26)
"This very" refers to the innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*).
"Great gnosis" (*mahājñāna*) is that which was indicated in the first chapter by the passage beginning, "And the great gnosis resides within the body," and so forth.

In that context, it is indeed called "great gnosis" because its nature is the experience of the emptiness of duality; and for that very reason, because there is no distinction from the vision of emptiness—which consists of great bliss—it is also "great bliss."
The body of all sentient beings is the "all-body.
It is non-dual because duality—the subject and object—is absolutely non-existent;
nevertheless, it has a dual form because it appears as a duality.

The existence of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and the non-existence of duality—of that which consists of both existence and non-existence—is what is meant by "having the nature of existence and non-existence.

The Lord Vajradhara, because his nature is the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) and because all phenomena are characterized as mere non-dual luminosity, remains pervading everything; nevertheless, due to the appearance of duality, he shines like one possessing a form of illusion (*māyārūpī*). || 24 ||
If, then, the experience of the emptiness of duality is beginningless for all sentient beings, would it not follow that they possess enlightenment from the very outset?
It would not; for although the experience exists, it is unperceived.
From what, then, does enlightenment arise?
Because that very [practice] is characterized by continuity.
If one asks, "By what means does he attain that continuity?", he says: "In the maṇḍala-cakra," and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the two yogas consisting of the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) of the Solitary Hero (*ekavīra*). || 25 ||
"Having forgiven" means having pardoned.
For what purpose?
To illuminate the very greatness of those [goddesses].
It is called a "city" (*pura*) because it is filled by all the Buddhas.
"What? means "for what reason? "Delusion" (*bhrānti*) refers to doubt (*vicikitsā*). || 26 ||

The Blessed One said: "The *vajrapañjikā* (the Commentary on the Vajra) is the *muktāvalī* (String of Pearls). It is said that the mandala is the essence; it is the great bliss of bodhicitta. Because it performs that taking (*ādāna*), it is considered a mandala (*maṇḍala*), which is understood as 'rubbing' (*malana*). || 27 ||
The wheel known as the space-element (khadhātu) is a collection that purifies the sense objects and so forth;
its bliss is realized through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*. (28)

Bodhicitta is great bliss (*mahāsukha*); it is the seed-syllable produced by the correct conjunction of the moon and sun within the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā, and the seed-syllable produced from that [conjunction] within the womb of the Goddess.
In the maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka, however, bodhicitta is that which has dissolved into the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*).
Both of these are great bliss.
That very essence is the maṇḍala.
It "takes" (lāti), meaning it grasps; for the arising of the body occurs through its own nature by virtue of grasping that essence, thus it is considered the maṇḍala.
"Mīlana" refers to the deities. (27)
"Cakra" (wheel) is the object to be characterized; its synonym is "gaṇa," which means the state of total unification.
Its definition is explained by means of "khadhātu" (space-element) and so forth. Because of its similarity to space, "khadhātu" refers to suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, when there is space, the space-element (khadhātu) also brings nourishment to yogins.
The meaning is that the emptiness (śūnyatā) of each of the sense objects and so forth is the circle of yoginīs (yoginīcakra).
For this very reason, he says it is the purification of the sense objects and so forth.
The meaning is that the objects, the sense faculties, and so forth, each possess a pure nature (*viśuddhasvabhāva*).

Now, if it is the case that they rest in the power of those [objects] by virtue of having pure objects of focus, he asks: "What is that power? and replies with the words "the wheel" (*cakra*) and so on.
That [power] is the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) because it brings about the blissful realization of the circle of Yoginīs (*yoginīcakra*).
The term "vimāna" refers to the wheel (cakra) because it serves as the support for that [wheel]. || 28 ||

In the *Hevajratantra*, in the chapter titled "The Sandhyābhāṣā" (The Esoteric Language), Vajragarbha asks in the *Muktāvalī* commentary on the *Hevajra*: "By what commitment (*samaya*) should one abide, and by what vow (*saṃvara*)?

The Blessed One replied. Then all the Yoginīs said this to the Blessed One: "What, moreover, are those sense objects (*viṣaya*), what are the sense faculties (*indriya*), what is the sense base (*āyatana*), and which are the aggregates (*skandha*)?
What, moreover, are those elements (*dhātu*)?"
What is the intrinsic nature of these? || 31 ||
False speech;
[the taking of] another's wife. || 29 ||
The Blessed One said: "The six sense objects;
living beings must be killed by you; that which is not given must be taken by you; there is service, a single mind, the killing of a living being, and the life-mind—this is what is intended.
'I shall deliver the worlds,' thus is false speech proclaimed."
A woman who gives her semen is a paramour; one's own beautiful wife is likewise [a paramour]. 30.

“*Ekacittaṃ* means the solitary mind (*āveṇikacitta*); it signifies the knowledge of *cittamātratā* (mind-only). That itself constitutes the taking of life here. It extends up to the point of not desiring an object that is a body consisting of a sentient being distinct from the mind;

this is the meaning of ‘becoming one. Furthermore, it is said: by the words ‘the space element (*ākāśadhātu*)’ and so forth, the definition and the object are taught. Because it shares the same characteristics as space, the space element is suchness (*tathatā*).”

Since it is both space (*ākāśa*) and that which causes yogins to expand (*vistaraka*), and is also an element (*dhātu*), it is the "space-element" (*ākāśadhātu*). That which is the emptiness of each respective object and so forth is called the "wheel of yoginīs. For that very reason, it is said to "purify objects and so forth," which means its nature is the individual purification of the sense faculties and so on. Now, if one focuses on purification, one will expand through enjoyment (*bhoga*); what then is that enjoyment? It is indicated by the words "Vajra" and so forth. Because one realizes the bliss of that wheel of yoginīs, it is "enjoyment. The celestial mansion (*vimāna*) is the "wheel" because it is the very support for that wheel. Why is it requested? It is for the purpose of teaching what is known as the "vow" (*saṃvara*) and so forth. Regarding "one-pointed mind": this refers to an unmixed mind; the meaning is the primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*). That, in this context, is the taking of life.
Form, sound, as well as smell, taste, and likewise touch, and the nature of the sphere of phenomena—these six are considered to be the objects. || 32 ||

And there are six sense faculties. "False speech" means that no sentient world is perceived; this is the intended meaning. "What is not given" refers to taking from others. [The rest follows the Tibetan text]. || 30 ||

"What is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of these [objects]? refers to those objects and so forth. "What is their intrinsic nature? [The answer is: suchness (tathatā). The sense is: by what knowledge does purification occur? [The answer is: "Its intrinsic nature is the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu)," meaning its essence is the realm of phenomena. || 31–32 ||

Regarding "action" (*karman*): it refers to the position that, apart from the mind, no body characterized as a sentient being is perceived, and so forth. Regarding "falsehood": the intention is that the world of sentient beings is not perceived. "Not given" means taking [a woman] from another. "Beautiful self-manifestation" refers to Nairātmyā and the others. If one asks, "In what sense are they the 'wives of others'? [it is because they are] supreme. As for what their nature is like: they are the objects and so forth. What is their nature? It is suchness (*tattva*). The intention is: by which primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) do they become purified? "The nature of the *dharmadhātu*" means having the essence of the *dharmadhātu*. **Hevajra Tantra, Chapter Three, titled "The Esoteric Speech" (*Sandhyābhāṣā*):** "The eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and likewise the mind—these six sense faculties are joined with Mohavajrā and the others. (33)
Through the object and the subject, there are the twelve bases; and the five aggregates, beginning with form and ending with consciousness, O Great Compassionate One. (34)
The sense faculties, their objects, and the consciousnesses of the sense faculties—these are declared to be the eighteen elements for the awakening of the Yoginīs. (35)
Intrinsic nature is primordially unarisen; likewise, it is neither true nor false. O Yoginīs, by your own will, you know all things to be like the moon reflected in water. (36)
"Endowed with Mohavajrā and the others" refers to those who were mentioned previously. "These six" refers to the eye and the other sense faculties. (33)

The objects of the senses are the sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth. Having placed the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) in the middle, he also speaks of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha), the aggregate of feeling (vedanāskandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha), and the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāraskandha). As it is said: "But one [cognition] is recognition, and the second is metaphorical. Both metaphor and discernment proceed from the mind alone. (34)

"Nature is primordially unarisen" means that the nature of objects and so forth is primordially unarisen. Likewise, it refers to the state of consciousness appearing as objects and so forth. These [objects] do not exist in accordance with how they appear; because they are non-existent, and because they are primordially unarisen, they are unarisen. They are "not real" because they lack existence in accordance with how they appear. They are "not false" because of the existence of mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*). "Like the moon in water" means that one aspect appears in the form of another aspect. "Knowing" refers to thorough knowledge. "And so forth" refers to what was previously stated. "These six" refers to the eye and so forth. "Subject" refers to the subjects, such as the eye and so forth. "Infinite formations" refers to the very fact that the aggregate of consciousness is placed in the middle—namely, the aggregate of form, the aggregate of consciousness, and the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations. As it has been said: "One is the consciousness of conditions, The second is the experiencer; Experience and discernment— Their nature is primordially unarisen. That which initiates its engagement is mental. This means that the nature of objects and so forth is primordially unarisen. Thus, regarding objects: *Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*: For example, when a fire-stick, a fire-drill, and the exertion of a person’s hand come together, why does fire arise? That fire does not abide in the fire-stick, nor in the fire-drill, nor in the exertion of the person’s hand. When sought in every possible way, it is not found even in any one of them. And yet, that fire is neither real nor false. In this same way, O Yoginīs, you should contemplate all phenomena in your minds.

Then all the Vajra-Ḍākinīs, headed by the Yoginī Nairātmyā, taking the five nectars and the samaya substances, worship the Blessed One Vajrasattva; they arouse passion through the *kunduru* yoga and cause him to drink the essence of the vajra nectar.
The meaning is: "If it is by your will," that is, if your desire exists, then such knowledge will come to pass.

The upper fire-stick (*uttarāraṇī*) is the shaft; the lower fire-stick (*adharāraṇi*) is that which is to be rubbed. "Depending upon" (*pratītya*) is the ellipsis, meaning "having reached. "Sudden" (*akasmāt*) means without an agent and without effort. "Does not exist" (*nāsti*) means it is not perceived. "Not real" (*na satyam*) because, contrary to how it appears, it lacks the nature of being either one or many. "Not false" (*na mṛṣā*) because the aspect of that [appearance], which is mere representation (*vijñaptimātra*), does exist. "Produce" (*kuruta*) means "should establish."
"Anurāgayantī" means they satisfy; "pibācayantī" means they cause them to drink.

Consciousness itself, appearing as [objects] such as forms and so forth, is the object and so on; yet it does not exist in the way that it appears. Because it does not exist [in that way], it is from the very beginning free from arising and is thus unarisen. "Not true" means that it is not as it appears. "Not false" means that it exists as mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*). "Like the moon in water" means that while it exists in one way, it appears in another way. "Knowing" refers to thorough comprehension. Regarding the phrase "if you desire," it means: "If you so desire, you shall understand it in that way. Then, after the Blessed One was pleased, he displayed his empowerment: "O, O Vajra-Ḍākinīs! Listen with interest to that which is honored by all the Buddhas! [Vajratantre, Chapter Three, titled "The Sandhyābhāṣa"] Thereafter, when the Blessed One was satisfied, he showed his blessing: "O, O Vajra-Ḍākinīs! Listen with desire to that which is saluted by all the Buddhas!"

"I shall now declare that reality which was kept secret by me through the power of the Vajra-worship. Then all the goddesses, having attained enthusiasm, placed their right knees upon the ground, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and listened to what the Blessed One spoke.
The Blessed One said: "One should eat and drink as obtained; one should not avoid women who may or may not be approached.
One should not perform ritual bathing or purification; one should not avoid sexual intercourse."
The wise one should neither recite mantras nor rely upon meditation; he should neither abandon sleep nor restrain the senses.
One should consume all the five-colored forces;
with a mind free from doubt, one sports with all women.
"When [the consort] is satisfied" means when she is pleased; that by which Vajrasattva bestows his blessing through its performance is "his empowerment," which he shows or reveals.
"Worship itself is the vajra" because of its firmness; "by its power" means by the force of that worship. "By desire" means with reverence.
The Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī: A Commentary on the Vajraśekhara Tantra Entitled "The Pearl Necklace"
One should not cultivate affection for friends, nor should one practice hatred toward those who are hostile; one should not pay homage to these deities made of wood, stone, or clay.
Since the yogi must always abide in the form of the deity, he should touch those who are difficult to touch— such as Dombas, Caṇḍālas,
leather-workers, and scavengers— as well as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others, just as he would his own body.

The five nectars (pañcāmṛta), molasses, wine, poison, neem, that which is born of a woman, the sour, sweet, and astringent tastes, and so forth; the foul-smelling, the fragrant, water, blood, and even that which is not food—likewise the bitter, salty, and pungent flavors [are all present].
One should consume with the thought of awakening, with the thought of awakening,
using a mind of non-dual gnosis.
Having obtained the *svayambhūkusuma*, one should place it in a lotus vessel;
then, having mixed it with phlegm and nasal mucus, the observer of the vow should drink it.
Having obtained a multicolored loincloth, ornaments made of clay shards,
and flowers from a cremation ground, he should bind his excellent hair.

"By the thought of awakening (bodhicitta)" means by a mind that appears as an illusion-like reflection or as being without appearance; this very point is stated as "by the non-dual gnosis-mind," where the gnosis of non-duality is without appearance, and "mind" (cetas) refers to conceptualization.

In touch is Īrṣyāvajrā, and in the mind is Nairātmyayoginī; O Mahāsattva, with these [mantras] one should perform the armor-rite for the purification of the sense faculties.

24. "Impure" means those whose sixfold number has been established without being purified by means of the forms of the deities; they are described as such. Therefore, the sense is: "Let their purification be stated.

Regarding the phrase "of every object": the purification of the deity for all objects of knowledge, such as the sense-objects and so forth, has already been stated previously; therefore, it is sought [here]—this is the intended meaning.
The purification of the eyes and so forth is to be established, as is their intrinsic nature, such as Mohavajrā and the others; therefore, from these [five], three case-endings arise.

*Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī* 41. Laughter, as well as gazing with the eyes, embracing, and likewise union; 42. even by means of the tantra, the intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣa*) of these four has not been expressed [literally].
The Blessed One said: "Vajragarbha, listen with a one-pointed mind to the detailed exposition of the conventions of the samaya."
46. I shall explain the twilight language (sandhyābhāṣa), the great language (mahābhāṣa), passion (madana), wine (madya), strength (bala), meat (māṃsa), sandalwood (malayaja), and union (milana).

By this, the state of being secret (*guhyatā*) has been stated; now he speaks of the state of being extremely secret (*atiguhyatā*) with the words beginning with "hasita" (smiling).
Among the four—Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Yogottara—that which is characterized therein by smiling and gazing, as well as by embracing and union:

for instance, in some Kriyā and other tantras, there is a smile indicating the passion between the Wisdom and Means of the deities; in some, a gaze upon the form; in some, an embrace; and in some, union.
Even by such [means] as the Kriyā and other tantras, this *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language) has not been uttered nor proclaimed;
it is to be proclaimed solely by the unsurpassed (*niruttara*) Yoga tantras.
Therefore, the sense is that it is "supremely secret."
If the mind has a single object, it is a one-pointed mind.

In the *Vajra-tantra*. 71. [The third chapter, titled "The Sandhyābhāṣa"] 73. O Vajragarbha, Mahāsattva! 74. The *asparśa* is declared to be the *ḍiṇḍima* drum; the skull-cup (*kapāla*) is the lotus vessel.
The food to be consumed is known as that which provides satisfaction, and the side dish is the fuel of jasmine.
Feces is said to be the four equal parts; urine is known as musk. Self-arisen [semen] is to be understood as camphor; semen is considered to be camphor.
78. Mahāmāṃsa is said to be that which is born of rice (śālija), and kunduru is the union of the two organs.
79. Vajra is known as bolaka, and padma is considered to be kakkolaka. 60.
The family (kula) is known to be fivefold, divided according to the distinction of castes (varṇa). Thus, by means of the twilight language (sandhyābhāṣā), there are the Buddhas and the five Kaulikas.
The Ḍombī is known as belonging to the Vajra family, and likewise the Naṭī belongs to the Padma family;
the Caṇḍālī belongs to the Ratna family, and the Brāhmaṇī is considered to belong to the Tathāgata family.
The washerwoman and the woman of the artisan caste—these mudrās grant excellent accomplishment. Their semen is the *vajra*; having worshipped it, the practitioner of the vow should drink it.
"The family (kula) is fivefold" is the intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā).
"By way of the distinction of colors" means having made the fifth [family] untouchable.
For here, the meaning of the seed-syllable (bīja) is the meaning of the family.
The Buddhas are the Kaulikas; it is through intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā) that they are thus called so, because of their arising from the Kula. 61.
89. A family (*kula*) is indeed a lineage (*kulī*); [these] are the lineages of the Vajra-family and so forth. Why are these called families?
Because 90. they bestow excellent accomplishment (*susiddhi*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Of these," and so forth.
"Vajra" refers to the fivefold bodhicitta. "Having worshipped" means having worshipped these very [deities]. (62–63)
