96. *Śvapacī*—Ga, Gha; *susiddhitāḥ*—Kha, Gha; *śukro*—Kha; *kulaniruttaratvam*—Gha. 97. *eva*—Gha; *svasiddhidāḥ*—Ka. 98–99. *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: O Mahāsattva, all that has been spoken by me should be respectfully received as the most wonderful *sandhyābhāṣa*. (64)
Whoever, having been consecrated here in Hevajra, does not speak in the sandhyābhāṣā (twilight language), for him there arises a violation of the samaya; of this there is no doubt. (65)
If he does not speak according to the intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*), he will die from planetary afflictions, fever, poison, and the like— even if he were a Buddha.
If one who knows their own tradition does not speak these words upon attaining [the state],
the Yoginīs born of the four seats (pīṭhas) will cause agitation.
The third chapter, titled "The Esoteric Language of the Introduction to All Tantras of Hevajra. || 64-65 ||
Even if he were a Buddha, he would not speak [of it].
The nidāna of all tantras and the intentional language (sandhyābhāṣa) that illuminates it have likewise been explained in this chapter.

In the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti, this is the third chapter, the Chapter on Intentional Language (*sandhyābhāṣa*), in the second section (*kalpa*).

The Fourth Chapter, titled *The Summary Meaning of the Seals of All Tantras of Hevajra*, known as the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*. Now, all the ḍākinīs, headed by Vajragarbha, having fallen into doubt and being overcome with dejection, spoke thus to the Blessed One, Vajrasattva:
"May the Blessed One dispel our doubt. (1)
Regarding that which was explained in the Caryāpaṭala—the song and the dance that bestow accomplishment—I have a doubt concerning them: what is the song, and what is the dance?

Regarding that which was taught concerning the sealing with hatred and the other [afflictions] following the consecration by the deities, a doubt arises in me: what is to be sealed, and by whom is the sealing performed? (3)
Regarding that which was taught in the Mantra Chapter concerning the seed-syllables of Nairātmyā and the others, a doubt has arisen within me: what is the seed, and whose seed is it? (4)
"May the Blessed Ones explain the purification of those channels consisting of thirty-two, which are proclaimed in the *Kulapaṭala*; an error has occurred in my [understanding]."
"Vajragarbha," and so forth.
"Foremost" means those who lead the way.
"Doubt" refers to...
Because it is difficult to distinguish [the two], there is doubt. || 1-2 ||
"By the deity-consecration" means: because of the statement in the chapter on the consecration of deities that "one being consecrated becomes the Lord of one's own family upon the crown of the head.
"Mudrā" means sealing. || 3 ||
"That which was proclaimed" refers to [the vowels] beginning with *a* and ending with *aṃ*. ||4||
In Kollaira they sing the *bolā*, in Mummuṇira the *kakkolāra*, and in Ghaṇakiviḍara the *ho-vājjai*; alas, in Karuṇe the *rolā* is not performed. 6.
There fine food is eaten and strong liquor is drunk;
O friend, the Dunduru drum resounds there at Kāliñjara.
Taking four-fold sandalwood, kacchuri, sihlā, and camphor, they eat their fill of this garland of fuel from the Śāliñja tree. || 7 ||
While swinging and playing with balls, they do not distinguish between the pure and the impure;
they climb onto limbs that are boneless and there they sell their very essence.
Along the path of the sandalwood and the musk, the drum sounds, excluding all else.
Kollagira is a particular sacred seat (pīṭha);
Mummuni is a particular field (kṣetra).
By this much, he indicates the instantaneous union of even those situated at a great distance.
*Ghaṇaa* is *ghamaka*; the suffix *ka* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). *Kipiṭṭa* is *kṛpīṭa*, meaning a small drum (*ḍamaruka*).
*Ho* is used as a vocative particle.
"Karuna" means with compassion.
"Kiai na" means it is not done. "Rolā" is a sound; it means a clamor.
*Māṇā* means crushing (*mardana*).
*Pijjaa*: the word *pijja* is a different verbal root. *Śāli* is that which is produced from non-śāli.
Bharu means abundant. || 6-7 ||
*aṅga* means "on the limbs";
*caḍābī* means "having placed upon";
*tahiṃ je* means "and there."
*Sarāveti* means *śrāvayati* (he causes to hear). *Paṇiai* means *praveśyate* (it is introduced).
By this much, four four-line verses have been stated; at the end of the two halves, the *sayamakā* [rhyme] has been mentioned.
In each foot of these [verses], there are three groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*).
In two of the *gāthās*, according to the previous rule, the third group consists of two morae.
At the end of all four *gāthās*, a refrain (*dhruvaka*) must be sung; this very point he expresses with the words beginning "malayaja" and so forth. (8)

In the Vajra Tantra, [the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing"]: One should perform the dance in the form of Śrī Heruka through the yoga of unimpaired mindfulness; one should practice meditation with a red-colored mind and a consciousness of unremitting cultivation. (9)
By the Vajradharmas, as well as by the Buddhas, the Yoginīs, and the Mothers—
through these two, song and dance— the Supreme is sung and danced.

By this very [mantra], there is protection of the community and likewise protection of oneself; by this very [mantra], one gains mastery over the world, and through it, the recitation of the mantra is accomplished.
Where it is sung with devotion and where it is danced with devotion,
placing the Lord of the Gaṇas at the forefront, there one should perceive the sense of smell.
One should perceive garlic as the first scent, then the vulture-scent, followed by camphor and sandalwood; thereafter, one should observe the locus of the song.
"Regarding 'nāṭya' and so forth:

the recollection of oneself in the form of Heruka which, due to its firmness, is not lost—that [recollection] is the basis for the yoga. By means of that, i.e., by possessing that state. Of that very recollection: cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the continuous occurrence; in this, the mind is attached (*rakta*), which is application with reverence (*satkṛtya-prayoga*). Continuous cultivation through uninterrupted practice is constant application (*sātatyaprayoga*). (9)

"By the Vajra-dharmas" means by those very three [deities] in the form of Padmanarteśvara. "By the Buddhas" means in the form of Vairocana. "By the Mothers" means by the Blessed Ladies in the form of Nairātmyā and so forth; such is the meaning. "Supremely" (param) means exceedingly. Alternatively, it means supreme through these two alone, and not through ordinary song and dance. || 10 ||
"Vaśam" means "submissive. "By this" means by this very [mantra]. || 11 ||
"Nose" refers to fragrance; "Malayaja" is sandalwood; the "abode of song" is its characteristic mark or sign, [perceived] by the yogis and yoginīs. || 12-13 ||
In the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*, it is stated: "The cry of a swan and the song of a bee are heard as remnants of music; one should also observe the sound of a jackal in the outer garden. (14)
Sealing, joining, and the family (kula) are characterized by the mark; if the family is disordered, there is neither accomplishment through the yoga of meditation nor a practitioner. || 15 ||
One should seal Nairātmyā with the seal of hatred, Vajrā with the seal of delusion, Gaurī with the seal of malice, and Vārī with the seal of passion. || 16 ||
One should worship Ḍākinī with the mudrā of envy, Pukkasī from the mudrā of hatred, Śavarī with the mudrā of delusion, and Caṇḍālī with the mudrā of malice. || 17 ||
One should worship Ḍombī with the mudrā of passion (rāga), Gaurī again with hatred (dveṣa), Caurī with the mudrā of delusion (moha), and Vetālī with the mudrā of malice (piśuna). || 18 ||

He states another sign, beginning with "rutam" and so forth. The phrase "even in an external garden" includes "also in the sky" by virtue of the word "api. By this much, the first question has been answered. || 14 ||

He speaks to provide a response to the second [point]: "Sealing" (mudraṇa) is the meaning. Sealing, embracing (liṅgana), and marking (aṅka) are synonyms. To whom does the embracing belong? He says: "By the mark (aṅka) the lineage (kula) is characterized. When a lineage is separated from another lineage—that is, when it is sealed by another lineage—if there is an application of meditation (bhāvanā) upon that [separated state], there is neither accomplishment (siddhi) nor a practitioner (sādhaka). Therefore, the sense is that one must exert effort in the rule of sealing, lest there be confusion regarding yoga. || 15 ||
"Selflessness," and so forth. Here, hatred, delusion, slander, passion, and envy correspond respectively to Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi. (16–18)

One should seal Khecarī with the Rāga-mudrā, Ghasmarī with the Rāga-mudrā, and Bhūcarī with the Moha-mudrā; one should understand this sealing according to one's desire, as stated in the Vajra-tantra. [This is the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing."]
The second [deity] from Vajrāli is Vāriyoginī. 20.

Āle is the first Nairātmyā; Āle is the third; Gaurī is the fourth; Vajraḍākī is the fifth; Pukkasī is considered the sixth; Śavarī is indeed the seventh; and Caṇḍālī is remembered as the eighth. || 21 ||
The ninth is Ḍombinī, and Gaurī again is the tenth; Caurī is known as the eleventh, and Vetālī is considered the twelfth. || 22 ||

Ghasmarī is the thirteenth, Bhūcarī the fourteenth, and Khecarī the fifteenth; these are the respective seed-syllables (*svabīja*) of the Yoginīs. Regarding the channels (*nāḍī*) described in the *Kulapaṭala* as consisting of thirty-two-fold [groups], each pair of channels corresponds respectively to one Yoginī, by means of her will—or rather, by mere intention (*icchāmātra*)—through faith. 19.
Thus it is considered. || 24 ||

Because of the explicit mention of the manifest [syllable], he says "āleḥ" and so forth in order to answer the third [question]. "Āleḥ" means the letter *a* is its beginning. "Nairātmye" means the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Nairātmyā. || 20 ||
"Two fives" refers to the tenth [chapter]. || 22 ||

He speaks to answer the fourth [question], beginning with "the chapter on the family" (*kulapaṭala*) and so forth. "Twice sixteen" means thirty-two. "Two pairs of channels" (*nāḍīdvayadvaya*) means two channels each. "The yoginīs one by one in sequence" means that each individual yoginī follows the proper order. || 24 ||

In the *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*, it is held that Lalanā, Rasanā, and Avadhūtī are considered the Yoginī Nairātmyā; one should diligently abandon all the others, since they do not possess the sixteenth digit (*kalā*).

Because it does not perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) would be the moon consisting of fifteen digits; its form is the *ālī*, which is great bliss, and the yoginīs are its rays.
Vajragarbha said: Why indeed is camphor not an offering for them, since it arises from all yoginīs, has the nature of innate bliss, is imperishable, substantial, and moves through the sky?

"Lalanā," and so forth. The three channels, beginning with Lalanā, are one [with] the Yoginī Nairātmyā. Now, there are thirty-two channels; half of that is sixteen *kalās*, which constitute the *Āli*. Why, then, is the sixteenth *kalā* abandoned? To this he says: "All," and so forth. "The remainder of all" means the very last, namely the syllable *Aḥ*. Why? He says: "The sixteenth," and so forth.

"Non-acting" (*akaraṇa*) means that which does not act; for thus, in the sequence of lunar days (*tithi*), fifteen lunar digits (*candrakalā*) manifest during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) and provide illumination for the world. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The thought of awakening" (*bodhicitta*), and so forth. "Parts" (*aṃśaka*) refers to the digits (*kalā*). Here, by the statement "just as the first Yoginī [is], so too are the three channels," it is stated by implication (*sāmarthyāt*); otherwise, there would be no inclusion of the two channels within the Yoginīs.

"Camphor," and so forth. This is an unprecedented question. The word "kiṃ" is used in the sense of a question. It is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because of its permanence. It is "pīvara" (plump) because of its pervasiveness. It is "khaga" (sky-goer) because its sole essence is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). [Regarding the variants: *nairātmaka*, *nairātmā* [variants *kha*, *ga*, *gha*]; *matā* [variants *ka*, *kha*, *ga*; *mataḥ* *ṭa*]; *śeṣā* [variants *ka*, *gha*]; *nāsti* [variant *gha*]; "because of being the instrument of action" [variants *ka*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *ṭa*; "because of being non-instrument" *kha*, *cha*, *jha*]; "consisting of fifteen digits" [variant *kha*; "consisting of fifteen digits" *gha*]; "parrots" [variants *ka*, *ghu*; "and his doubt" *ga*]; "camphor" [variant *ka*; "camphor" *gha*]; "the source of all Yoginīs" *gha*; "Cāveya" *ga*, *gha*; "pīvara" *ga*, *gha*; "likewise by the statement of the channel-array" *ka*, *kha*. This is indeed unprecedented. In the *Vajratantre*, in the chapter titled "The Essential Meaning of the Seals" (*Mudrāpiṇḍārtha*), the fourth, and in the *Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*: "In this very way, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); apart from cyclic existence, there is no other nirvāṇa"—thus the Blessed One said. "It is exactly as you say. Vajragarbha asked: "By what means is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) to be generated?"

The Blessed One said: By means of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, and through the process of self-consecration, one should generate the bodhicitta which consists of both the ultimate and the conventional forms.
Closed, it resembles a kunda flower; opened, it has the form of bliss.
It is the very nature of the syllable EṂ, located within the *kakkola* of the woman in the Sukhāvatī.
Precisely because it protects happiness, it is called "Sukhāvatī," the support for Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajra-holders.
The meaning is that what you say is not to be abandoned.
"Maṇḍalacakra and so forth"—the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes even the yoga of the solitary hero (*ekavīrayoga*).
The stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*) and the stage of generation (*utpannakrama*) are those taught in the eighth chapter.
To the question "Where is it to be produced? he says: "A woman," and so forth.
How is it that it is called "Sukhāvatī"? He says: "Of happiness," and so forth.
[The root] *ava* is used in the senses of protecting (*rakṣaṇa*), going (*gati*), delighting (*prīti*), satisfying (*tṛpti*), and understanding (*avagama*).
It is called Sukhāvatī because it constantly protects (*avati*) and establishes (*sthāpayati*) happiness.
It is derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes like *vasati*.
How is it the support of the Vajradhara?
Because the Vajrin is great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
How [is it] for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
Because they are gathered by them.
—This section is not present in manuscripts *ka* and *gha*.
*Maṇḍala* [is attained] by means of the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth—*ka*, *kha*.
*Adhiṣṭhāna*—*ka*.
Gha: *vivṛti*—ka, kha, ga; *saṃvṛti*—ka; *saṃvṛte*—ga; *saṃvṛtiṃ*—gha.
*Kuṇḍa*—ka, kha, gha; *kundu*—ga.
*vivṛttim*—ka, gha; *vivṛtim*—ga | *strīkakkole svarūpakam*—ka; *strīkakkole*—kha.
gha | "The Lord"—ka. gha; "from the very definition of the Lord"—kha.
śābditaṃ—ka; trisandhitaṃ—ga | dhāriṇaḥ—ka, gha; dhāriṇaṃ—kha; dhārināḥ—ga |
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Dra-prathama-kalparāja*.
Nirvāṇa is described in this very way.
Form, sound, and the rest are saṃsāra; feeling and the rest are saṃsāra.
The sense faculties themselves are saṃsāra; hatred and the rest are saṃsāra.
These very phenomena are nirvāṇa, yet through delusion they take the form of saṃsāra.
For one who wanders through cyclic existence without delusion, that very saṃsāra becomes nirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is the bodhicitta, which takes the form of the manifest relative truth—
a woman with a beautiful face and wide eyes, adorned with beauty and youth.
"But surely this happiness exists only within saṃsāra, while we are seekers of nirvāṇa?
To this he says: "In this very way," and so forth.
Here, both saṃsāra and its path are called "saṃsāra," and both nirvāṇa and its path are called "nirvāṇa."
It is understood that he practices accordingly.
He states the logical justification with the words beginning "saṃsāra" (cyclic existence) and so forth.
"These" refers to form, sensation, the eye, hatred, and so on.

They are "nirvāṇas" from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because all phenomena (*dharma*) are merely non-dual luminosity; because that which appears as duality lacks a substantial body (*aśarīra*); and because those appearances, being errors, are adventitious.
How, then, is this very [reality] saṃsāra? To this he says: "from delusion," and so forth.
"From delusion" means from ignorance; that is to say, from the error of duality.
"The undeluded" refers to one who is free from error; "saṃsāra" refers to the state of one who wanders in saṃsāra.
"Extending to extinction" means it becomes like nirvana.
He asks, "How so? and says: "For *nirvṛti* is the bodhicitta, while *vivṛti* has the form of *saṃvṛti*.
Because for one who is undeluded, *vivṛti* is like the *dharmakāya*, and *saṃvṛti* is like the *sambhogakāya*.
By this much, it is consistent with the statement that "one should not abandon the camphor."
He states what constitutes the abandonment of that [desire]: "The lovely-faced one," and so forth.
— *saṃsāre* — Ka, Ga; *saṃsāro* — Gha.
The phrase "evameva tu" is not present in the Ka manuscript.
One does not attain nirvāṇa elsewhere—ka, kha, ga, gha; one attains what is called "nirvāṇa"—he, paṃ, mu, va; saṃsāra is seen—cha; saṃsāra is perceived—jha.
[The suffixes] śabda-ādayaḥ—cha; śabda-ādayaḥ—jha. Ami—ga, gha.
But the dharmas— tu-kha.gha;
from nirvāṇa— ka.gha, nirvāṇā— hepaṃmuva, nirvāṇa— khaga.
Formless—kha.
Born from the flow of nectar, O you who go to nectar—ga.
Cessation—ka.
*Gha*, *dra*—the reading is *hepaṃmuva pāṭhaḥ*; *nirvṛtibodhicittaṃ*—*ṅa*. *ca*. *ṭa*; *hi*—*ka*. *ga*. *gha*. *hepaṃmuva*. *he yo ra mā*.
*nirvṛti-saṃvṛti*—cha, jha; *vivṛtirūpakaṃ*—ja; *saṃvṛti-vivṛti*—bho;
*cāruvaktrā*—ka.

Ga Gha | Viśālākṣī— Ka Kha Ga Gha | Maṇḍitāḥ— In the *Vajratantro*, the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of the Seals": [One should seek] a woman who is dark-complexioned, steadfast, of noble lineage, and born from the essence of musk and camphor.
But [one who is] consecrated by oneself in Hevajra, with beautiful hair and dear to the practitioner. || 36 ||
One should cause her to drink the *madana* (intoxicant) and then drink it oneself;
afterwards, one should arouse passion in the *mudrā*.
Having inserted the *bolaka* into the *kakkola*, the observer of the vow produces the *kunduru*; the wise one should not discard the camphor that has arisen from that union. || 38 ||
Of Bala indeed. || 39 || || 40 ||

It cannot be grasped by the hand, nor by mother-of-pearl, nor by conch shells; it is the nectar to be taken with the tongue for the sake of increasing [wisdom]. Camphor itself is *nairātmyā* (selflessness), whose form is blissful selflessness; its bliss is established as *mahāmudrā* in the circle of the navel. She, whose nature is the primordial vowel (*ādisvara*), is conceived by the Buddhas as *dhīti* (insight).
She alone is the Blessed Lady Prajñā, through the yoga of the *utpannakrama* (completion stage). (41)
"Mudrā" refers to the very one under discussion [in the preceding context]. || 37 ||
"For fuel" means for growth. || 39 ||
"Having the form of selflessness" means having the nature of selflessness (*nairātmyā*).
"Of that" refers to [the goddess] Nairātmyā.
"Bliss" refers to the bliss of *bola* (semen), which has the nature of Heruka and the form of the syllable *HŪṂ*, located in the navel-mandala. (40)
"Sā" means selflessness (nairātmyā).
"Dhī" means wisdom (prajñā).
"Prajñā" means supreme knowledge (prakṛṣṭajñāna).
"Yogataḥ" means in yoga. || 41 ||
The *Hevajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* states: "It is neither long nor short, neither square nor round;
transcending taste, smell, and flavor, it brings about innate bliss. (42)
In her the yogi arises and he enjoys her bliss; together with her comes accomplishment, the Mahāmudrā who bestows happiness.
Form, sound, as well as smell, taste, and likewise touch, and that which has the nature of the dharma-element, are experienced by wisdom alone. (44)
She alone is the divine Yoginī of great bliss, whose nature is the innate (sahaja);
she alone is the mandala-circle, whose very form is the five wisdoms. 45.
She is the embodiment of the wisdom of equality, she is the nature of the mirror-like wisdom, she is the discernment of reality, and she is indeed the wisdom of accomplishing activities. (46)
That very one is the utterly pure dharmadhātu; she herself is I, the Lord of the Maṇḍala.
She herself is the Yoginī Nairātmyā; her own nature is the dharmadhātu. (47)

In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing"]: Vajragarbha said: "The Blessed One previously taught the arising of the deities according to the path of meditating on the wheels; now, please tell me the *saṃvara*. (48)
The Blessed One said:
"The syllable A, abiding as the *saṃvara* within the body of the Yoginī—just as it is externally, so it is internally; that *saṃvara* has been revealed. (49)
Vajragarbha said:
What did he say? He spoke the sixth question beginning with "the wheel" (*cakra*) and so forth.
In the context of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), this is the meaning: the wheel is the maṇḍala consisting of the support and the supported.
The path of cultivation is the very sequence of its arising.
Regarding "the emergence of bliss for the deities":
it is just as the production of bliss occurs for the deities there.
In the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*), however, this is the meaning: the wheel is non-conceptual bliss;
cultivation is movement; the path is the lotus and the vajra;
and the arising of the deities' bliss is the lunar fluid—all of this has been explained in detail in the eighth chapter.
"Not a new restraint"—the remainder of the question is "of what kind? This much constitutes the inquiry;
"tell me" is the request. (48)
He said: "What did he say? [The reply is:
"The answer beginning with 'by the Yoginī,' and so forth."
The "middle of the body" is the navel.
"The letter A" refers to the first vowel.
"Situated" means it is indeed stable and eternal.
"Of the Yoginī" refers to Nairātmyā.
"Saṃvara" means restraint (*saṃvara*).
He explains the meaning of the word "saṃvara" with the words beginning with "yathā" (as follows).

Just as it is externally, so too should it be viewed internally; the meaning is that it is not less than that. Because it is enclosed within the body, or because it is more condensed, the sense is that it is a "confinement" (*saṃvara*).
Thus, it is stated here that just as the body belongs to the Nairātmyā, so too does the *Skāra* located at the navel. || 49 ||

2. Arising of Bliss (Sukhodaya); 3. The Blessed One (Bhagavān) Kha; 4. All the limbs of restraint (Saṃvaraṅga), not something new; 5. The letter A of the Yoginī; 6. The restraint (Saṃvara) abiding; 7. Fully revealed; 8. The accomplishment of the arising of bliss (Sukhodayasiddhi); 9. By means of the lotus and vajra; 10. The arising of bliss of Hevajra, the melting of the moon (Candradrava), the melting of the moon according to the arising of the deities; 11. The question; 12. One's own mind (Ātmaceta); 13. Not remaining at all; 14. The restraint (Saṃvara); 15. "Then," and so forth (Athetyādi); 16. The bliss of the *bola* (Bolasaukhya); 17. The Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī; 18. Mahāmudrā is the vajra-sphere (Vajrāyatana), the skillful means (Upāyaka).
19. By means of this secret union, the external pair is illustrated. || 50 ||

20. The three bodies (trikāya) within the center of the body are said to exist in the form of wheels (cakras). 21. The five wisdoms of the three bodies are considered to be the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukha). 51.
22. Likewise, there is the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*), the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
23–24. These three bodies are established in the womb, the heart, the throat, and the head. || 52 ||

25. Wherever there is the birth of all sentient beings without exception, 26. there the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) exists; the emanation is stable. 27. It is thus proclaimed. 28. This is the view. || 53 ||

30. *Bolasaukhyam* (the bliss of the *bola*): when the tip of the *bola* has reached the letter *A* at the navel, the syllable *HŪṂ* has reached the tip of the letter *A* at the heart. 31. *Bolasaukhyam*: that is Mahāmudrā; the meaning is the *saṃvara* (vow/union) of the yogin, the deity Heruka.
That itself is the *vajrāyatana*. 32. *Bodhicitta*: that indeed is the *upāya* (skillful means).
[This occurs] through the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of the two secrets, the letter *A* and the syllable *HŪṂ*.
The external pair (33) is the sexual union of Nairātmyā and the body of Heruka.
The meaning is that it is "shown" by being cast forth, which is to say, it becomes manifest. || 50 ||
34. "The three bodies," and so forth.
For each of all the Buddhas, there is an infinite *nirmāṇakāya*, an infinite *dharmakāya*, and an infinite *saṃbhogakāya*; these constitute the "three bodies.
That [deity] resides in the center of that body.
How is that demonstrated? By which restraint (*saṃvara*)?
By means of the form of the wheels—that is, by means of the three wheels beginning with the *nirmāṇa*-wheel—in the shape of lotuses having sixty-four petals, eight petals, and sixteen petals.
The thorough knowledge of those very three bodies is the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*), the *svābhāvika-kāya*.
That very same infinite fourth body of the Buddhas is the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
The meaning is that it is demonstrated by way of the *saṃvara* in the form of the wheel of great bliss, in the shape of a thirty-two-petaled lotus. || 51 ||
40. He states the names of the wheels: "Dharma," and so forth.
He states the locations: "Yoni," and so forth.
The yoni-location (41) is the yoni, which is below the navel of women and men.
"Three bodies"—the remainder [of the sentence] is "together with the fourth. || 52 ||
42. To demonstrate the reasoning regarding the connection of the locations, he says: "of all without exception," and so forth.
"Wherein" means in which womb.
43. "Is sung" means it is well-known.
In that context, the word "syāt" (it may be) is used because [the object] is proximate by virtue of being the means for producing a magical creation (*nirmiti*).

44. *bolasaukhya* (ka. ga. gha) 45. *mahatsukhaṃ* (ka. ga) 46. *mahatsukhaṃ* (ga) 47. *yoginyā* (kha), *yoginī* (ga), *yoginyo* (cha. jha) 48. *trayo* (ka. gha) 49. *yata utpatti* (ka) 50. *pratīyate* (ka), *pratiyate* (kha. ga), *nimīyate* (cha), *utpadyate* (ja), *pramīyate* (jha) 51. *nirvāṇa* (ka. gha) 52. *sthaviraṃ* (ka), *sthavaraṃ* (kha. gha) 53. *yataḥ* (ka. gha. he0paṃ0 mu0va0) 54. *svaratam* (ka) 55. *yoginītyādi* (ka) 56. *caturthaḥ* 57. *vajratantre* 58. [The Chapter titled "The Summary Meaning of the Seals" (*mudraṇapiṇḍārtha*)] 60. That by which [something] arises or is created is considered the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇika*). 61. But Dharma is the nature of the mind; thus the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*) resides in the heart. || 54 ||
62. Enjoyment is said to be that which experiences the sixfold nature of the tastes.
63. The wheel of enjoyment (saṃbhogacakra) is at the throat, and great bliss (mahāsukha) is situated at the head. 55.
Furthermore, emanation is "stable" because the emanations of the bodies and so forth of the Buddhas and Vajradharas remain for as long as there is work to be done for the benefit of sentient beings.
Therefore, by virtue of this stability, the womb (*yoni*) itself is its locus due to proximity. How is the womb stable?
Because of its triangular nature, it shares the same properties as the earth. || 53 ||

67. [Objection: Is it not the case that when the *nirmāṇakāya* arises, the agent (*kartṛ*) is the creator, while the womb (*yoni*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*); therefore, the two are not equal in their status as means of production? 68. [Response: He says: "It arises," and so forth; "it is emanated" (*nirmyate*), meaning it is emanated (*nirmīyate*). 69.
The meaning of this is that "it arises" is used in the sense of the reflexive passive (*karmakartari*).

Buddhas are born by means of the *nirmāṇakāya*, yet they are not born from a womb. Sentient beings are born by means of a womb; and that which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is also the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in "he cooks in a pot" or "he cooks with a pot.
Thus, in these two cases, their status as an instrument for the act of arising is equal.
"Dharma" refers to the correct discernment of all phenomena.
"The nature of the mind" means it is not distinct from the mind.
"The Dharma-body" refers to the locus of the Dharma-body, because it is the locus of the mind. || 54 ||
74. "Of those having the nature of rasa" means of the *rasas*.
The word "throat" (*kaṇṭha*) is connected with what precedes.
75. And "the wheel of enjoyment" (*sambhogacakra*)—the word "throat" is understood here—the sense being that it is due to the commonality of enjoyment (*sambhoga*).
What, then, is the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)? It is the teaching of the secrets of the Dharma. "Great Bliss" is the fourth body.
"Situated on the head" means on the head itself; the sense is that it is so because it is the location of the Moon and because it is the highest limb. || 55 ||

78. *utpadyante* (kha), *utpādyate* (ṭa) 79. *nirmayante* (kha), *nimyate ca* (ga) 80. *nirmāṇikai-* (kha), *kāya-* 81. *nairmāṇikaṃ* (ga) 82. *smṛtam* (kha); this portion of the verse does not exist in the manuscripts *ka* and *gha*. 83. *dharmaṃ citta0* (ka, kha) 84. *dharmadhātu0* (ga; *he0*, *paṃ0*, *mu0*, *va0*) 85. *dharmakāyaṃ ca* (ka, kha, ga, gha; *dharmakāyaṃ* in *he0*, *paṃ0*, *mu0*, *va0*) 86. *rasarūpiṇām* (ga, ṅaja, *he0*, *paṃ0*, *mu0*, *va0*; *rūpiṇā* in cha, jha) 87. *cakraṃ tu* (kha; *saṃbhogacakraśca* in *he0*, *paṃ0*, *mu0*, *va0*) 88. *sthāvaraṃ* (gha) 89. *dharmam iti cittaṃ* (Bhoṭa)
90. *Hevajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* 91. Within the syllable *Evaṃ*, there is the outflow (*niṣyanda*); from the wheel of Dharma, the ripening (*vipāka*);
92. the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) in the wheel of enjoyment (*sambhoga*), and stainlessness (*vaimalya*) in the wheel of bliss (*sukha*). (56)
93. The fruit is said to be fourfold, distinguished by the outflow (niṣyanda) and the others.
94. The Blessed Wisdom is the enjoyer of karma, impelled by the wind of karma. || 57 ||
95. As it was done, so it is experienced; this is designated as "outflow" (*niṣyanda*). 96. Its opposite is "ripening" (*vipāka*); even from a small action, there is a great fruit.
97. "Human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) is acquisition; "purity" (*vaimalya*) arises from the purification of yoga.
98. || 58 || O Bird, from the Wheel of Dharma, the wheel-crest is produced as a natural outflow (*niṣyanda*).

Human effort (*puruṣakāra*), human exertion, and the person—all this is stainless, yet it is not differentiated from action; for action is designated as the wind of action. In the application of slight stainlessness within action, there is no verbal expression of the fruit of purity through the yoga of stainlessness. This verse begins with "atha" and so forth; see the *Abhidharmakośa*. In the *Vajratantropiṇḍārtha*, chapter four, titled "The Summary Meaning of the Seals," it is said in the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: "In the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*), the emanation is stable (*sthāvara*) because it is stable."
In the Sarvāstivāda and in the Wheel of Dharma, there arises the discourse on the Dharma.
Because consciousness resides in the enjoyment wheel at the throat, it is the Great Assembly; and because great bliss resides in the wheel of great bliss at the head, it is the Great Bliss.

The "nikāya" (assembly) is said to be the body; from one who is free from passion, the belly becomes [the assembly]. The womb is called the "residence" (*jarāyu-vihāra*), and the blazing garment is [the residence]. Likewise: the cupped hands at the head;

the preceptor (*upādhyāyī*) is likewise the mother; salutation, the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), the duties of the world, and the recitation of mantras—I am the "Immovable One" (*sthāvarī*) due to my connection with immovability.
Because all true doctrines arise from this, it is the Sarvāstivāda, the source and cause of all philosophical systems.
Because of the conjunction with consciousness, it is consciousness;
because of its extreme hardness, it is the "Great Assembly" (Mahāsaṃgha) head; and because of that conjunction, it is the "Belonging to the Great Assembly" (Mahāsaṃghī).
Therefore, he says: "What is that by which one is established? The terms *sthāvarya* and so forth are synonyms for the terms *sthāvarī* and so forth.
In that regard, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā through the secret union has been described;

by means of the four wheels (*cakras*), there is the attainment of the four bodies (*kāyas*), the attainment of the fruit of all virtues, the attainment of the state of a Śrāvaka, and the attainment of the assembly of noble Bodhisattvas—in brief, because of the acquisition of the three or four bodies.
Now he describes in detail the excellence of the assembly of bodhisattvas, beginning with the words "the womb":
"the womb" refers to the mother's belly;
at the time of birth, they are free from passion (*vītarāgau*).
Because there is an absence of passion even during friction, it is free from the membrane of the womb, radiant, and unfading.
The breath is "I" (aham), and the recitation of the mantra is "so be it" (tathā) just as "I" (yathāham); likewise, there are the syllables *akāra* and *haṃkāra*.
The syllable *bha* is the womb of the wheel, and the syllable *ha* is that of great bliss;
the monk born [therein] is the sounding mantra, naked, with his head and beard shaven.
Through these collections of conditions, sentient beings are indeed Buddhas, without a doubt;
the ten stages and the ten months are the sentient beings who are masters of the ten stages.
Then all the goddesses, headed by the Yoginī Nairātmyā—
namely Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, Cundā, Parṇaśavarī, Ahomukhā, and others such as these— numbering as many as the atoms in Mount Sumeru, were struck with supreme amazement.

Having heard these words of Bhāratī, they fainted, were terrified, and fell to the ground; seeing all those goddesses overcome by fear, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin) praised them in order to restore them.
"Uttering the mantra"— this very triad is "naked," meaning one whose girdle is unbuckled.
He is called the "Lord of the Ten Stages" at the time of birth; thereafter, he is called "Buddha" because of his awakening to all things stable and moving.
Furthermore, the stomach and other internal organs are to be seen as the vows (*saṃvara*) for external dwellings and so forth, for the purpose of establishing others in the ten stages.
"This speech" refers to the statement that "beings are indeed Buddhas."

The syllable *Aṃ* is the wheel of Yoginīs; the syllable *Haṃ* and the syllable *Hūṃ* are the mantra of wealth. With the ritual implements (*sāmagrībhiḥ*)—naked, with shaven heads and beards—all the goddesses, Nairātmā, Māmikā, Pāṇḍarā, and Cundā, likewise with faces turned downward, fell down, terrified by the visualization of the two Yoginīs. Shaking all those goddesses, there is no lineage [superior] to the Lord of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*). This is the fourth chapter in the Vajra-tantra, titled "The Sealing and the Summary Meaning" (*mudraṇapiṇḍārtha*). O Earth, Water, Wind, Fire, and Space, you brothers, listen, O Goddesses! I shall speak that which no one at all knows.
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, which were like a dream, they all regained their lives.
The Blessed One said: "Sentient beings are indeed Buddhas, but they are obscured by adventitious defilements;
through the removal of those, sentient beings are indeed Buddhas—of this there is no doubt."
Regarding the passage beginning with "earth and water" (*kṣitijala*), etc.:
why is it that in the case of the unjoined (*ayukta*) and so forth there are fourteen *mātrās*, whereas in the case of the joined (*yukta*) and so forth there are twelve *mātrās*?
This is a crossroads of earth, water, air, and fire; O sisters, O goddesses,
I shall explain the truth of this beautiful manifestation to you— the meaning being that no one at all knows this object of measurement.
Sentient beings are indeed Buddhas; for suchness itself, when perfectly purified, is the Buddha, and that is perfectly pure by its very nature.
If it is asked, "Why is this not realized?
he says: "But... and so forth. (Verse 69)
The goddesses of the *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī* said: "So it is, Blessed One; this is true, not false. (70)

The Blessed One said: "Eat that poison for which there is no remedy—those who are free from delusion and worldly attachment, whose minds are fixed on the Supreme Reality, they alone shall be satisfied. (71)
Likewise, those who know the means for liberation and have exerted themselves in the Hevajra tantras are not seized by ignorance and the like, nor by the bonds of delusion and so forth. (72)
There is not a single being who is not a Buddha, because of their own respective awakening as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, asuras, and humans. (73)

The statement beginning with "evam" (thus) refers to the goddesses: "evam" is the general designation, "satyam" (truth) is the specification, and "na mṛṣā" (not false) is the counter-specification, provided they are not covered by impurities. || 70 ||
They are indeed obstructed by these [afflictions]; for what reason, then, do they possess awakening? To this he says: "For whom," and so forth. The world reels at the consumption of poison;

but he who is devoid of consciousness (*niścetana*) regarding the non-poisonous state possesses mental activity (*manaskarma*) here as true consciousness (*cetanā*), because of his knowledge of the true nature of poison, which is free from delusion (*moha*).

One whose mind is fixed on the reality that removes poison is "one whose mind is fixed on reality" (*tattvamanāḥ*); the word "he" (*yaḥ*) from the previous verse carries over here. For him, supreme sorrow is severed—sorrow produced by the affliction of having consumed poison.
This is the illustration. || 71 ||
He states the application to the subject at hand with the words beginning "in the same way":
*nirvṛtiḥ* means liberation;
*sukṛtaśramāḥ* means those who have well-performed their exertion.

Non-afflicted ignorance is *avidyā*; here, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes envy, anger, indolence, and others which are designated as *avidyā*. Defilement (*kleśa*) is delusion (*moha*); from the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), hatred, passion, and others are included; these alone are the bonds, by means of which [one is bound]. || 72 ||
Regarding the point that "sentient beings are indeed Buddhas," he states another logical argument beginning with "abuddha" and so forth;
"sattvaika" means even a single sentient being.

"From awakening" (*saṃbodhāt*) means from the awareness (*saṃvedanāt*) of one's own mind; the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), and the singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāv ekavacanam*), meaning "by all minds.

To the question "of what is there awareness by them?", he says: "and of one's own. In the *Vajratantre*, [the fourth chapter titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing"]: "But worms and such that dwell in filth are eternally happy by their very nature."
For they do not know the happiness that belongs even to the gods and the asuras. 74.
The Buddha is not found elsewhere; for he is indeed the perfectly awakened one who is nothing but the mind itself. Nowhere in the world-realms is a Buddha manifested other than as this. || 75 ||
Even those such as Caṇḍālas and Caṇḍakāras, whose minds are intent on the purpose of killing, achieve accomplishment by resorting to Hevajra; there is no doubt in this matter. (76)
Enveloped by ignorance and unaware of this goal,
these fools wander through the prison of existence within the six realms of rebirth.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis, meaning "of the very intrinsic nature" (*svarūpasyaiva*).

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is precisely the absence of duality; the vision of that is the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and that alone is awakening (*bodhi*). Thus, all sentient beings are indeed Buddhas.
Enlightenment is certainly not merely the vision of emptiness;
what then? It is great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
And yet, do those in the hells and other such realms not possess that happiness?
To this he says: "In the hells," and so forth. (73)
"By way of intrinsic nature" means by way of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); the meaning is "by way of equality," which is to say that there is no distinction in the mere perception of emptiness.
Now, one might object: is it not the case that the happiness of the gods and asuras is such that the happiness of those in the hells and other realms does not exist?

It should not be thought that they do not know this, for even the happiness of gods and asuras is not truly seen by the noble ones as happiness; because it is impermanent and thus involves the suffering of separation, and because, being subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), it serves as the cause for further suffering.
Therefore, great bliss alone is true happiness;
and just as it exists for the gods, so too does it exist for those in the hells, by virtue of non-conceptual equanimity.
He states another argument with the words "not the Buddha" and so forth;
"elsewhere" means other than one's own mind;
therefore, as [it is] at the end...
The very mind of sentient beings is enlightenment, because their minds were already equal even prior to that. || 75 ||

With the words beginning "caṇḍāla," he speaks of the greatness of the tantra: "Hevajra" means that by the syllable *he*, compassion (*karuṇā*) is intended, which is the meaning of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); "Vajra" means wisdom (*prajñā*), which is the meaning of the vision of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
"Having approached" (*āgamya*) means having brought this Hevajra to manifestation through the logical arguments just mentioned.
"Gati" means "nīti" (policy or conduct). || 76-77 ||

Having obtained the means, they purify the Hevajra and the Vajragarbha, and they shall attain the sense objects. Vajragarbha said; the Blessed One said: "O Great Compassionate One, it is indeed unsurpassed. (78)
The earth is known as Pukkasī; how can there be the sealing by Akṣobhya? Since hardness is delusion (moha), the body is considered Vairocana.
O Lord, it is logical that Pukkasī is the sealing by delusion—that is the appropriate sealing. || 79 ||
Once the body has been left behind, the mind’s play cannot occur elsewhere;
therefore, O Vairocana, one should seal the mind with the body by means of the mind. || 80 ||
"They purify the sense objects" means they transform all phenomena into the means for achieving enlightenment;
by this entire [explanation], the answer to the question regarding restraint (*saṃvara*) has been given,
and the answer to the question regarding sealing (*mudraṇa*) has been provided through such statements as "sealing is the mark and the limb," and so forth.
In that very context, there are eight further questions and eight answers. || 78 ||
He states those [points] with the words beginning "earth" and so forth.
Here, these are the verses of inquiry belonging to Vajragarbha:
solidity indeed is earth; that is delusion and the body, and those two are Vairocana.
Therefore, the meaning of the question is: why is it appropriate for the sealing (*mudraṇa*) to be by that very [deity] and not by Akṣobhya?
"Graceful play" (*lalita-vilāsa*) elsewhere in the support refers to Vairocana; thus, it resides in Vairocana.

Then, "the body" refers to the intrinsic nature of the body; "by the mind" refers to Akṣobhya. [Regarding] *upāyeka* (in the Ka and Gha manuscripts), *mahāmahaṃ* (Ka and Gha), *mahāmaha* (Kha and Ga), *mahāmahā* (Cha and Jha), and *mahāmahī* (Ja).
It is purified: kha ye ka kha ga gha moha kha gha.
Hardness—ka, kha, ga, he, paṃ, va. Hardness (kakkhaṭattaṃ)—gha.
Body—kha; [the word] "body" does not exist in kha.
pūjyate—cha; pūjyante—ja; pūjyan—jha; this reading follows the manuscript ‘kha’;
prabhoḥ—kha. cha. jha.
* This half-verse portion does not exist in the manuscripts ka, ga, and gha.
Devoid of *ga*,
[it is] Vairocana— *ka kha ga gha*; sealing with *kha ga gha*.
They perform the sādhani— ka kha he ta 2.4.15;
and there are eight [of them]— gha.
The verse:
*ka kha* refers to the state of hardness (*kakkhaṭatva*); *kakkhāṭatva* is the play of the great glory of *pheromahodaya*—*gha*.

In the *Hevajratantra*, in the chapter titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing" (*mudraṇapiṇḍārtha*), Vajragarbha asks and the Blessed One replies: "The water element is known as Śavarī; Akṣobhya has the nature of fluidity. O Lord, it is appropriate that Śavarī be sealed by the seal of Akṣobhya."
Apart from the mind, no other state of the body is perceived;
therefore, the mind should become delusion, and the mind should be sealed by delusion.
Vajragarbha asked: "The Blessed One has stated that Teja is known as Caṇḍālī; how is sealing with Ratna appropriate?
For Caṇḍālī, there is no sealing other than by the seal of Rāga."
Since passion (rāga) is known as that which is colored (rakta), and Rakta is Ratnasambhava,
one should seal passion with Piśuna because its nature is fiery redness.
Vajragarbha said: "O Lord, since the Ḍombinī is the Amogha wind and possesses the form of the wind, her sealing with the Amogha-mudrā is appropriate."
"Śavarī" refers to the state, support, arrangement, and locus of Śavarī;
"mind" refers to that which resides in the mind; and "delusion" refers to the body.
And for this reason, "sealing the Śavarī with the mind through delusion" means sealing by means of Vairocana and not by another; it is "not sealing by another."

And "red" refers to female menses; therefore, because fire has a red form, [the consort] Caṇḍālī is [associated] with passion (rāga) by means of Piśuna, who is Ratnasambhava. — Akṣobhya — [is indicated by] ka, kha, ga, gha.
The liquid form— by way of the letters ka, kha, ga, gha— the letter ga; by way of the seal (mudrā) of Akṣobhya, the letter gha— ka.
is worshipped—cha. jha; are worshipped—ja;
of the Lord—ka. gha; of the sky—ka. gha.
O nihilist, there is no other state [than this] that can seal it.
There is none— O Ga, O Teja Caṇḍālinī— Ka.Ga.Gha Kaṃ— Gha.
ratneśa—ka, gha; ratnaiḥ—kha; ratnasya—ga;
mudraṇa—ka, kha, ca; caṇḍālyo—cha, jha.
In the version with *rāga*, there is *ka kha ga gha*; in the version with *rakta*, there is *kha gha*; in the version with *ga*, it does not exist.
sambhavam—ka, kha, gha; sambhavām—ga; raktasvarūpa—ka, ga, gha; raktasvabhāve—kha;
piśuna—ka, gha.
— there is none — kha;
as in — ka; therefore — ga; there is none — gha;
the wind is unfailing — ka kha ga gha.
The form of Vāyu: Ka Kha Ga Gha Ḍombinī Amogha; Ka Ga Gha are offered as oblation (juhyate). Ka. Ga. Gha.
Juhyate. Ka.
The Lord said: "Who is it that has broken the manuscript hereafter at the letter 'Gha'?
[The disciple replied: 'Having abandoned passion (rāga), there can be no occurrence of envy (īrṣyā) elsewhere.'"
Therefore, the wise one should seal the Ḍombinī with the mudrā of passion.
Since form is solidity, Vairocana is considered the consort of Gaurī;
by the very same logic previously stated, she should be sealed by Citteśa alone.

*Kṣaṇa-vajrapañjikā-muktāvalī* 195: If, by means of this offering, yogins perform worship to all beings for the sake of auspiciousness;
Then there would be untroubled happiness among them, and the gods would be gratified, as would the world's prosperity.

Subjugation, malevolent rites, the destruction of enemy armies, expulsion, killing, and summoning—as well as pacification, happiness, and nourishment—will come to pass; and one should offer the *bali* here to the assembly of spirits if one desires permanence.
Vajragarbha asked: "By which mudrā is the *khecarī* [attained], and by whose mudrā is the *bhūcarī*?"
O Lord, how was it that I did not previously know that this printing should be performed?
Thus, he states the benefits of offering the bali-oblation with two verses, beginning with "By this" and so forth.
"Bhūtān" means "of the bhūtas";
"teṣu" means "among them."
"Blissful and undisturbed" refers to stainless joy.
"And the gods" means the deities.
"Jagatsubhūtayaḥ" means those from whom the world's excellent prosperity and well-being arise.
This means the mantra-deities of the five families.
*Vaśya* (subjugation) and *abhicāra* (sorcery) together constitute *vaśyābhicāra*. *Nāśana* (destruction) is *nāśa* (annihilation).
“Killing and summoning” refers to *māraṇa* and *ākarṣaṇa*.
“Pacification” refers to *śāntika*, and “nourishment” (*pauṣṭika*) likewise belongs to that; the word “should be” is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
The connection is: “he who would offer the *bali*.”
"Here" refers to the vajra;
"beings" refers to Indra and the others;
"eternally" means perpetually.
Vajragarbha said, meaning he asked:
"Why did he not ask earlier?
[The answer is: because of the difference in reasoning (*yukti*).
"Khecarī" means by means of Khecarī;
"bhūcarī" means by means of Bhūcarī; "of what mudrā? means by which mudrā.
"It was not known by me before" means it was not previously known by me.
The world-born beings— cha; the dull-witted Vināyakas— ja,
kha, cha.
he0 paṃ0 mu0 va0, śaśvat-jha. he0 paṃ0 yo0 ra0 mā0 | nāsti - ka. kha. ga. gha. jha |
The Blessed One said: [In the *Vajra-tantra*, Chapter Four, titled "The Summary Meaning of Sealing"]: "The three secrets are within the center of the wheel, distinguished by body, speech, and mind;
the lower, upper, and middle positions are established within the center of the wheel."
Bhūcarī is the body-mudrā, downward-facing, and the embodiment of the Body-Vajra;
Khecarī is the passion-mudrā, upward-facing, and the embodiment of the Speech-Vajra.
Cittavajrī and Nairātmyā are the mind; the mind has the form of Nairātmyā.
The mind is the central place of Nairātmyā; therefore, she is born from the center.

They say there are six kinds of families; one should explain them in detail. They are said to be threefold and fivefold as well; listen, O Yoginī! Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitaprabha [Amitābha], Amoghasiddhi, and Vajrasattva—these are to be meditated upon.
How indeed is there happiness from hatred, delusion, malice, passion, and envy through this sequence of purification?
The "three secrets" are distinguished by body, speech, and mind.
To the question of how that [occurs] in the center of the wheel, he says: "Below," and so forth.
The connection is according to the sequence.
Because Kāyavajriṇī has the nature of the body-vajra, she is therefore Kāyamudrī.
*Madhyajā* means born in the middle.
There are six types of families; thus, the family is sixfold:
Akṣobhya, Vairocana, and Ratnasambhava are three; Amitaprabha and Amoghasiddhi are two; and Vajrasattva is one.
He states by which purification these are to be meditated upon: "hatred, delusion, malice, passion, envy, and pleasure"—this is a collective *dvandva* compound.

The vowel *i* of *īrṣyā* undergoes *guṇa* substitution [with the following *a*], and the long *ā* is shortened; by means of this purification, one reveals the void (*kha*). "Pleasure" (*saukhya*)—[as stated in] Hevajra-pañjikā-muktāvalī.
Setting aside the one called Vajrasattva, the Vajrapañjikā Muktāvalī subsequently presents five families;
thereafter, it proceeds to a threefold division by means of delusion, passion, and hatred.
The single family is the Lord of Mind, Akṣobhya, whose form is hatred;
this is the power of Hatred-Vajra, and the family is considered to be fivefold within the sixfold [classification].
The fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning of the Seals of All Tantras of Hevajra."
Through the purification of hatred and the other [afflictions].
"In sequence" means according to their respective order.
Thus are the six families.
197. As for how there are five, three, and one here, he states this in two verses beginning with "vihāya":
"the group of six and the group of five" means the hexad and the pentad.
"Entire tantra" (*sarvatantra*) refers to this very *Hevajratantra* in its entirety. "The entire tantra and the sealing" (*mudraṇa*):
the separate mention of "sealing" is for the purpose of indicating its preeminence.
Its "piṇḍārtha" means its summarized meaning. The chapter that elucidates this is thus described.
This is the fourth chapter on the summarized meaning of the mudrās in the second kalpa of the *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*, composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti.
*Mahādveṣarāgakaiḥ*—ka, kha, gha; *mahādveṣānurāgake*—ga. *Citteśa Akṣobhya*—ka, gha; *Akṣobhyaṃ dveṣarūpiṇām*—ga.
Thus, *iti śrīhevajranairātmāsarvatantramudreṇa piṇḍārtho*—ka; *iti śrīhevajra sarvatantramudraṇaṃ*—kha; *iti śrī hevajre ḍākinījālasaṃvare sarvatantramudreṇa*—ga.
[The reading "nāsti" is absent in manuscripts ka, kha, ga, and ca. Now, the Lord Hevajra, the Great King, the Vajrin who bestows all things,
whose very self is the nature of all forms, shall fully reveal the mandala.

Seated in Sukhāvatī, possessing the nature of all forms,
he is the Lord of the Maṇḍala, perfected by means of the seed-syllable of Cittavajra.

The goddess Nairātmyā herself questioned the Lord, who has sixteen arms, eight faces, and four feet; who is terrifying, wears a garland of skulls, is heroic, has his neck embraced by Nairātmyā, and bears the five mudrās.
This wheel described by you, surrounded by fifteen [deities], is your mandala;
O Lord, its nature was not previously known by me.
Having kissed Nairātmyā, placed the vajra in her skull-cup, and massaged her breasts, the Lord should reveal the mandala.
Mouths are faces; feet are the collective term for thighs, shanks, and toes;
and the neck is the throat. || 3 ||

"From us" (*asmaccakra*) means my own mandala. It is so described because it is surrounded— meaning encircled— by the five yoginīs situated in the inner enclosure and by the ten situated in the outer enclosure.
"Because it was not previously known," since the deity was not mentioned. || 4 ||
The skull-cup (*kapālaka*) is so called because it protects the bliss of the lotus.
It "shines forth" (*samprakāśate*), meaning it perfectly illuminates.
[5] Fifth: In the *Hevajrapañjikā Muktāvalī*, the wheel (*cakra*) is as previously described, adorned with necklaces (*hāra*) and half-necklaces (*ardhahāra*).
It is four-cornered, with four gates, and adorned with vajra-lines.
There, O fair-faced one, I am present in the center together with you,
by virtue of the nature of innate bliss through the passion of great attachment.
Eight-faced and four-legged, adorned with sixteen arms,
he tramples upon the four Māras and is terrifying even to fear itself.
Wearing a necklace made of a garland of severed heads, standing upon the sun and engaged in the *tāṇḍava* dance,
he holds a universal vajra upon his head and is terrifying with his black complexion.
One should emanate the syllable *hūṃ* from the mouth, [visualizing] one whose body is smeared with ashes, engaged in the union of passion, and joined with Nairātmyā. (10)
"Cakra" refers to my own foundational maṇḍala;
"just as previously described" means that it is exactly like yours. || 6 ||

"I" refers to the Blessed One Vajrasattva, who has manifested in the form of Śrī Heruka through the sequence of the fivefold realization (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) that will be described; "one should know" means one should meditate [upon him]. "Together with you" means accompanied by Nairātmyā, who has manifested in the form of Māmakī.

The joy (*prīti*) preceding the culmination of *vicāraṇā* is the great passion (*mahārāga*) called bliss (*ānanda*); following that is passion, which is joy or attachment (*anurāga*). The culmination of *vicāraṇā* is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); therefore, both of these are experienced as the great passion and are characterized by it.

Following that, from the perspective of the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), innate bliss alone is the essential nature, because there is a subsequent realization of the form of the time of non-perception.
The meaning is that it is characterized by that [nature] from that [source], by that very form alone.
The subsequent portion of the text is for the most part out of its proper sequence; we shall explain it according to the order of connection, not according to the order of the recitation. || 7 ||
[The Hevajrābhyudaya, the fifth chapter of the Vajra Tantra, which has attained waveless bliss: He whose nature is waveless;
his primary face is intensely black, and the right is like a kunda flower. (11)

The left face is red and most terrifying, with its head at the top and twenty-four eyes; the remaining faces issued forth while you and I were sporting in the beautiful city of old. Gaurī is in the eastern direction, at the eastern gate, [with] Vikarālin;
[the others] are like bees in color. 12.
Filled with intense delight, she was perfectly situated. || 13 ||
Again, by means of the union of the churner and the churning, Caurikā emerged;
having emerged at the southern gate, that Caurī became the guardian of the gate. (14)
Through the union of bola and kakkola, Vetālī emerged once more;
having emerged at the western gate, she sat down as the destroyer of Māra. 15.
Furthermore, during the great union, Ghasmarī emerged;
having emerged, she sat at the northern gate, possessing a terrifying form.
From the friction and union of the two, Pukkasī emerged once more;
having emerged, she sat in the northeast corner, possessing a fierce form.
Again, by means of the method of churning, Śavarī is in the southeast corner,
Caṇḍālī is in the southwest direction, and Ḍombī is in the northwest corner.
Then the Vajrin, having become liquefied through great passion together with his consort, is impelled by the goddesses with various offerings of song. (19)
Arise, O Bharāḍa, essence of compassion! Protect me, O Pukkasi!
Abandon me, O Mahāsu, in the union of passion; [abandon] me in the meditation on emptiness. 20.
Immediately after the phrase "by virtue of having the nature of innate bliss" (*sahajānandasvarūpataḥ*), the five verses beginning with "Then the Vajrin" (*tato vajrī*) are to be understood.
"That" (*tat*) refers to immediately following that.
"The Vajrin" (*vajrī*) refers to that very same Vajrasattva.
"From great passion" (*mahārāgāt*) means from the cause that is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which is known as great passion.
"Become liquefied" (*drutaṃ bhūtam*) means having attained the state of the fluidity of gnosis (*jñāna*).
"By one's own wisdom" (*svavidyayā*)—the instrumental case is used here in the sense of association with the object; the word "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) is to be supplied.
The meaning is that one should meditate on both as dissolved.
"Then" means immediately after their dissolution.
"The goddesses" refers to Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombikā, who have arrived from their respective directions and are seated upon their own thrones.

"Citing" means they urge him, with various songs, to emerge from the meditative absorption of dissolution (*vilaya-samādhi*). Each individual verse is an offering (*upahāra*), that is, a presentation (*ḍhaukana*) made to him. (19)
There, at the beginning, Pukkasī urges him: "Uṭṭha bharāḍo" means "Arise, O Lord," being one whose mind is filled with compassion (*karuṇāmanaska*). "Pukkasī mahu" means "Pukkasī, me."
"Paritāhi" means "protect me.

To the question "How?", he says: "Mahāsukha," etc. "Mahāsukha" is the bliss of great liberation; for that purpose, the yoga is the form of Hevajra arising from the fluid. Through that yoga, "kāmayasva" means "enjoy me. "Chaḍḍahi" means "abandon [me]."
"Suṇṇasamāhī" means the meditative absorption (samādhi) characterized by emptiness (śūnyākāra), that is to say, its liquid nature.
Even in the reading "chaḍḍahiṃ suṇṇasahāva," the meaning remains this very same "liquid nature"; however, [in that case] the poetic figure of yamaka would be disrupted. || 20 ||
*vajri*—kha. gha;
*drutaṃ bhūtaṃ*—ka. kha. ga. gha. cha. ja. jha. he paṃ mu va;
*svavidyayā*—he paṃ mu va.
maṇḍalaṃ-kha; ‘karuṇa’ is missing—kha; karuṇamaṇḍala—ga; karuṇamana—he paṃ mu va mahu—ṅaca. ṭa | paritohi—ga; paritāhi—he paṃ mu va mahasu—ka. ga gha | mahu—ka. gha. ṅa. ṭa. he paṃ mu va |
With six—ka. gha; with six—cha; with six—jha.
Of empty nature—ka. gha.
Because of the great passion, which is the causeless form of innate bliss—ka.
"Paritrāhi" (Save me)—this is the reading in manuscript *ka*. "Chattahi" (Protect me)—this is the reading in manuscript *ka*; however, from manuscript *gha*, it begins again as "dravatārūpata."
For the purpose of recitation: *gha*. In the *Vighaṭana*:
*ka kha*. In the *Vajratantre*: *hahuṃ uṭṭhehiṃga uṭṭhehiṃ tuhuṃ tohyā vihuṇe marami hahuṃ chaḍḍahi sunnasabhāvaḍā śavaria sihyāu* [The Hevajrābhyudaya, Chapter Five]. *Hevajra*.
Action || 21 ||
"O Lord of the Gods, you have been invited; why do you remain in this empty place? I am a Caṇḍālī who has come to petition you, yet though I petition you, you do not even look at me. (22)
O Indīālī, rise up! I know your heart; we are *ḍombīs*, O jewel of skill—do not show such misplaced compassion. || 23 ||
Then Śabarī says:
*tojjū* means "of you.
*Vihuṇṇe* means "by separation"; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), meaning "by the state of being separated," that is, by separation.
*marami havu* means "I am dying.
*Uṭṭhehi tuhuṃ hevajja* means "Arise, O Hevajra!
*Chaḍḍahi suṇṇasahāvaḍā* means "Abandon the nature of emptiness," which signifies the state of being in a liquid form.
"May the task of the Śavarī be accomplished," meaning "may the Śavarī's purpose be fulfilled.
Then the Caṇḍālī says:
"Having invited the entire world," that is, having invited all people by means of purposeful action.
"O Lord of the Suras!"—thus [he addresses him].
"Why do you remain in the void?"—that is, why do you abide in the form of a fluid within the void?
Why?
"I, a Caṇḍālī, inform you"—thus I, a Caṇḍālī, make my request. What do you request?
"Without you, I am not seen; without you, I cannot discern the directions."
The meaning is: "I see nothing but darkness. || 22 ||
Then the Ḍombī says: "Indīālī, arise! You!"—meaning, "O Indrajālika, arise; this is your magic trick. [The magician asks: "If you say, 'I am not a magician'?"
She said: "Hauṃ! I know your mind"—I know your mind, which is full of guile.
"We are clever ḍombīs"—we ḍombikās are skillful. (Regarding the variants: *toju*—ka, *tojyā*—kha, *tojhā*—ga, *tojjhu*—gha;
*vihuṇe*—ka, gha, *vihunna*—jha).

Siktaukajja—Ka. Gha; Sijjaukajja—Ga.
He paṃ mu va.
Nimantritā—Ga.
kisu—ka gha;
