Hau-ka-kha; Viṇu-ka-kha, Viṇḍa-gha;
I do not infer the direction—gha.
*Indrī* (ka, kha), *indīyālī* (gha); *tuhaṃ* (ka, kha).

In the eight skull-bowls of the right [hands], the elephants, horses, donkeys, oxen, camels, humans, *sarabhas*, and *autukas* are to be known as the two-legged beings and so forth, in their respective order. (24)
Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Fire, the Moon, the Sun, Antaka, and Dhanada are the guardians of the eight quarters starting from the left. (25)
It is endowed with the dramatic sentiments (rasas) of laughter, fear, the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the pathetic, the marvelous, and the tranquil. || 26 ||
With the syllables Aṃ, Hūṃ, and Bhyāṃ, the Great Vajra-Holder arose from his liquid form,
spreading his feet upon the earth and threatening the gods and asuras.
Citizens!
Know this: "maṇḍa" means "we cannot be deceived"—this is the sense.
Therefore, do not act in vain;
do not cause the interruption—that is, the cessation—of compassion through haste. Or rather, do not allow it to be distracted by compassion, cast aside as if it were a mere material object. || 23 ||
Within this pentad of verses, one verse beginning with "aṃ hūṃ" and so forth is to be seen.
"Mahāvajrī" means the Vajra-holder.
"Arisen from the state of melting" means that he has arisen, having abandoned the state of liquefaction in accordance with the injunction of the four songs.

"Aṃ-hūṃ-bhyām" means produced from the syllable *hūṃ* together with the syllable *aṃ*, arising from the process of melting and withdrawal (*drava-saṃhāra*). "Sphālayan" means causing to expand or vibrate.
"Tarjayan" uses the accusative case in the sense of the nominative.
The same applies to [the passages] beginning with "evam aṣṭāsyam" and so forth. || 27 ||
As [stated] in the versions *ka*, *gha*, *kha*, *ga*: "donkey, ox, camel, human, *sarabha*, boar, dog"—and in *ga*: "hand, elephant, horse, donkey, ox, camel, human, *sarabha*, boar, dog.
[The term] "wind" appears in *ka*, *ga*, and *gha*.
[The term] "infinite" appears in *ga*.

In the left [hand], with eight skull-cups—ka. gha. ṭa; with eight skull-cups on the left—kha; with eight [skull-cups] on the non-right side—ga. Possessing the heroic, the loathsome, the comic, and the wrathful—ka. gha; possessing the heroic, the loathsome, the wrathful, and the comic—ga. Endowed with the nine sentiments of drama—ka. gha; endowed with the nine sentiments of drama—kha. ṭa; endowed with the nine sentiments of drama—ga. Ā HŪṂ—ka. gha; A HŪṂ—kha.
Of those two, [the reading] "vajrī" is in kha; "tato" is in jha;
"ucchrito" is in ka and gha; and "caraṇāt" is in ka and kha, while "caraṇān" is in ga and gha.
*sphālayet* — *ka*; *sphālayan* — *ga*.
*he paṃ mu va tarjayantam* — *ka. kha. gha. cha. jha*; *vajrayantam* — *ga. ja*. *karuṇayā* — *gha*.
In the *Vajra-tantra*, immediately following this single verse [which is the fifth chapter, the *Hevajrābhyudaya*],
there are five verses beginning with "eight-faced" (*aṣṭāsya*).
"Faces" (*āsya*) means mouths.
The feet, thighs, shanks, and toes constitute the collection [of members]. He is so called because the four Māras have been stepped over by him.
"Of fear" means of the terrifying. (8)
It is so described because he has made a necklace from a garland of shaven heads.
*Tāṇḍava* is a fierce dance.
He is dark-complexioned, appearing as terrifying as possible. || 9 ||
"Sphārayet" means "while expanding.
"Vigraha" refers to the body.

"Rati" is supreme bliss; that itself is the "pair" (dvandva) because it possesses conceptualization (savikalpatvāt). He has "attained that" (tatsamāpanna), because he has previously brought it face-to-face.
Regarding what the seal is according to this reality, he says: "In union with Nairātmyā"; that is, [the union] with Nairātmyā. (10)

"Waveless" (*nistaraṅga*) means free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); "bliss" (*sukha*) is innate joy (*sahajānanda*). "Having attained that" refers to one who is reaching it. By what reality [is this so]? Thus, the reality of these two is as follows: in the *Hevajra*-cakra it is one way, while in the *Nairātmyā*-cakra it is the reverse due to the difference in the leaders. To explain which of the eight faces is what kind, he says "at the root," and so forth.
[He is] Mahākṛṣṇa, exceedingly black-bodied;
Vikarālin, with formidable fangs;
and Caturviṃśatinetrādya—what [is meant by this]?
That group of eight faces has three eyes because of its three-eyed nature. || 12 ||

Immediately following these five verses, there is one verse beginning with "śṛṅgāra" (the erotic). The erotic sentiment prevails in all [the white] faces; the peaceful sentiment is in the white [face];
and the furious sentiment is in the non-white [faces].
In the remaining cases, [the application is] according to what is appropriate. || 26 ||
Immediately following this are two verses beginning with "elephants, horses," and so forth.
*Khara* means a donkey;
*gāvaḥ* means cows.
Otuka is the cat.
These are the emblems on the eight skull-cups located on the right hands of the two legs;
those on the left hands, which consist of the eight skull-cups beginning with Earth, are as follows.
By all of this, the samādhi named Ādiyoga is indicated. || 24-25 ||

Immediately following this is the set of six verses beginning with "By you and by me. In a delightful and beautiful city-circle, "by you" means together with Nairātmyā, and "by me" refers to Hevajra; thus, it means "play," while "me" refers to Hevajra who is playing.
How does she play?
With "rati-nirbharaiḥ"—*rati* being *māyā*, that is, sexual union; with the intensities (*nirbhara*) of that, meaning its excesses.

Having emerged—that is, having issued forth according to the analogy of fire produced by the friction of kindling wood—the goddess Satī became Gaurī and was well-established, meaning properly situated, at the eastern gate.

The term "Indra's direction" (indradiś) is connected to all eight [directions]. It is called "Indra's direction" because its view (dṛk)—that is, its sight—is directed toward Indra as its own lord; the vowel *i* is used here according to Vedic usage (ārṣa). || 13 ||
One should emanate these [goddesses] by means of the seed-syllables *gaṃ*, *vaṃ*, *vaṃ*, *vaṃ*, *paṃ*, *śaṃ*, *laṃ*, and *ḍaṃ*;
and the presiding lord by means of the two seeds of passion (*ratibīja*), *hūṃ* and *aṃ*, which are blue and terrifying with flames.
One should thus meditate upon the Lord within the delightful city of the circle of Mothers (*mātṛcakra*).
Black in color and most terrible, it bestows unhappiness upon Nairātmyā. || 29 ||
Indeed, on the right hand of Gaurī there is a tortoise, and likewise on the left a Rohita fish;
on the right hand of Cauryā there is a fire-wood cutter (kṛpīṭa), and on the left hand a boar.
To the right of Vetālī is a tortoise, and to her left, a lotus vessel;
to the right of Ghasmarī is a snake, and in her left hand, a yogic bowl.
For Pukkasī, there is a lion on the right and likewise an axe on the left;
for Śavarī, there is a mendicant on the right and likewise a khikkhirikā on the left.
It is called *mantha* because it is churned; it is called *manthāna* because by means of it [the churning] is performed.
"Again" (*punar*) means subsequently. || 14 ||
The "great duel" is the "great rati.
The rest is easy to understand. || 16 ||
Immediately following this group of six verses, there is a single verse beginning with "ga~ ca~" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "one should create these," it means that one should emanate these eight yoginīs in their proper sequence.
To the question "From where? he says: "The sovereign," and so on.

The sovereign is the Lord of the Mandala (Maṇḍaleśvara), and Rati is Nairātmyā; from the seed-syllables of these two—namely *hūṃ* and *aṃ*, which consist of the liquid essence of the mind situated within the lotus, marked by the syllables *hūṃ* and *aṃ*—they both become formidable with flames and blue in color. (28)
Immediately following this single verse is the group of eight verses beginning with "gauryāḥ. Rohita is a fish;
kṛpīṭa is a hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
Varāha means a boar. || 30 ||
MAD [is the seed-syllable] of Caṇḍālī; she holds a discus in her right hand and likewise a plough in her left.
Of Ḍombī, there is a vajra in the right and likewise a raised index finger in the left.
Gaurī and the others are considered to have two arms, standing in the *ardhaparyaṅka* dance posture;
they possess three eyes, have upward-streaming hair, and are adorned with the five mudrās. (34)
Gaurī shall be black in color, Caurī resembles the sun,
Vetālī has the luster of molten gold, and Ghasmarī is like an emerald.
Pukkasī has the luster of sapphire; Śavarī has the radiance of a moonstone; Caṇḍālī is dark blue like the sky; and Ḍombī is considered to be the color of karcūra.
Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Rudra,
Nairṛti, and Vemacitrin are the seats for Gaurī and the other goddesses.
Candramaṇi is the moonstone (candrakānta). || 36 ||
Upendra is Viṣṇu;
Vaivasvata is Yama;
Vittanāyaka is Kuvera.
The *viṣṭara* is the seat;
[they are used] in their respective order. || 37 ||
Immediately following these eight verses is a single verse beginning with "mātṛcakra.
*Cakra* means an assembly.
By all of this, the second meditative absorption (samādhi), named Maṇḍalarājāgra, is indicated.
The third [section], the *Karmarājāgri*, is a classification of mantra-yoga; according to the tantra, it should be observed in other tantras as well.
Thus, by means of these three meditative stabilizations (*samādhi*) together with the recitation of mantras, one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and so forth. || 29 ||
— Having adorned the *bolaka* and worshipped the Blessed One with devotion, Nairātmyā asks for the mantra with firm embraces and kisses. (38)
The mantra that brings women under one's control, as well as that which threatens the wicked;
the mantra that causes the subjugation of serpents, and that which crushes the gods and demons. (39)
Therefore, O Goddess who bestows happiness, I shall speak of this; listen!
I have taught this nowhere else except among the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. (40)
O Goddess, regarding what was done by Vajrasattva concerning this mantra in the past, I am extremely afraid; nevertheless, I shall speak it out of deference to you. (41)
Having drawn the mandala, which was formidable with its garlands of flames,
he drew Tilottamā in order to bestow the consecration upon Vajragarbha.
Therefore, in this context, the Blessed Lady asked about the mantra; the Blessed One, introducing both [the mantra and its application], said: "The *bolaka*," and so forth.
He explains what kind of mantra it is by saying: "Of women," and so forth, which is easy to understand. (38–39)
"Then I," and so forth, is the speech of the Blessed One. "That" refers to the mantra as desired. (40)
"Yat" means that which is the action;
"kṛṣṭā" means drawn forth. || 41-42 ||
By means of a beautiful, long-sounding resonance, clear through ten thousand recitations, and joined with the yoga of Hevajra, all women are attracted. (43)
Then, the goddess Sārā, gratified by the practice of churning with the churning-stick, asked for a beautiful mandala through intense embraces and kisses. (48)
There, the Teacher, possessed of great wisdom, himself draws the mandala with a joyful mind and in meditative absorption through the union of the vajra and the lotus. (49)
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, this practitioner whose self is yoga performs all rites;
with a mind free from doubt, through the vajra-yoga of the syllable *he*. (44)

One enclosure with four gates, provided with four archways, the very first of the Vedas, adorned with a crescent moon and a bindu; thereafter, [the mantra] "to the eight-faced one" (aṣṭānanāya) and "to him whose path is tawny and upward-pointing hair" (piṅgordhvakeśavartmane).
To the one with twenty-four eyes, followed by sixteen arms;
whose body is like a dark cloud, who wears many garlands of skulls; whose mind is exceedingly cruel toward the end of existence, and who has fangs like a half-moon. 46.

Kill! Kill! Make them act! Make them act! Roar! Roar! Threaten! Threaten! Dry up! Dry up the seven oceans! Bind! Bind the eight nāgas! Seize! Seize the enemies! Ha hā hi hī hu hū hai hai ho hau haṃ haḥ phaṭ svāhā! || 47 ||
By means of this very mantra, the yogi becomes one whose self is yoga;
the rest is easy to understand. || 43-44 ||
He states the mantra: "Of the Vedas," and so forth.
The first syllable is the *praṇava*.
It is adorned by its very nature. || 45 ||
At the end of the mantra are twelve *ha* letters joined with the vowels; at the very end are *phaṭ* and *svāhā*. || 47 ||
It is filled with various rays of light and adorned with vajra threads. ||50||
With rice-husk ashes and the like, as well as with charcoal from a cremation ground. || 51 ||
Then one should draw eight jars joined with five lines;

either with powders made of the five jewels or even with bricks from cremation grounds. In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus together with its filaments, and upon the pericarp, one should draw Naraka, white in color and divided into three parts.
When asked, "What is the mandala?"—meaning the mandala to be drawn—the Teacher spoke in response; this is the ellipsis.
The master of great wisdom should draw the mandala himself at the outset, and not have it drawn by a painter. (48–49)
"One should draw the vases" means one should paint them;
"eight" refers to the vases of the goddesses, which implies the *vijaya-kalaśa* and the *sārvakarmika-kalaśa*.
To the question of with what colored powders (*rajas*) one should draw the mandala, he says: "with five jewels," and so forth.
"In the middle of that" means in the center of the outer enclosure (bāhyapuṭa) there is a lotus whose nature is that of the inner enclosure (garbhapuṭa).
"Puṣkara" refers to the pericarp (karṇikā).
One should also draw a Śarabha in the northeast, a mendicant (bhikṣu) in the southeast corner,
a wheel in the southwest, and a vajra in the northwest.
One should draw a knife at the eastern gate and a fire-pot at the southern;
one should likewise draw a tortoise at the western and a serpent at the northern.
These eight symbols are proclaimed according to the specific colors of the goddesses.
In the center, one should draw a white skull-cup marked with a double vajra. || 55 ||

Then one should present the victory-pitcher (vijayakalaśa), which has sprouts at its mouth, is well-wrapped in cloth, divine, filled with śāli rice, containing five gems within, and—what more need be said—is completely full. 56.
It should be performed in the same manner as the mandala ritual described in the Tattvasaṃgraha. || 57 ||
"Śarabha" means a lion. || 53 ||
"Of the goddesses," and so forth;
the meaning is that the colors of their emblems are the same as those of the goddesses themselves.
One should draw the white skull-cup in the center, marked with a double-vajra (viśvavajra). || 55 ||
Then one should offer the victory-vase; this is understood by implication. Afterwards, the remaining vases are to be placed in their respective positions. || 56 ||

In the northeast, one should draw a monk; in the southeast corner, a sword; in the northwest, a sickle; and in the west, a tortoise and a serpent. In the center of that, there is a skull-cup of Śukra and a vase—this is the reading. It should be gathered in its true nature with a fine cloth. The Lion King, the Vajrapañjikā, the Muktāvalī, and the Maṇḍala should be introduced; and the eight Vidyās of Great Bliss, twelve years old and sixteen years old, adorned with necklaces and anklets. (58)

The mother, the sister, the daughter, the sister’s daughter, the wife of the maternal uncle, the mother’s sister, the husband’s sister, and likewise the father’s sister—these eight are proclaimed as the Vidyās. (59)
The yogi should worship these [goddesses] with firm embraces and kisses;
he should consume camphor there, by which the mandala is consecrated.
The yogi should cause them to drink [it], and he shall quickly attain success;
therein, madana should be drunk, and one should eat that which is born of balashali.
Having stripped her naked, he should kiss her vulva again and again;
and by them, his *bola* is aroused, while he sings and dances most excellently.
And there, sport is performed through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*;
afterwards, in the second watch, one should cause the disciple to enter there. (63)
"They should be made to enter" means they should be caused to enter;
"of sixteen years" means those who are sixteen years old.
It has been stated that there are eight sciences; as to what they are, he says "the mother" and so forth—these are to be understood by their names and so on, and not by their actual physical forms.
"Śvaśrū" refers to a mother-in-law.
"Of these" means "these.

In the maṇḍalas, a sixteen-year-old girl of the Bhāgavata lineage, the sister of my brother, a yoginī of mantra, should drink [the sacrament] there; she should sprinkle the maṇḍala, and one should cook with *madana* [fruits]. Their strength and power are then sucked; furthermore, they dance and sing. One should strike [her] in the glorious play and cause her to enter. Covering the eyes with a cloth made of *vajra-tantra*, the maṇḍala is shown afterwards, and the initiation is bestowed there at midnight in a secluded house. (Hevajrābhyudaya, Chapter Five)

Just as the empowerments have been described according to the distinctions of the master and so forth, and just as the praise and worship have been explained, they should be inferred by well-trained disciples as before. 65.

And there he should teach the reality (tattva) beginning with the Stage of Cessation (virama) and ending with the Ultimate (parama), which has been concealed in all tantras and is revealed here as the very pinnacle of the pinnacle. || 66 ||
To him who asks there, that goddess [said]: "O Lord, O Great Master, tell me at that very moment what the application of the vajra-worship is like. (67)
The Blessed One said: "There is neither beginning nor end; there is neither birth nor nirvāṇa there.
This is that supreme great bliss—neither other than the self, nor the self."
"According to what was explained" refers to the chapter on consecration;
"praise and worship" means both praise (*stuti*) and worship (*pūjā*). || 65 ||
"Beginning with cessation" means prior to the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*); "ending with the supreme" means after the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
What, then, is that? He says: "the end," which means the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*).
And this has been concealed in all the tantras and not made manifest.
"Revealed at the end" means it is revealed at the very conclusion of this tantra; by this, it indicates that this is the *uttaratantra* (supreme tantra) among all tantras. || 66 ||
The question "What is that moment like? is intended for the purpose of making it extremely clear. || 67 ||

The Blessed One said: "Ā i na" and so forth; the meaning of the five instances of the word "na" is "not. Having carefully covered his eyes, he spoke of the house at midnight; as for his own consecration, it should be understood as previously explained. Then, showing that which begins with the beginning and ends with the supreme in all tantras, and what kind of final mantra is spoken by the Lord: "O Majjanau, be our Nirvāṇa; therein is our own supreme great bliss. O Naurapara, worship the Self! Thus, "Ā i ṇa" and so forth, the beginning and end are, respectively, the Supreme (Parama) and the Cessation (Virama).
Existence and nirvāṇa are those very same two:
passion and dispassion. Apart from that, in that context, they are called "beginning" because of their priority relative to the innate [nature], and "end" because of their supremacy.
It is called *bhava* because existence arises from this; it is *nirvāṇa* because it is the cessation of that [existence];
it is *rāga* (passion) because its simultaneous object is that which is about to arise; it is *virāga* (dispassion) because its simultaneous object is that which has just ceased;

and since it is inferior even to those two, the first joy (*prathamānanda*) itself is thus called "desire" (*kāṃkṣā*), while the middle is called "middling," just as one speaks of a "middling body" or "middling livelihood."

He who is not even these three—beginning with the *virama* and ending with the *parama*, as has just been explained—is this very one, the Supreme Great Bliss (*paramamahāsukha*), meaning the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Thus, the determination of its moments has been stated;

now he describes its essential nature: "Neither the other nor the self" (*nau para nau appāṇa*)—that which is manifested does not appear as the "other," the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), nor does the "self," the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*), appear.

That which shines forth as the mere supreme bliss, non-dual, free from appearances, and infinite—that is the meaning of "innate bliss" (*sahajānanda*). And it is said in the *Melāpakapaṭala*: "Through *ānanda* there is some degree of pleasure; *paramānanda* is greater than that; in *viramānanda* there would be detachment; but innate bliss remains as the remainder."
The first is characterized by a desire for touch; the second by a longing for pleasure;
the third by the destruction of passion; and by that [third], the fourth is cultivated.
Existence (*bhava*) is said to be supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), and nirvāṇa is [said to be] from the absence of passion (*virāga*);

There is neither passion nor dispassion; the middle is found only by abandoning these three. That which is not perceived is called *sahaja* (the innate). the *ḍākinī* is the fifth vowel *u*.
The *praṇava*, the eldest of letters, [is *oṃ*].
Rambhā and Tilottamā are the two apsarases.
(21) The syllable *praṇava* is the family of delusion (*mohakula*);
it is the fourth letter of the first [vowel group], joined with *vajraḍākinī*, together with the *visarga*. (22)
The first [syllable] of the first [group] is ‘ka’; the second of those situated at the end is ‘ra’; the first of the first [group] is ‘ka’; the third of those situated at the end is ‘la’. || 23–24 ||
One should join the syllable *hrīḥ* there, adorned above by *caurī* and conjoined with the *vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*, and then perform it again, ending with *svāhā*.
The mantra of Kurukullā. || 25 ||
Adorned with a skull-bowl and joined with a lotus-stalk and a vajra. || 26 ||
Beginning with Oṃ, the third of the fourth [varga], the fourth of the semivowels (antasthā), and the fourth of the sibilants (ūṣman) adorned by Pukkāsī;
[this] is conjoined with the Void (Śūnya) and tripled. Then the second of the fifth [varga], and the first of the third [varga], ending with Svāhā—this is the heart-mantra of Hevajra. || 27 ||
Vairocana and so forth are joined with the blazing, blazing [fire]; the fourth of the fifth [vowels] is joined with the first of the semivowels (antasthā) and adorned by Ghasmarī. || 28 ||
By that very power, Caurī is the eleventh vowel: "E. || 25 ||
The third of the fourth [group], 'da', at the end; the fourth of the semivowels, 'va'. || 26 ||
The fourth of the sibilants (ūṣman) is 'ha';
the second of the fifth [class] is 'pha';
the first of the third [class] is 'ṭa'. || 27 ||
The fourth of the fifth [group], 'bha', at the end; the first of the semi-vowels (*antasthā*), 'ya'; the devourer (*ghasmarī*), which is the thirteenth vowel, 'o'. || 28 ||

In the Vajra Tantra, the mantra of the Four-Armed One ends with *svāhā* and consists of: the fourth of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), conjoined with the Void (*śūnya*) and tripled; the second of the fifth group (*pañcama*) and the first of the third group. || 29 ||
The first [mandala] of Vairocana and the others is adorned with Gaurī in the inner circle; and the first [mandala] of the third is likewise adorned with Gaurī in the inner circle. || 30 ||
Having doubled the third letter of the fifth [vowel], the third letter of the second [vowel] adorned with fire (ṛ),
joined with three *hūṃ* syllables, the second letter of the fifth [vowel], and the first letter of the third [vowel], ending with *svāhā*, is the mantra of the six-armed one. || 31 ||
The first [syllable] of the fourth [group], Vairocana and so forth, joined with fire (ra) and adorned by Vetālī;
the third of the semivowels (antasthā), adorned by Ghasmarī;
the first of the first [group], joined with the first of the semivowels and adorned by Vajrā. || 32 ||
The letter *kṣa*, adorned by Caurī;
the first of the fifth [class] and the fourth of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), adorned by Vajraḍākinī.
The mantra for the two-armed [form] consists of the syllable ŚŪṂ, followed by three repetitions of ĀKRAṂTA, and ends with PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. || 33 ||
The third vowel, 'i', is Abhyantaragaurī. || 30 ||
What is that which is doubled?
It is this word "kiṭi" mentioned immediately above. || 31 ||
The first [syllable] of the fourth [quarter] is 'ta', Vetālī is 'ai', Vajrā is 'ā'. || 32 ||
The first [syllable] of the fifth [section] is "pa. || 33 ||

[Chapter] Nine: *Vajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*. [The mantra is: the first of the first [vowels], the first of the second, the first of the third, the first of the fourth, the first of the fifth, the first of the semivowels (*antasthā*), and the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*); beginning with Vairocana and ending with *svāhā*.
This is the mantra for agitating the city, to be recited one hundred thousand times. (34)
The second of the semivowels (*antasthā*), namely the two *kṣa* syllables,
are placed in the middle; furthermore, the second of the semivowels is [repeated], interspersed with three *hūṃ*s from Vairocana onwards and the *phaṭ* syllable, ending with *svāhā*.
The mantra for purifying the ground.
|| 35 || Then, the mantra for the consecration of food and drink, beginning with Vairocana and ending with the vajra syllable *hūṃ*. || 36 ||
Following Vairocana and the others, there is the letter *a*, which is the first of the vowels (*akāra*); the third of the sibilants (*ūṣman*);
and the fourth of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), adorned above by fire.
Following that, there is the *vajra* because all phenomena are unarisen from the beginning: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The mantra for the bali offering to all elemental beings. || 37 ||

The ninth chapter on the extraction of mantras. Regarding the phrase "the second of the semi-vowels (*antaḥsthāna*) and the letter *kṣa*," the meaning is that these two, taken as a collective whole, are to be doubled. 35.
Following that, "vajrā" with the visarga is "āḥ. || 36 ||

The third of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), *sa*, and the fourth of the semi-vowels (*antaḥsthāna*), *va*. This concludes the ninth chapter, the Extraction of Mantras, in the second section of the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti. The tenth chapter, named the Chapter on Recitation, concerning Vajrasattva, the single vow of all phenomena.
Now, therefore, having kissed Nairātmyā, he reveals the subject of recitation. || 1 ||
Stambhana (paralysis) is performed with crystal; for vaśya (subjugation), one should recite with red sandalwood;
abhicāruka (malevolent rites) with a piece of glass, and likewise vidveṣa (causing enmity) with boneless materials.
Exorcism is performed with the bone of a horse; attraction with the bone of Brahmā; bringing rain with elephant bones; and killing with the bone of a buffalo. || 3 ||

For the rite of paralyzing (stambhana), one should drink milk; for subjugation (vaśya), one may act according to one's own will; for killing (māraṇa), sihṇaka resin is prescribed; for attraction (ākṛṣṭi) and inciting enmity (vidveṣa), rice-based substances are taught; and for expulsion (uccāṭana), the "fourfold equal" (catuḥsama) compound is used. || 4 ||
Musk,
or else *antaśvam*, *ādiśvam*, *nādim*, *gādim*, and likewise *hādim*.

The tenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Recitation" (Jāpapaṭala). Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth: "atha" signifies immediate succession; "āha" signifies restriction, meaning "immediately thereafter.
"Ekasaṃvaram" means the singular, condensed [teaching] that is without a second.
*Japanaṃ* is *jāpa*; regarding that, the object associated with it is the *jāpamakṣasūtra* (the rosary for recitation).
The rest is easy to understand.

This concludes the tenth chapter, the Chapter on Recitation (*jāpapaṭala*), in the second section of the *Hevajrapañjikā*, the *Muktāvalī*, composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti. [Regarding the variant readings: "antaḥsthaṃ ādiśca" is found in manuscripts ga and gha; "antaścamādiśca" is found in manuscript kha.

In the *Śrī Hevajra Tantra*, the tenth chapter, titled "Recitation" (*jāpa*): [ka]; the tenth chapter on recitation in the *Hevajra-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*: [ga]; the tenth chapter, titled "Recitation of Hevajra": [gha].

The eleventh chapter, titled "The Meaning of the Innate" (*sahaja*): Embracing Hevajra firmly and pressing his lower lip with her teeth, Nairātmyā asks him there concerning the family-forms (*kularūpaka*) of embodied beings. (1)
"Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, thus spoke the Lord of the Wheel:
'I shall describe the own-family (*svakula*) of embodied beings; listen, O Prajñāpāramitā! (2)
On the base of the ring finger of whichever woman or man there may be a vajra, that is the supreme Akṣobhya family.
The wheel of Amitābha should be a lotus;
Ratnasaṃbhava [should hold] a great jewel, and that of the Karma family a sword. || 4 ||
For whichever yogi is Kṛṣṇa, Akṣobhya is his deity;
for whichever yogi is Mahāgaura, Vairocana is his family deity.
The nine-tongued [deity] belongs to Vairocana; for the yogi who is dark blue, his deity is Amoghasiddhi. For the yogi who is deep reddish-brown, Ratneśa is his family deity.
"By means of the firm," and so forth.
"He said this" means he spoke as follows. || 1-2 ||
"Akṣobhyakula" means the family (kula) of Akṣobhya; such is the meaning. || 3 ||
"Of Vairocana" means one belonging to the family of Vairocana; this is because the family and the one belonging to the family are treated as non-different through metaphorical identification. ||4||

Embracing firmly—*ka*. Embracing with firmness—*ga gha*. Pressing the lips—*ka. gha*; Śrīdhara—*ga*. With teeth likewise—*ga*. Nairātmā—*kha. gha*. Having established him—*ka. gha*. Named Cakra—*ka. gha*. I shall speak—*ka. kha. gha*; I shall speak—*ga*. Prajñāpāramitā—*ka*; Pāramitā—*gha cha*. At the root—*ka. kha. gha*. Ninefold—*ga*. Of the family of Akṣobhya—[omitted]. Bhavacakre—*ga*; *cakre*—*gha*. Of Amitanātha—*ka. kha. gha*. Of Ratnasambhava—*ka. gha*; Ratnasambhavā—*kha*. Khaḍgakarma—*ka. kha. ga. gha*. Black—*ka. ga. gha*. Deities—*gha*. Mahāgaurī—*ka. ga. gha*. Vairocana—*ka. kha. ga. gha*. The deity of the family—*ga*. Kulaśyāmā—*ka. kha. gha*. Amogha, the supreme deity—*ka*; Amoghaṃ, the supreme deity—*gha*. *Piṅge*—*ka. gha*. "Embracing Hevajra firmly," etc.—Bhoṭa [Tibetan].
Immediately following this, the reading "sambhava iti sambhavaḥ" is found as an addition in the Tibetan manuscript.
In the *Vajra-tantra*, [the eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Meaning of the Innate"]: "The yogin who is reddish-white has Amitābha as his family deity (*kuladevatā*).
The yogin who is whitish-yellow belongs to the Vajrasattva family. (7)
Living beings should not be held in contempt nor harmed by those who have reached the further shore of yoga;
for they belong to the family of the Tathāgatas, having resorted to a conventional form.
The characteristics of women are exactly the same as those of men; their families likewise exist according to their concealment, conduct, and appearance. (9)
There, the Great Vajra-holder, delighted by the kissing of the bhaga and liṅga, awakened Nairātmyā; listen, O Goddess, to the method of worship. (10)
In a garden, in a secluded place, or within the interior of one's own house, the knower of yoga should always worship the Mahāmudrā after having made herself naked. 11.
*Sattva* refers to Vajrasattva. *Kulāḥ* means those belonging to a family (*kulinaḥ*) or their progeny. *Saṃvṛtim* means the worldly [convention]. (7–8)
"Bodhayāmāsa" means he addressed [him]. || 10 ||
In the *Hevajrapañjikāmuktāvalī*: Having performed kissing and embracing, as well as the touching of the vulva, the testicles, and the tip of the nose, one drinks the honey of the lower lip. (12)
He always performs the ritual actions with the hands of Madanāṅga,
and likewise with the elbows and well-stretched fingers of Dolāṅga.
The wielder of the vajra should desire [union] again and again, and gaze both downward and upward;
he attains vast accomplishment and becomes equal to all Buddhas. || 14 ||
There, camphor is drunk, and especially the *madana* fruit;
one should consume *bala* there for the sake of the camphor.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Meaning of the Innate."
"Madana" refers to the arising of knowledge; its "aṅkas" (marks) are nail-scratches and the like. Thus, he is "madanāṅkakaraḥ" (one who makes marks of passion).
"Bolavān" means one whose penis is erect. "Karma" refers to sexual union. || 13 ||
Yoga has the meaning of the co-emergent (*sahaja*); this chapter elucidates that.
This is the eleventh chapter, on the meaning of the co-emergent, in the second section of the *Vajrapañjikā*, the *Muktāvalī*, composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti.

The second chapter of the *Māyājāla*, the Great King of Tantras. Now, therefore, the Vajra-holder spoke of the four empowerments, just as the sons of enlightenment were consecrated by the Buddhas of the past:
"By me, you have been consecrated with the secret empowerment through the stream of mind."
"Seize, seize her, O Great Being—the goddess who bestows delight and accomplishment, who possesses a universal form and is enchanting; having seized her, perform worship.
This knowledge is exceedingly subtle, the adamantine essence, like the sky."
You are yourself that very father—dustless, bestowing liberation, and peaceful.
"Then he said" means immediately thereafter.
"Established in the vajra" means firmly situated in the state of being a Vajradhara. || 1 ||
Bodhi is wisdom; the sons of that [wisdom] are the bodhisattvas. || 2 ||
Rati is joy;
her abode is the bodhicitta;
the goddesses are Prajñā, Viśvanārī, and so forth. ||3||
It is also "greatly subtle" because it is inexpressible.

The "Vajras" are the Tathāgatas; their "maṇḍa" is the essence. [Twelfth: Oṃ vajrapañjikā muktāvalī padma sukhādhāra vajrapadmādhiṣṭhānamantraḥ. (The mantra for the consecration of the vajra-lotus: Oṃ, O Vajra-commentary, O pearl-necklace, O lotus, O support of bliss, [this is] the mantra for the empowerment of the vajra-lotus.)
O Great Passion, bestower of bliss, whose nature is the four joys, O Viśva, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ, accomplish my purpose! || 5 ||
Oṃ! O Vajra, Great Hatred, bestower of the four joys!
O Lord whose single flavor is the face of the sky, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Accomplish my purpose!
[One should place] the syllable Oṃ on the head, the syllable Hūṃ at the heart, and the syllable Ā in the pericarp. (6)
The second [chapter] of the Mahātantrarājamāyākalpa.
It is like space because it is without appearance;
it is stainless because of the exhaustion of afflictions;
it bestows liberation because of the exhaustion of existence.
It is peaceful because it is free from affliction;
you are his father because you are the seed;
and you yourself have attained a body composed of that very essence. 4.
The "face of space" (*khagamukha*) is the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of the *bodhicitta*, because it has suchness as its object and because it is without appearance.
Because it has that as its intrinsic nature, the "vajra" is the single flavor of the face of space;
the "stamen" (*kiñjalka*) is that of the lotus. (6)
Having composed this extensive commentary (*pañjikā*) upon the heart of the Vajra—the treasury of the tantras’ incomparable exposition of vast meaning—I have accumulated great merit.

By this, may I ascend to the glorious state of the majestic Vajradhara, whose majesty is all-encompassing; and may all people without exception certainly emerge from cyclic existence by means of the three vehicles.

In the *Muktāvalī*, a commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Hevajra* composed by the great scholar and master Ratnākaraśānti, this is the twelfth chapter, the second [chapter] of the *Mahātantrarājamāyākalpa*.
The Pañjikā of the Vajra Yoginī Tantra is completed.
This is the work of the venerable Ratnākaraśānti.
The unsurpassed *Sarvatantra* known as Śrī Heruka has not been understood by those who do not know Hevajra, the unsurpassed *Sarvatantra*.
